taxonomy.title: Perioperative — risk, medicines and recovery
taxonomy.scopeIn: Preoperative assessment, cardiac/pulmonary/geriatric risk, medication continuation/interruption, VTE prevention/bridging, recovery, delirium and general diagnostic safety.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Anesthetic delivery/reversal belongs to anesthesia-analgesia-pharmacology. Cirrhosis-specific decisions belong to liver-benign-portal-infection. Nutrition belongs to nutrition-support-metabolism.
taxonomy.priorityReason: Broad everyday general-surgery decisions merit audit despite substantial related clinic content.
researchAgenda: Frailty, pulmonary risk and postoperative delirium
VTE prevention versus bridging and recovery planning
taxonomy.coverageReason: Live identities cover part of this scope. The research agenda flags breadth to check, and the topic worker must judge redundancy and question quality.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

concepts.displayName: Heparin bridging and VTE prophylaxis are separate
concepts.learningObjective: Keep the decision against routine therapeutic AF bridging separate from indicated postoperative surgical VTE prophylaxis.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Scored-objective override after reading the concept objective.

concepts.displayName: A local contrast event despite an allergy label
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish a localized injection-site contrast event from a generalized allergic-like event using the actual distribution and timing.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Postoperative SGLT2 restart after a fasting course
concepts.learningObjective: Use present clinical stability and oral intake to determine postoperative SGLT2 resumption rather than carry forward a preoperative interval as an automatic restart clock.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Progression after contrast leaves an IV
concepts.learningObjective: Escalate progressive local injury after contrast injection while preserving a separately documented earlier allergic-like event.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Reconcile current postoperative recovery with an imminent second fasting procedure when scheduling SGLT2 resumption.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: An urgent limb change during contrast administration
concepts.learningObjective: Separate progressive local-pressure injury from an arterial-pulse endpoint and a different historical systemic reaction. Direct the urgent review to threatened hand compartments rather than rely on pulse mapping or pursue an allergic explanation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Two heparin orders with different purposes
concepts.learningObjective: The therapeutic order derives from an AF interruption, while the lower-intensity order derives from the cancer operation; a low INR does not merge those indications. Remove the unnecessary bridge without inadvertently cancelling surgical prophylaxis.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Scored-objective override after reading the concept objective.

concepts.learningObjective: Reconcile sleepiness and OSA-probability reports, then document and communicate risk without making a screening diagnosis.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Use discordant sleep reports in perioperative communication
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish sleepiness from apnoea-probability information and decide what should drive current anaesthetic risk communication without requiring diagnostic confirmation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Continuation of a chronic beta blocker
concepts.learningObjective: Continue a tolerated chronic beta blocker through noncardiac surgery when no contraindication is present.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Avoid routine therapeutic-dose heparin bridging when warfarin is interrupted for selected nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Use drug-specific U.S. labeling to plan elective preoperative interruption of empagliflozin versus ertugliflozin without assigning every SGLT2 inhibitor one interval.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Treat a medication-withdrawal driver of postoperative agitation
concepts.learningObjective: Integrate the actual home drug interruption with autonomic/neurobehavioural observations rather than applying a generic delirium drug prohibition.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Communicate a tailored nonpharmacologic multicomponent prevention plan to the hospital perioperative team for an at-risk adult.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Extended VTE prophylaxis after selected cancer surgery
concepts.learningObjective: Use about four weeks of postoperative pharmacologic prophylaxis for a selected high-VTE-risk patient after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted ultrasound to characterize an uncertain superficial collection after benign breast excision.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Observation of an uncomplicated postoperative seroma
concepts.learningObjective: Observe a small simple asymptomatic postoperative seroma without infection, wound tension, implant, or functional limitation.

concepts.learningObjective: Use a structured multidimensional frailty assessment rather than inferring frailty from age or comorbidity before elective major abdominal surgery.

review.title: Recognize a withdrawal exception in a postoperative medication decision
fairness: The learner must identify a withdrawal pattern from the medication chronology and autonomic findings, then apply the exception to routine avoidance of benzodiazepines in postoperative delirium. Lorazepam is the most defensible offered etiologic treatment.

Haloperidol and dexmedetomidine are plausible symptom-management temptations but do not substitute for treating the likely withdrawal cause. The omitted doses are necessary chronology, not an authored instruction to give the keyed drug.

Importance: high postoperative medication reconciliation and delirium management. Realism: the inpatient syndrome is coherent. This does not establish a dose, route, monitoring level or that every alternative delirium cause has been excluded.
suggestions: Preserve the medication chronology and autonomic findings; keep subsequent teaching explicit that symptom suppression does not replace withdrawal treatment and reassessment.

review.title: Heparin bridging and VTE prophylaxis are separate
fairness: The reader must distinguish an atrial-fibrillation bridge from cancer-surgery VTE prevention and reconcile overlapping orders. Low INR alone cannot determine both decisions. These are consequential, distinct indications.

Stopping the therapeutic bridge while retaining appropriate postoperative prophylaxis is defensible for this represented history. The plan is initial reconciliation during warfarin resumption, not authorization to continue duplicate anticoagulants indefinitely.
The lack of previous thromboembolism/valve replacement establishes the relevant risk context and does not simply disclose the answer. No confident clinical error identified.
Importance: high, medication safety and perioperative thrombosis prevention. Realism: duplicate heparin orders and a subtherapeutic restarted INR are plausible.
suggestions: Retain both indications and the risk history. Ensure subsequent teaching specifies reassessment of prophylaxis when therapeutic anticoagulation is established; do not make the present key an indefinite combination order.

review.title: Postoperative SGLT2 restart after a fasting course
fairness: The balanced two-by-two schedule offers no unique wording, length or convergence advantage. The learner must reconcile apparent recovery with another imminent fasting procedure and choose the restart condition; current glucose is a credible competing anchor.

The keyed schedule is best among those offered. Oral-recovery restart is shorthand, not a complete statement of all restart requirements; it must not imply that oral intake alone establishes readiness.
Importance: high, practical perioperative medication reconciliation. Realism: plausible clinic decision, although the indication for ERCP and the prolonged-fasting plan are not developed.

Review scope: the input contains 39 items, not 40. It has no literal after blocks; the current clinicalCase presentation and decision-node exhibit, stem and answer-choice labels were reviewed as the corresponding visible fields. No separate current-update field is present. Titles were retained as identifiers, not treated as learner-visible answer cues. Historical verdicts and author self-checks were not used to establish correctness. Both referenced image exhibits were inspected. Importance and realism are recorded in fairness to preserve the requested schema. All difficulty estimates are qualitative PGY-2/3 predictions. This is an offline editorial review without fresh source verification or clinical approval; all drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Importance/ABSITE relevance is an editorial judgment of general-surgery applicability, not verification against a current examination blueprint. A clinical finding is not automatically a cue: necessary safety and eligibility observations should be retained even when the item is judged too easy.
suggestions: Preserve the two-procedure timing conflict and balanced schedule options. At clinician sign-off, ensure the shared restart definition includes clinical stability as well as recovered intake without supplying the correct schedule in the stem.

review.title: Investigate an awake abnormality before relying on the sleepiness report
fairness: The resident must recognize that the awake oxygenation/total-CO2 findings raise a current ventilatory or acid-base question not settled by the sleepiness history, then choose a blood gas rather than a sleep-only investigation.

Arterial blood-gas analysis is the most defensible offered immediate investigation. The supplied findings do not establish obesity hypoventilation syndrome: body habitus and alternative causes are not provided. That limitation does not prevent assessing awake gas exchange.

Importance: high perioperative respiratory assessment. Realism: screening can uncover daytime abnormalities; a saturation reference is more naturally a clinical range than a 'laboratory reference band', but the intended observation is understandable.

Owner flag F13: fully resolved in this displayed replacement. The alone options and informal-impression shortcut are absent, and the apparently reassuring sleepiness report now competes with objective awake findings. This changes the task from screening-tool selection to evaluation of an abnormal preoperative assessment; it is not clinical approval of the new objective.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between sleep-risk screening and evaluating awake physiology; avoid diagnosing a specific hypoventilation syndrome from this record alone.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Tessa Lane's operative record describes elective mesh abdominal-wall repair without bowel entry or infected tissue. Cefazolin was first given before incision, repeated during the operation and then carried onto the discharge medication list. She now has an intact incision, expected mild tenderness, no spreading erythema and no fever. A drain retained for a postoperative seroma has been present since surgery. A specimen from its disinfected port now reports MSSA susceptible to cefazolin and cephalexin; no new cavity was accessed. Wound and drain reassessment will continue with every medication plan.
decisionNodes.stem: Which cefazolin-related medication plan is most appropriate for Tessa Lane at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the cefazolin prescription
answerChoices.rationale: The operative/dose chronology supplies an incision-related indication, not a current infection. A positive longstanding-drain report without clinical infection does not create a new treatment indication.

answerChoices.label: Continue the cefazolin prescription
answerChoices.rationale: Cefazolin is active against the isolate, but neither the carried-forward operative doses nor this drain report establishes an infection requiring an ongoing IV course.

answerChoices.label: Replace cefazolin with oral cephalexin
answerChoices.rationale: Changing route reduces IV burden but still treats a laboratory result without establishing a postoperative infection.

decisionNodes.explanation: The medication timing and operative findings explain why cefazolin appeared in the record. They do not establish treatment of an infection, and prophylaxis does not need continuation after closure because a drain remains. The new port isolate must be interpreted as an indwelling-device sample alongside the benign clinical course; it does not justify IV continuation or oral conversion.

question.stem: Which medication-associated complication best fits this patient's laboratory pattern?

answerChoices.label: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied lactate is within the laboratory reference range, while ketones are elevated.

answerChoices.label: Insulin-associated hypoglycemia
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied glucose is not low, while the record explicitly identifies ketone excess and acidosis.

answerChoices.label: Isolated SGLT2-related dehydration
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This label omits the documented ketone excess and metabolic acidosis.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis.” The implicated SGLT2 drug should be interrupted and the patient sent for immediate medical assessment; medication association does not replace evaluation for other contributors.

question.stem: What does this patient's near-normal glucose mean when the supplied ketone and acidosis findings are present?

answerChoices.label: Excludes SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This treats the glucose value as an exclusion test despite the supplied ketone/acidosis evidence.

answerChoices.label: Establishes a harmless medication effect
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reassuring glucose does not make the supplied acidosis and ketone excess harmless.

answerChoices.label: Proves the medication caused the episode
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Glucose alone does not establish causation; the drug association still requires clinical evaluation.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “Does not exclude ketoacidosis.” Interpret the supplied ketone and acid-base evidence; a near-normal glucose value neither excludes the complication nor proves its cause.

question.stem: What is the appropriate device-clearance step before this patient's MRI?

answerChoices.label: Proceed using any MRI scanner
answerChoices.distractorRationale: MR Conditional labeling does not authorize unrestricted scanning.

answerChoices.label: Exclude all MRI examinations permanently
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An implant is not automatically a permanent prohibition when a suitable protocol can be verified.

answerChoices.label: Use a prior CT as clearance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A CT experience does not test the device in an MR environment.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “Verify device-specific MR conditions.” Send the identifying record to the MRI and device teams; the clinic does not independently authorize unrestricted scanning.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Past tolerance alone does not verify the current scanner and protocol.

answerChoices.label: Use absence of symptoms as clearance

question.stem: What should happen before this patient's implant is cleared for MRI?

answerChoices.label: Clear the implant based on size
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Implant size alone does not establish magnetic, heating, or device risks.

answerChoices.label: Clear the implant based on age
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Time since implantation is not device-specific MR safety labeling.

answerChoices.label: Ban MRI for all implanted metal
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The safe next step is identification and specialist assessment rather than a universal permanent ban.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “Verify identity and MR label.” Defer clearance while the MRI team obtains reliable identification and an appropriate safety assessment.

Give a readily available single ART tablet

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The reconciled medication list includes cobicistat. The anesthesia team now asks about its interaction with midazolam.
decisionNodes.stem: Which mechanism explains the midazolam interaction with cobicistat?
decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Inhibition of CYP3A-mediated metabolism.” Reduced metabolism can increase midazolam exposure and prolong sedation. The booster warning concerns metabolic inhibition rather than increased renal elimination. Reduced absorption does not explain increased exposure from CYP3A inhibition. The relevant booster effect inhibits rather than induces midazolam metabolism.

question.stem: Which combined medication plan should be agreed with {patientName}'s surgical team?

answerChoices.label: Continue ART; plan individually titrated intravenous midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Preserves ART while coordinating parenteral midazolam, monitoring and individualized dose reduction when appropriate.

answerChoices.label: Continue ART; plan individually titrated oral midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Treats monitoring/titration as sufficient to overcome the contraindicated oral boosted-PI combination.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt ART; plan individually titrated intravenous midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Unnecessarily interrupts a complete regimen instead of coordinating the procedural medicine.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt ART; plan individually titrated oral midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adds ART interruption and assumes this permits an oral combination without an established interaction-management plan.

question.explanation: Coordinate the interacting procedural medicine while maintaining ART when feasible. Oral midazolam is contraindicated with boosted protease inhibitors. Parenteral use requires an appropriately monitored setting and individualized dosing, including consideration of dose reduction, particularly with repeated doses.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During induction, the patient develops repeated generalized convulsions without regaining awareness between them. Intravenous midazolam stops the convulsions and the procedure is abandoned. Assisted ventilation is now maintaining oxygenation while the capnography trace remains infrequent and spontaneous chest movements are shallow.
decisionNodes.stem: Which reversal instruction should guide {patientName}'s care while assisted ventilation continues?

answerChoices.label: Withhold flumazenil
answerChoices.rationale: Midazolam was used to control a potentially life-threatening seizure state; antagonizing it is contraindicated even though respiratory support is needed.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil now
answerChoices.rationale: Respiratory depression does not remove the contraindication when the benzodiazepine was required for seizure control.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil after another antiseizure drug
answerChoices.rationale: An additional antiseizure drug does not make the stated benzodiazepine-antagonist contraindication disappear.

decisionNodes.explanation: The reason a benzodiazepine was administered changes whether its antagonist is appropriate. Repeated convulsions without recovery of awareness required seizure control; flumazenil is contraindicated when benzodiazepines are used to control a potentially life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus. Maintain supported ventilation and specialist seizure/anesthesia care. Boosted exposure increases the temptation to reverse sedation, but does not override this boundary.

laterNodesForSequenceAudit.currentUpdate: During induction, the patient develops repeated generalized convulsions without regaining awareness between them. Intravenous midazolam stops the convulsions and the procedure is abandoned. Assisted ventilation is now maintaining oxygenation while the capnography trace remains infrequent and spontaneous chest movements are shallow.
laterNodesForSequenceAudit.stem: Which reversal instruction should guide {patientName}'s care while assisted ventilation continues?

answerChoices.label: Withhold flumazenil
answerChoices.rationale: Midazolam was used to control a potentially life-threatening seizure state; antagonizing it is contraindicated even though respiratory support is needed.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil now
answerChoices.rationale: Respiratory depression does not remove the contraindication when the benzodiazepine was required for seizure control.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil after another antiseizure drug
answerChoices.rationale: An additional antiseizure drug does not make the stated benzodiazepine-antagonist contraindication disappear.

laterNodesForSequenceAudit.explanation: The reason a benzodiazepine was administered changes whether its antagonist is appropriate. Repeated convulsions without recovery of awareness required seizure control; flumazenil is contraindicated when benzodiazepines are used to control a potentially life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus. Maintain supported ventilation and specialist seizure/anesthesia care. Boosted exposure increases the temptation to reverse sedation, but does not override this boundary.

answerChoices.label: Pause midazolam; assess and support ventilation; continue ART
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the respiratory observations despite apparent wakefulness/maintained oxygen saturation, while avoiding an uncoordinated ART interruption.

answerChoices.rationale: Misreads movement and oxygen saturation as permission for another dose despite the ventilation observations.

answerChoices.rationale: Responds to ventilation but treats interruption of one ART component as the immediate interaction-management solution.

projection.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan. The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

question.stem: Which reconciliation of the heparin orders fits {patientName}'s recorded indications?
question.explanation: Read the order's purpose rather than the subtherapeutic INR as a universal heparin trigger. Routine bridging for the represented atrial-fibrillation interruption is not supported. Postoperative cancer-surgery prophylaxis has a separate purpose while the INR remains subtherapeutic. Cancel the therapeutic bridge order and retain the prophylactic prescription with routine prescribing review. The case does not direct overlapping heparin regimens or prescribe a dose, start interval or duration.

cells: Atrial fibrillation for eight years; no previous stroke, systemic embolus, venous thrombosis or valve replacement
Warfarin restarted; INR 1.3; wound dry; hemoglobin unchanged on consecutive measurements; walking limited after major abdominal cancer surgery
Therapeutic intravenous heparin until warfarin becomes therapeutic, entered for the atrial-fibrillation interruption
Prophylactic subcutaneous enoxaparin for the postoperative cancer-surgery course

projection.learningSummary: Read the order's purpose rather than the subtherapeutic INR as a universal heparin trigger. Routine bridging for the represented atrial-fibrillation interruption is not supported. Postoperative cancer-surgery prophylaxis has a separate purpose while the INR remains subtherapeutic. Cancel the therapeutic bridge order and retain the prophylactic prescription with routine prescribing review. The case does not direct overlapping heparin regimens or prescribe a dose, start interval or duration.

question.stem: Which empagliflozin schedule should be agreed for {patientName}'s next procedure?
question.explanation: Reconcile both procedures rather than treating the first recovery as the end of the medication problem. Empagliflozin labeling advises interruption for at least three days when possible before surgery or a procedure associated with prolonged fasting. A new dose 48 hours before the next fasting procedure would interrupt that protection. After the second procedure, resumption again depends on clinical stability and oral intake, not glucose in isolation.

question.stem: Which assessment method should be used to classify {patientName}'s preoperative risk of obstructive sleep apnoea?

question.stem: Which entry should be made in {patientName}'s preoperative assessment?

answerChoices.label: Suspected OSA; communicate perioperative risk

question.stem: Which request should accompany {patientName}'s anaesthetic referral now?

answerChoices.label: Send the apnoea-probability result for planning
answerChoices.rationale: The different domains do not cancel each other. The current probability assessment and witnessed breathing history should inform anaesthetic planning even before diagnostic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Repeat daytime-sleepiness assessment before planning precautions
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second sleepiness measure does not resolve the apnoea-risk question. Its reassuring result is the credible but inappropriate basis for delaying risk communication.

answerChoices.label: Obtain diagnostic polysomnography before planning precautions
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A diagnostic study can resolve the diagnosis, but making it a prerequisite for communicating and assessing current perioperative risk confuses the purposes of screening and confirmation.

question.explanation: The reports address sleepiness and apnoea probability, which can disagree. A reassuring sleepiness result does not cancel the reported breathing pauses or the probability assessment. Send the current apnoea-risk information for perioperative planning while distinguishing it from a confirmed diagnosis. This communication decision does not determine whether surgery must be delayed or prescribe a precaution regimen.

definition.intendedInference: Determine which reported domain addresses the breathing-risk question despite low sleepiness. Then: Use that information in current perioperative assessment rather than making another sleepiness screen or diagnostic confirmation a communication prerequisite.

question.stem: Which request should accompany {patientName}'s anaesthetic referral now?

answerChoices.label: Send the apnoea-probability result for planning
answerChoices.rationale: The different domains do not cancel each other. The current probability assessment and witnessed breathing history should inform anaesthetic planning even before diagnostic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Repeat daytime-sleepiness assessment before planning precautions
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second sleepiness measure does not resolve the apnoea-risk question. Its reassuring result is the credible but inappropriate basis for delaying risk communication.

answerChoices.label: Obtain diagnostic polysomnography before planning precautions
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A diagnostic study can resolve the diagnosis, but making it a prerequisite for communicating and assessing current perioperative risk confuses the purposes of screening and confirmation.

question.explanation: The reports address sleepiness and apnoea probability, which can disagree. Send the current apnoea-risk information for perioperative planning while distinguishing it from a confirmed diagnosis. This communication decision does not determine whether surgery must be delayed or prescribe a precaution regimen.

question.stem: Which ART plan is appropriate when the prescribed regimen can be continued perioperatively?

answerChoices.label: Continue ART with the perioperative team
Withhold ART during surgical recovery
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART.

answerChoices.label: Use a single-drug ART formulary substitute
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen.

answerChoices.label: Continue the unboosted ART components

laterNodesForSequenceAudit.stem: What is the appropriate response to proposed oral midazolam with ritonavir-boosted ART?

answerChoices.label: Revise sedation for the ART interaction
Retain the planned oral midazolam order
Increase the proposed oral midazolam dose
Withhold the ART regimen for oral sedation

laterNodesForSequenceAudit.explanation: The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During induction, the patient develops repeated generalized convulsions without regaining awareness between them. Intravenous midazolam stops the convulsions and the procedure is abandoned. Assisted ventilation is now maintaining oxygenation while the capnography trace remains infrequent and spontaneous chest movements are shallow.

answerChoices.label: Withhold flumazenil
answerChoices.rationale: Midazolam was used to control a potentially life-threatening seizure state; antagonizing it is contraindicated even though respiratory support is needed.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil now
answerChoices.rationale: Respiratory depression does not remove the contraindication when the benzodiazepine was required for seizure control.

answerChoices.label: Administer flumazenil after another antiseizure drug
answerChoices.rationale: An additional antiseizure drug does not make the stated benzodiazepine-antagonist contraindication disappear.

decisionNodes.explanation: The reason a benzodiazepine was administered changes whether its antagonist is appropriate. Repeated convulsions without recovery of awareness required seizure control; flumazenil is contraindicated when benzodiazepines are used to control a potentially life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus. Maintain supported ventilation and specialist seizure/anesthesia care. Boosted exposure increases the temptation to reverse sedation, but does not override this boundary.

Parenteral use requires an appropriately monitored setting and individualized dosing, including consideration of dose reduction, particularly with repeated doses. The reason a benzodiazepine was administered changes whether its antagonist is appropriate. Repeated convulsions without recovery of awareness required seizure control; flumazenil is contraindicated when benzodiazepines are used to control a potentially life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus. Maintain supported ventilation and specialist seizure/anesthesia care. Boosted exposure increases the temptation to reverse sedation, but does not override this boundary.

question.stem: Which perioperative antiretroviral medication plan is most appropriate for this elective operation?

answerChoices.label: Keep the complete regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes feasible regimen continuity rather than repeating a stated permission to continue ART.

answerChoices.label: Suspend the complete regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Overgeneralizes perioperative medication withholding to an effective regimen that can be administered.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Overgeneralizes perioperative medication withholding to an effective regimen that can be administered.

answerChoices.label: Omit the regimen's booster
answerChoices.rationale: Attempts to avoid interaction concerns by removing part of a regimen without coordinated review.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Attempts to avoid interaction concerns by removing part of a regimen without coordinated review.

question.explanation: Coordinate continuation of the complete prescribed antiretroviral regimen when it can be administered. Surgery itself does not justify interruption or uncoordinated removal of regimen components. If an interruption becomes unavoidable, involve the HIV clinician and perioperative team.
question.teachingPoint: Coordinate continuation of the complete prescribed antiretroviral regimen when it can be administered. projection.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan. The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

projection.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan. The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

question.stem: Which plan correctly separates {patientName}'s AF bridging decision from her postoperative VTE prevention?

answerChoices.label: Omit bridge and give prophylactic LMWH
answerChoices.rationale: AF bridging and surgical VTE prophylaxis address different indications; avoiding routine bridging does not cancel indicated prophylaxis.

answerChoices.label: Add bridge and give prophylactic LMWH
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied AF indication does not establish a need for routine therapeutic-dose heparin bridging.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied AF indication does not establish a need for routine therapeutic-dose heparin bridging.

answerChoices.label: Omit bridge and withhold prophylactic LMWH
answerChoices.rationale: This incorrectly extends the no-bridge decision to the separate postoperative prevention indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This incorrectly extends the no-bridge decision to the separate postoperative prevention indication.

answerChoices.label: Add bridge and withhold prophylactic LMWH
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses both purposes, substituting a routine bridge for separately indicated prevention.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses both purposes, substituting a routine bridge for separately indicated prevention.

question.explanation: Routine therapeutic heparin bridging is not recommended for the represented AF interruption scenario. Selected high-risk abdominal/pelvic cancer-surgery patients may still have a separate postoperative LMWH prevention plan. The timing and dose of either regimen require the treating team's plan; none is invented here.

decisionNodes.stem: Which reconciliation of the heparin orders fits {patientName}'s recorded indications?

answerChoices.label: Stop therapeutic heparin; continue prophylactic enoxaparin
answerChoices.rationale: Routine full-intensity bridging is not established by this history, whereas the cancer operation supplies a different preventive indication.

answerChoices.label: Continue therapeutic heparin; cancel prophylactic enoxaparin
answerChoices.rationale: A treatment-level anticoagulant would subsume prophylaxis while given, but this assigns therapeutic bridging to an interruption without the represented indication.

answerChoices.label: Defer both heparin prescriptions during initial warfarin resumption
answerChoices.rationale: Correctly avoiding routine bridging does not remove the separately represented postoperative prophylaxis indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the order's purpose rather than the subtherapeutic INR as a universal heparin trigger. Routine bridging for the represented atrial-fibrillation interruption is not supported. Postoperative cancer-surgery prophylaxis has a separate purpose while the INR remains subtherapeutic. Cancel the therapeutic bridge order and retain the prophylactic prescription with routine prescribing review. The case does not direct overlapping heparin regimens or prescribe a dose, start interval or duration.

cells: Atrial fibrillation for eight years; no previous stroke, systemic embolus, venous thrombosis or valve replacement
Warfarin restarted; INR 1.3; wound dry; hemoglobin unchanged on consecutive measurements; walking limited after major abdominal cancer surgery
Therapeutic intravenous heparin until warfarin becomes therapeutic, entered for the atrial-fibrillation interruption
Prophylactic subcutaneous enoxaparin for the postoperative cancer-surgery course

question.stem: Which preoperative and early postoperative heparin plan should have been recorded for {patientName}?
question.explanation: Keep indication and timepoint separate. The preoperative decision is whether AF interruption requires a therapeutic bridge. The postoperative decision is prevention after a major cancer operation with limited mobility and the represented hemostatic course. Avoiding routine therapeutic bridging does not cancel indicated prophylactic LMWH. The plans refer to different phases, not concurrent therapeutic and prophylactic doses.

cells: Warfarin indication: atrial fibrillation; no additional therapeutic heparin indication recorded
Major abdominal cancer resection; walking limited to bed-to-chair trips; incision dry; hemoglobin 10.1 then 10.2 g/dL

answerChoices.label: No preoperative bridge with postoperative LMWH prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: Routine AF bridging is not recommended in this represented interruption. The cancer operation and limited mobility create a separate postoperative prevention decision, with supplied hemostatic observations supporting pharmacologic prophylaxis.

answerChoices.label: Therapeutic preoperative bridge with postoperative LMWH prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: This correctly retains postoperative prevention but adds routine therapeutic bridging for the represented AF indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This correctly retains postoperative prevention but adds routine therapeutic bridging for the represented AF indication.

answerChoices.label: No preoperative bridge with postoperative pneumatic compression
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding routine AF bridging does not by itself remove the separate indication for postoperative pharmacologic prevention alongside the already used compression.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Avoiding routine AF bridging does not by itself remove the separate indication for postoperative pharmacologic prevention alongside the already used compression.

answerChoices.label: Therapeutic preoperative bridge with postoperative pneumatic compression
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a preoperative therapeutic bridge for the separate postoperative prevention decision.

answerChoices.rationale: Localized pain and swelling at the injection site fit extravasation rather than a generalized contrast reaction.

answerChoices.rationale: The copied prior label does not replace the current local findings, which lack the described generalized allergic-like features.

answerChoices.label: Transient systemic physiologic flushing
answerChoices.rationale: Isolated warmth does not account for the focal visible swelling and pain at the IV site.

question.stem: Which urgent assessment best addresses {patientName}'s later findings?
question.explanation: Separate the earlier urticarial event from the current local injury and use the trajectory rather than the preserved radial pulse as reassurance. Progressive tense swelling, sensory change and pain with passive stretch require urgent hand-surgical evaluation for threatened compartments/tissue. The earlier hives remain recorded; nothing here authorizes deleting that history. The case does not select an exact operation or use an extravasated-volume threshold. Exact compartment-evaluation priority is source-held for direct verification.

answerChoices.label: Resume after the original postoperative calendar date arrives
answerChoices.rationale: Elapsed postoperative time does not substitute for the unresolved oral-intake requirement.

answerChoices.label: Resume after the next fasting glucose reassessment is acceptable

decisionNodes.stem: Which empagliflozin schedule should be agreed for {patientName}'s next procedure?

answerChoices.label: Continue interruption until ERCP with oral-recovery restart
answerChoices.rationale: The next fasting procedure is too near to restart safely now; restarting afterward depends on recovered intake and clinical state.

answerChoices.label: Resume until ERCP morning with oral-recovery restart
answerChoices.rationale: The eventual recovery condition is appropriate, but resuming until the procedure morning fails the recorded advance interruption requirement.

answerChoices.label: Continue interruption until ERCP with glucose-triggered restart
answerChoices.rationale: The preprocedure interruption fits, but a glucose rise does not establish recovery of intake and clinical state.

answerChoices.label: Resume until ERCP morning with glucose-triggered restart
answerChoices.rationale: This combines inadequate advance interruption with a restart criterion that does not establish postoperative recovery.

decisionNodes.explanation: Reconcile both procedures rather than treating the first recovery as the end of the medication problem. Empagliflozin labeling advises interruption for at least three days when possible before surgery or a procedure associated with prolonged fasting. A new dose 48 hours before the next fasting procedure would interrupt that protection. After the second procedure, resumption again depends on clinical stability and oral intake, not glucose in isolation.

definitions.name: Marcus Reed
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old man, attends clinic the afternoon before elective hernia repair. The medication list includes metoprolol, originally prescribed for hypertension. His current blood pressure is 126/74 mmHg and pulse is 72/min on amlodipine. The bottle dispensed three months ago still contains all 60 tablets; he says he put it aside when the amlodipine arrived. The record contains no coronary disease, heart failure or arrhythmia. Tomorrow’s copied orders include his listed metoprolol dose.

nodes.conceptVersionReason: Changes the scored decision from continuation of tolerated chronic therapy to recognizing that a stale list would create new operative-day exposure.
nodes.objective: Distinguish actual chronic beta-blocker exposure from a stale list before accepting an operative-day restart.
nodes.task: Which metoprolol instruction should Marcus receive for tomorrow’s operation?

choices.label: Omit metoprolol tomorrow and review its longer-term indication
choices.rationale: The untouched supply and administration history show that the copied list does not represent current beta blockade. Controlled hypertension does not create a reason to introduce it on the operative day.
choices.temptation: Reconcile actual exposure before applying the chronic-continuation rule.
choices.correctUnder: The represented unused medicine and controlled hypertension apply.

choices.label: Give the listed metoprolol dose tomorrow
choices.rationale: This would introduce treatment after a prolonged interval rather than continue tolerated current therapy.
choices.temptation: Treat a copied prescription as evidence of current administration.
choices.correctUnder: Consistent current dosing with demonstrated tolerance would support continuation.

choices.label: Postpone repair to resume metoprolol and assess tolerability
choices.rationale: A new independent indication could warrant advance treatment, but none is represented; an old hypertension prescription does not establish a need to delay this operation for beta blockade.
choices.temptation: Correct the stale list by delaying surgery to reinstate every listed drug.
choices.correctUnder: A newly established independent indication needing evaluation and treatment before elective surgery would change the preparation plan.

nodes.explanation: First reconcile what Marcus has actually taken: an unused bottle and his account contradict ongoing metoprolol exposure. Then use the indication and decision time. This is controlled hypertension without another represented beta-blocker indication, so tomorrow’s copied order would be an operative-day introduction, not continuation.

gate.interpret: Infer absent current beta-blocker exposure from the untouched dispensing quantity plus actual administration history, rather than from the imported medication list.
gate.apply: Distinguish continuation from new exposure and use the controlled-hypertension indication to avoid either a surgery-day start or an unsupported postponement.
gate.decidingObservation: The dispensed supply is untouched and Marcus describes setting it aside; normal treated blood pressure does not establish a new beta-blocker requirement.
gate.counterfactual: If the dispensing and administration record instead showed uninterrupted daily metoprolol use with current tolerance, give the listed dose tomorrow becomes the appropriate continuation plan.
gate.deletionTest: Without actual administration evidence, the imported list cannot distinguish continuation from initiation. The established indication and tomorrow timing resolve whether earlier reassessment or operative-day action is being asked. No dose or titration interval is invented.
gate.cueAttack: Removed “first replacement dose for cardiac risk reduction.” Three concrete instructions use the same time anchor. The key lacks a unique team-coordination phrase; the postponement plan is a real reconciliation error rather than an unrelated replacement drug.
gate.stageAudit: One instruction for the immediately upcoming operative day; all options address metoprolol administration/preparation.
gate.difficultyReason: The familiar continuation rule competes with neutral dispensing evidence and a separate indication assessment. The ceiling is moderate; this is not claimed hard.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone revised case; no prior continuation feedback is visible.
gate.limitation: One current guideline supports the medication rule. Fictional tablet counts and vital signs are observations, not evidence-derived treatment cutoffs.

definitions.name: Nadia Brooks
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old woman, attends clinic before elective colectomy. Warfarin is prescribed for atrial fibrillation. Her record shows no prior stroke, systemic embolus, venous thrombosis or valve replacement. The surgeon is comparing anticoagulation instructions for the bowel resection.

nodes.objective: Apply the bleeding implications of major bowel surgery and the actual AF indication to therapeutic bridging.
nodes.task: Which anticoagulation plan fits Nadia before the colectomy?

choices.label: Interrupt warfarin with no therapeutic heparin bridge
choices.rationale: Temporary interruption for major surgery does not create a routine therapeutic-bridging indication for this AF history.
choices.temptation: Separate procedural interruption from thromboembolic indication.
choices.correctUnder: The represented AF and operation apply.

choices.label: Interrupt warfarin and use a therapeutic heparin bridge
choices.rationale: This adds treatment-level anticoagulation despite the represented AF indication, increasing bleeding exposure without the routine benefit assumed.
choices.temptation: Treat any subtherapeutic interval as requiring a bridge.
choices.correctUnder: A different very-high-risk thrombotic indication would require specialist assessment; this option is not endorsed as an automatic exception.

choices.label: Continue therapeutic warfarin at the usual dose
choices.rationale: The bleeding implications of major resection differ from a minor low-bleeding-risk procedure.
choices.temptation: Generalize an uninterrupted plan from minor procedures.
choices.correctUnder: A low-bleeding-risk procedure with a supported uninterrupted-warfarin protocol would be a different decision.

nodes.explanation: Interpret both the planned resection and why warfarin is prescribed. Avoid routine therapeutic bridging for this AF interruption. Postoperative surgical VTE prevention has its own indication and must be planned separately.

gate.interpret: A major bowel resection and AF without represented prior embolic events are distinct inputs.
gate.apply: Interrupt therapeutic warfarin without automatically adding a treatment-dose bridge.
gate.decidingObservation: The anticoagulant indication is AF, with the documented thromboembolic history shown.
gate.counterfactual: If the operation were canceled and no procedure or new bleeding problem remained, continuing the established therapeutic warfarin regimen would replace perioperative interruption.
gate.deletionTest: The operation makes uninterrupted warfarin a meaningful competitor; the indication/history distinguishes interruption from bridging. The prior beta-blocker story is removed.
gate.cueAttack: Deleted the legacy sentence announcing that interruption is required and the permanent-cessation caricature. Three concrete anticoagulation plans answer the same task.
gate.stageAudit: Preoperative therapeutic anticoagulation, not a matrix of pre- and postoperative phases.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error is unnecessary treatment-dose bridging during an anticipated low-INR interval.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; frozen N2 order reconciliation is not appended.
gate.limitation: No high-risk bridging exception is keyed or resolved; CHEST and AHA scope differences are preserved. No exact interruption timing.

definitions.name: Elena Foster
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after colorectal cancer surgery. The founder reviews an outside hospital decision from postoperative day 2. She had a prior postoperative DVT and was still transferring from bed to chair with assistance. After hemoglobin had been unchanged on two measurements, it fell from 10.0 to 8.1 g/dL while the abdominal drain filled with fresh blood. The next prophylaxis orders were being selected during the surgical reassessment.

nodes.objective: Select prevention while active postoperative bleeding competes with a major-surgery thrombotic risk.
nodes.task: Which VTE-prevention order best fits Elena at that recorded decision point?

choices.label: Use intermittent pneumatic compression
choices.rationale: The new blood loss changes the current bleeding balance despite strong postoperative VTE risk. Mechanical prevention is the best offered immediate approach during reassessment.
choices.temptation: Integrate both thrombosis risk and the new trajectory instead of treating cancer risk as permission for heparin.
choices.correctUnder: The represented new blood loss applies.

choices.label: Give prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin
choices.rationale: Major cancer surgery, prior DVT and limited mobility favor pharmacologic prevention when bleeding risk permits, but the new drainage and hemoglobin change oppose starting it at this point.
choices.temptation: Apply the strong VTE indication without updating the competing bleeding risk.
choices.correctUnder: The same VTE risk with stable hemostatic observations would favor pharmacologic prevention.

choices.label: Give prophylactic subcutaneous unfractionated heparin
choices.rationale: Changing the heparin preparation does not remove the current concern from new blood loss.
choices.temptation: Treat selection of another prophylactic heparin as a solution to the risk-state change.
choices.correctUnder: An appropriate major-surgery patient without the represented bleeding concern could receive prophylactic UFH under the treating team’s plan.

nodes.explanation: The prior DVT, cancer operation and limited mobility establish a strong prevention need. The new hemoglobin and drainage trajectory nevertheless changes which form is appropriate now. Use mechanical prevention during this reassessment; neither offered heparin preparation removes the current bleeding concern.

gate.interpret: Read a new fall after stable hemoglobin together with fresh bloody drainage as a change in current bleeding risk, not a static postoperative laboratory result.
gate.apply: Weigh that change against prior DVT, cancer surgery and immobility when selecting the prevention modality.
gate.decidingObservation: Fresh drain blood accompanies a new hemoglobin fall after earlier stable values.
gate.counterfactual: If the new drainage were nonbloody and serial hemoglobin remained stable after source control, pharmacologic prevention such as the offered LMWH would become appropriate for the continuing high VTE risk.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the trajectory leaves a high-risk cancer patient for whom a heparin plan could be appropriate. Prior DVT and observed mobility are the competing-risk facts; no arbitrary blood-loss cutoff is taught.
gate.cueAttack: Removed both “active bleeding assessment” labels and the prophylactic IVC-filter foil. All options are named prevention modalities with no explanatory qualifiers in their labels. Two heparin preparations represent a plausible agent-substitution error.
gate.stageAudit: Immediate VTE-prevention order during a historical hospital assessment, not treatment of established VTE.
gate.difficultyReason: A strong prior-VTE prevention indication competes with a newly changed risk state. This retains a fair moderate ceiling; warning signs are not hidden to manufacture difficulty.
gate.sequenceAudit: Split into a standalone chart-review case. No explanation announces the following resumption answer; later course nodes are absent.
gate.limitation: ASH recommendations are conditional and evidence certainty is low/very low. This is the best offered immediate modality, not a quantitative bleeding threshold or universal timing rule.

definitions.name: Elena Foster
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after colorectal cancer surgery. The founder reviews her outside discharge orders from postoperative day 8. She had a previous postoperative DVT. At discharge she walked only from bed to the doorway with a walker. LMWH had been restarted after an earlier reoperation for bleeding. A small injection-site bruise had not enlarged; three successive hemoglobin results were unchanged and the abdominal wound had no new swelling. She was eating, creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL (0.6–1.1), and no VTE had been diagnosed.

nodes.objective: Reconcile total extended prophylaxis with discharge before mobility recovery after major cancer surgery.
nodes.task: Which discharge LMWH plan best fits Elena’s recorded course?

choices.label: Continue prophylactic LMWH to about four weeks after surgery
choices.rationale: Major abdominopelvic cancer surgery, prior DVT and persistent mobility limitation support an extended total course when the present bleeding balance permits it.
choices.temptation: Use the actual risk and recovery record instead of the discharge boundary or an isolated stable bruise.
choices.correctUnder: The represented high-risk major cancer operation and current tolerated prophylaxis apply.

choices.label: Stop prophylactic LMWH when she leaves the hospital
choices.rationale: Discharge does not remove this represented extended-prophylaxis indication.
choices.temptation: Transfer an inpatient-only course to a high-risk major cancer operation.
choices.correctUnder: Completion of an appropriate shorter course in a patient without an extended-course indication could support stopping at discharge.

choices.label: Withhold prophylactic LMWH pending a bleeding reassessment
choices.rationale: A stable small injection-site bruise without a new blood-count or wound trajectory does not recreate the earlier bleeding episode.
choices.temptation: Treat any visible bruise as equivalent to renewed surgical blood loss.
choices.correctUnder: An expanding wound hematoma or new hemoglobin fall would require reassessment of further anticoagulant exposure.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the current bruise and serial course separately from the earlier bleeding episode. Then apply the major cancer operation, prior DVT and persistent mobility limitation to the discharge course. The supported plan totals about four postoperative weeks; it does not mean four additional weeks starting at discharge.

gate.interpret: A stable local bruise and unchanged serial hemoglobin differ from an expanding surgical bleeding process.
gate.apply: Recognize the high-risk cancer-surgery extended-course indication rather than let discharge or any bruise determine the duration.
gate.decidingObservation: The bruise is not enlarging and serial hemoglobin and wound observations remain unchanged while mobility is still markedly limited.
gate.counterfactual: If the bruise finding were instead an expanding abdominal wound hematoma with a new hemoglobin fall, withholding further LMWH pending bleeding reassessment would become the appropriate offered plan.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting current bleeding observations makes further LMWH uncertain after the previous reoperation. Deleting the cancer/prior-DVT/mobility profile weakens the extended-course indication. Day 8 is a neutral constructed time point, with no four-week hint in the vignette.
gate.cueAttack: Removed the answer-bearing “well before four weeks.” Three discharge medication plans compare continue, stop and withhold; none uses a uniquely explanatory key label. The precise duration appears only after the learner interprets eligibility.
gate.stageAudit: One discharge prophylaxis prescription, not treatment of established VTE.
gate.difficultyReason: The resident must distinguish a stable bruise from renewed bleeding before applying an extended course to a still-limited patient. Moderate is the fair ceiling for this guideline application.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone discharge-record review; no preceding resumption feedback is available.
gate.limitation: Selected high-risk population and acceptable bleeding balance. No dose, exact stop date or universal four-week instruction for every operation.

definitions.name: David Chen
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic to finalize an elective abdominal operation requiring fasting. The imported medication list says empagliflozin. His current pharmacy dispensing record and the bottle he brings both say ertugliflozin; empagliflozin has no recent refill. His last dose from the current bottle was Monday at 08:00. He is well and eating normally. The booking list offers Thursday at 08:00, Friday at 08:00 or the following Monday at 08:00.

nodes.objective: Reconcile the actual SGLT2 medicine before applying its U.S. label-based elective interruption minimum.
nodes.task: Which listed operation slot first meets the labeled preoperative interruption minimum for David’s current medicine?

choices.label: Friday at 08:00
choices.rationale: Reconcile the current ertugliflozin exposure, then count four full days from Monday at 08:00. Friday is the first offered slot meeting that label minimum.
choices.temptation: Use the actual dispensed medicine and last administration time rather than the imported medicine name.
choices.correctUnder: The represented ertugliflozin exposure applies.

choices.label: Thursday at 08:00
choices.rationale: This is three full days after the last dose. It applies the empagliflozin interval to the current ertugliflozin exposure.
choices.temptation: Use the old medication-list entry rather than the bottle and dispensing record.
choices.correctUnder: If the current administered medicine were empagliflozin instead, this first offered three-day slot would meet its labeled minimum.

choices.label: The following Monday at 08:00
choices.rationale: This meets the minimum but is not the first offered slot that does so; the extra delay is not required by the represented label rule.
choices.temptation: Apply a blanket one-week hold to all diabetes-related preoperative medicines.
choices.correctUnder: A separate clinical reason to delay until that date could change booking, but no universal one-week SGLT2 minimum is established here.

nodes.explanation: Identify the medicine actually taken, not the carried-forward list entry. Ertugliflozin’s labeled minimum is four days when possible: Monday 08:00 to Friday 08:00. Thursday supplies only the three-day interval used for empagliflozin. This comparison tests the medication/calendar discrepancy, not overall fitness or automatic permission to operate.

gate.interpret: Resolve the imported empagliflozin entry against concordant current dispensing, bottle and administration evidence for ertugliflozin.
gate.apply: Apply the correct drug-specific interval to the recorded last dose and select the earliest offered slot meeting it.
gate.decidingObservation: Current dispensing and the administered bottle identify ertugliflozin, while Thursday and Friday differ at the relevant four-day boundary.
gate.counterfactual: If both current dispensing and the administered bottle instead identified empagliflozin with the same Monday 08:00 last dose, Thursday at 08:00 would be the first label-concordant offered slot.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the exposure discrepancy reduces this to interval recall. Deleting the last-dose/booking record prevents applying that interval to the actual operation. The extra unexplained instruction sheet is gone.
gate.cueAttack: No sheet is called old or incorrect and no drug-specific number appears before the choices. All options are actual booking times. The task states the limited comparison so meeting a medication minimum cannot be mistaken for full surgical clearance.
gate.stageAudit: One elective booking decision under a defined medication interruption constraint.
gate.difficultyReason: Current exposure reconciliation and a clinically consequential calendar application create a fair moderate item; arithmetic is simple and does not create an artificial hard label.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no earlier item teaches the current drug’s interval.
gate.limitation: U.S. labels, when possible, govern this narrow minimum. Dates/times are constructed; no interval beyond the sourced label minimum or whole-patient clearance claim.

definitions.name: Priya Shah
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, attends clinic after recovery from an outside operation. The founder reviews the earlier hospital record. She had taken empagliflozin through surgery and then vomited while eating little. After initial intravenous fluid replacement she was alert, blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. The team was choosing the next infusion plan using the following results.

nodes.objective: Interpret postoperative ketone-associated acidosis despite modest glucose and select an insulin/fluid plan that can correct it without creating hypoglycemia.
nodes.task: Which next infusion plan best fits Priya at that hospital decision point?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Glucose
items.value: 172 mg/dL

items.label: Venous pH
items.value: 7.25 (laboratory interval 7.32–7.42)

items.label: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate
items.value: 5.8 mmol/L (less than 0.6)

choices.label: Intravenous insulin with dextrose-containing fluid
choices.rationale: The ketone/acidosis pattern requires insulin despite the modest glucose. Dextrose supports continued insulin treatment while limiting hypoglycemia.
choices.temptation: Treat the ketone process rather than use glucose alone to decide whether insulin is needed.
choices.correctUnder: The represented ketone-associated acidosis and modest glucose apply.

choices.label: Intravenous insulin with saline lacking dextrose
choices.rationale: Insulin addresses ketone production, but the current glucose is already below the usual point for adding dextrose during DKA treatment.
choices.temptation: Transfer the initial high-glucose DKA fluid plan to a euglycemic presentation.
choices.correctUnder: With the same acidosis but markedly high glucose before it falls, insulin with isotonic fluid before dextrose becomes necessary could fit initial treatment.

choices.label: Saline replacement with intravenous insulin deferred
choices.rationale: Volume replacement is necessary, but it does not resolve this represented DKA pattern by itself.
choices.temptation: Treat a modest glucose concentration as evidence that insulin can wait.
choices.correctUnder: Volume depletion without the represented ketone-associated metabolic acidosis could support fluids without a DKA insulin infusion.

nodes.explanation: Integrate ketones with acidemia and low bicarbonate rather than let the glucose value exclude DKA. After initial volume replacement, the insulin plan must still address ketone production. Because glucose is already modest, pair intravenous insulin with dextrose-containing fluid. No insulin dose, fluid rate or post-DKA SGLT2 restart rule is tested.

gate.interpret: Recognize ketone-associated metabolic acidosis in a patient with diabetes and perioperative SGLT2 exposure despite glucose of 172 mg/dL.
gate.apply: Choose an insulin/fluid combination that treats ketone production while accommodating the low current glucose after initial fluid resuscitation.
gate.decidingObservation: Ketones and acidosis remain substantial even though glucose is modest; potassium is not low in the represented sample.
gate.counterfactual: If glucose were instead 520 mg/dL at the same initial post-volume assessment, saline with intravenous insulin before adding dextrose as glucose falls would be the appropriate offered initial combination.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting ketone/pH/bicarbonate information allows an ordinary volume-depletion interpretation. Deleting glucose prevents distinguishing the two insulin-fluid plans. Potassium and completed initial volume replacement are needed treatment-stage eligibility observations.
gate.cueAttack: Changed the diagnostic-label task to three parallel infusion plans. Removed lactate and HHS labels that separately eliminated options. Neither the presentation nor the task names euglycemic ketoacidosis or the need for dextrose.
gate.stageAudit: One next infusion decision after initial volume replacement; all options specify fluid plus whether insulin is being given.
gate.difficultyReason: The nearest plan correctly gives insulin but fails to adapt the fluid to modest glucose. The competing error is delaying insulin because glucose is not markedly elevated.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone outside-record review. The former restart companion is parked, and no later recovery data are exposed.
gate.limitation: One multisociety consensus publication directly supports this treatment distinction, with the FDA label corroborating recognition rather than the full infusion plan. No dose/rate or complete DKA protocol is taught.

nodes.conceptVersionReason: Changes the scored meaning from naming the adverse-effect pattern to selecting insulin/fluids after interpreting ketone-associated acidosis with modest glucose.

definitions.name: Aaron Cole
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old man, attends clinic before elective abdominal surgery. His BMI is 43 kg/m2. His partner reports loud snoring and breathing pauses at night, although he reports little daytime dozing. He speaks comfortably in full sentences and has no new dyspnea. On two clinic visits his resting room-air oxygen saturation was 92–93%. Serum total CO2 was 32 and 33 mmol/L (laboratory interval 22–29); creatinine was normal. He takes amlodipine and metformin, with no diuretic use or vomiting. Diagnostic sleep testing is booked.

nodes.objective: Recognize possible awake hypoventilation in obesity and select a test of PaCO2 rather than substituting a nocturnal screening result.
nodes.task: Which additional investigation best resolves Aaron’s persistent chemistry abnormality before anesthesia planning?

choices.label: Arterial blood-gas analysis
choices.rationale: The combined obesity, sleep-breathing history and persistent chemistry pattern warrant measuring arterial carbon dioxide rather than assuming the chemistry is diagnostic or waiting for a sleep-only assessment.
choices.temptation: Recognize that elevated total CO2 may reflect compensated ventilatory failure and needs direct assessment.
choices.correctUnder: The represented high-suspicion population and persistent unexplained abnormality apply.

choices.label: Attended diagnostic polysomnography
choices.rationale: Sleep testing remains needed for the sleep-breathing question, but it does not substitute for resolving the current possible daytime ventilatory abnormality.
choices.temptation: Treat the entire physiology question as ordinary nocturnal obstruction.
choices.correctUnder: After a current arterial assessment established normal daytime ventilation, the pending diagnostic sleep study would address the remaining nocturnal question.

choices.label: Repeat serum total CO2 measurement
choices.rationale: A further copy of a reproducibly abnormal screening value would not establish its acid-base mechanism or arterial carbon dioxide.
choices.temptation: Use repeated screening as confirmation of the physiologic diagnosis.
choices.correctUnder: An isolated result with a specific sample-quality concern could merit repeat chemistry before interpreting persistence.

nodes.explanation: The chemistry is a clue, not the diagnosis. Integrate it with severe obesity and the breathing history, then directly assess daytime ventilation. ATS supports arterial PaCO2 assessment when suspicion is high; neither an awake oxygen number nor raised bicarbonate alone establishes OHS. The sleep study remains relevant to a separate part of the evaluation.

gate.interpret: Integrate the reproducible high total CO2 with severe obesity and sleep-breathing observations; little reported dozing does not settle the ventilatory question.
gate.apply: Choose a measurement that resolves the acid-base/daytime ventilation uncertainty before treating sleep testing or repeat screening as a substitute.
gate.decidingObservation: Persistent total CO2 of 32–33 with the represented high-suspicion clinical context remains unexplained; the patient is clinically stable rather than acutely deteriorating.
gate.counterfactual: If a current arterial sample had already established normal PaCO2 without acidemia, repeating arterial sampling would not answer the remaining nocturnal question; the offered diagnostic polysomnography would become the relevant next investigation.
gate.deletionTest: The actual values and laboratory interval replace hidden degrees of abnormality. Stability limits the item to preoperative assessment. The medication/vomiting history constrains common nonrespiratory explanations; no SpO2 cutoff is proposed as a decision rule.
gate.cueAttack: The task names the unresolved chemistry question rather than the diagnosis or PaCO2. Replaced the duplicate overnight-oximetry foil with a plausible repeated-screening plan. The key is not inferred solely from contrasting awake with two overnight labels.
gate.stageAudit: One additional investigation for a current preoperative physiologic uncertainty; the booked sleep study is not canceled by choosing it.
gate.difficultyReason: An ordinary OSA workup and a repeated chemistry check compete with interpreting a persistent compensation clue. Values make the item fair rather than claiming difficulty from hidden severity.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no previous gas interpretation is supplied.
gate.limitation: ATS recommendation is conditional with very low certainty. All numbers are constructed observations, not invented diagnostic thresholds. Old F13 remains held; this exact new version requires review.

definitions.name: Rosa Bennett
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for bowel obstruction. The founder reviews how frailty was assessed before that admission’s operation. During dehydration on the ward she needed two people for transfers and could not sustain conversation. Her daughter’s dated account from two weeks before the illness describes help with shopping and medicine organization, but independent dressing, toileting and transfers. A two-year-old annual review describes gardening and managing all household tasks independently.

nodes.objective: Interpret acute loss versus recent baseline decline and choose the functional history that should anchor Clinical Frailty Scale assessment.
nodes.task: Which baseline functional state should Rosa’s team use for the Clinical Frailty Scale assessment in that operative episode?

choices.label: Instrumental-task dependence with personal-care independence
choices.rationale: The recent account describes support for shopping and medication organization while personal care and transfers were independent. Current ward dependence represents an additional acute loss.
choices.temptation: Use the recent corroborated baseline rather than the worst current or best remote state.
choices.correctUnder: The represented recent pre-illness account applies.

choices.label: Dependence for basic personal care and transfers
choices.rationale: This imports the acute ward decrement into the baseline rather than using the recent pre-illness abilities.
choices.temptation: Treat current illness-related dependence as the usual baseline.
choices.correctUnder: If the recent pre-illness account itself documented help for dressing, toileting and transfers, this would describe baseline.

choices.label: Independence in personal and instrumental daily tasks
choices.rationale: This matches the much older record but omits recent pre-illness support for shopping and medicines.
choices.temptation: Anchor on the best historical state instead of the recent baseline.
choices.correctUnder: If corroborated recent function still included independent shopping and medicine management as well as personal care, this baseline description would fit.

nodes.explanation: First distinguish the acute ward loss from the recent pre-illness state. Then classify what help was already needed: shopping and medicine organization required assistance, while personal care and transfers did not. That recent baseline should inform the CFS assessment; neither current dependence nor remote independence should replace it. No numerical CFS score or treatment exclusion is being taught.

gate.interpret: Separate a sudden illness-related decrement from persistent recent support needs, then interpret which daily activities actually required assistance before illness.
gate.apply: Use that recent functional state for the baseline CFS assessment rather than substitute current ward dependence or best remote function.
gate.decidingObservation: The daughter’s dated pre-illness account already contains some support needs but not the ward dependence.
gate.counterfactual: If the recent pre-illness account instead documented help with dressing, toileting and transfers, dependence for basic personal care and transfers would become the correct offered baseline.
gate.deletionTest: The dated recent account is necessary to distinguish instrumental assistance from basic-care dependence and from remote independence. Current and remote records supply credible but wrong temporal anchors; no protected numerical CFS descriptor is copied.
gate.cueAttack: Three mutually distinguishable functional states use comparable scope. Removed the earlier source-selection counterfactual that made two records equivalent when both described the same baseline. The key requires the recent activities to be interpreted rather than a date-word match.
gate.stageAudit: One baseline functional description entered for a historical operative frailty assessment, not a numerical score plus a treatment decision.
gate.difficultyReason: Both current dependence and remote independence are plausible anchoring errors; the trajectory is needed to choose the recent baseline. This is a fair moderate assessment decision.
gate.sequenceAudit: New standalone case. The exact PASS recovery-support node keeps its original header, update and wording in a separate case.
gate.limitation: BGS professional good-practice guidance supports the pre-illness anchor. No copied scoring scale, exact individual prognosis or automatic treatment exclusion is taught.

nodes.conceptVersionReason: Changes the scored meaning from selecting a generic multidomain assessment to selecting the appropriate supported baseline from a competing functional trajectory before acute operative illness.

definitions.name: Rosa Bennett
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 76-year-old woman, attends clinic before elective colectomy. Her comorbidity list is short.
