questions.stem: Which investigation should {patientName}'s hospital team prioritize for this new episode?

answerChoices.label: Bedside postvoid bladder ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: Acute fluctuating inattention warrants cause assessment; small voids do not exclude retention when postvoid lower-abdominal fullness persists.

answerChoices.label: Noncontrast head CT
answerChoices.rationale: The local urinary observations identify a current targeted question; no focal finding or head-injury history is supplied to prioritize CT.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The local urinary observations identify a current targeted question; no focal finding or head-injury history is supplied to prioritize CT.

answerChoices.label: Electroencephalography
answerChoices.rationale: The voiding/examination observations warrant assessment before choosing a seizure investigation for this course.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The voiding/examination observations warrant assessment before choosing a seizure investigation for this course.

questions.explanation: Quiet behavior can still be an acute delirium pattern. Interpret the postvoid fullness and small-volume voids, then assess residual bladder volume. This does not establish urinary retention as the only contributor.

questions.stem: Which ART plan should {patientName}'s team have used during that documented interval?

answerChoices.label: Coordinate temporary interruption of the complete oral regimen
answerChoices.rationale: When the complete regimen cannot be delivered despite route review, expert-coordinated interruption avoids unplanned partial treatment.

answerChoices.label: Continue the regimen components that can be obtained separately
answerChoices.rationale: Availability of individual agents does not establish an effective complete regimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Availability of individual agents does not establish an effective complete regimen.

answerChoices.label: Continue the complete regimen with repeated tube dosing
answerChoices.rationale: The actual repeated vomiting and return of administered tablets show that repeated dosing is not reliable delivery of the regimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The actual repeated vomiting and return of administered tablets show that repeated dosing is not reliable delivery of the regimen.

questions.explanation: Avoid routine interruption when ART can be delivered. Here actual route and formulation review establishes an unavoidable interval, so coordinate the complete-regimen plan with the HIV clinician rather than improvise partial treatment.

questions.stem: Which investigation should {patientName} undergo next for the current 2 o’clock incision-site fullness?

answerChoices.label: Targeted ultrasound at the marked 2 o’clock incision
answerChoices.rationale: The completed examination covered the old inferior scar, so its negative result does not characterize the current site. Ultrasound can characterize the localized postoperative collection.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic mammography of the left breast
answerChoices.rationale: This may be appropriate for a different new palpable-lesion workup, but it does not replace the missing targeted characterization of this early localized postoperative site.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This may be appropriate for a different new palpable-lesion workup, but it does not replace the missing targeted characterization of this early localized postoperative site.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the 2 o’clock fullness
answerChoices.rationale: A drainable collection at the current site has not been demonstrated. Targeted imaging should establish what the finding is before a therapeutic aspiration is selected.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A drainable collection at the current site has not been demonstrated. Targeted imaging should establish what the finding is before a therapeutic aspiration is selected.

questions.explanation: First match the actual acquisition to the current clinical target. A complete negative study of the 6 o’clock scar does not assess the 2 o’clock postoperative bed. Then choose focused characterization of that early wound-site change rather than escalate because of a supposedly adequate negative study or aspirate uncharacterized tissue.

questions.stem: Which current management plan best fits {patientName}’s postoperative incision-site collection?

answerChoices.label: Clinical observation with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The current functional course differs from the earlier symptomatic episode. Reappearance or a modest imaging increase does not by itself establish a need for another invasive procedure in this uncomplicated pocket.

answerChoices.label: Repeat image-guided needle aspiration
answerChoices.rationale: Aspiration helped the earlier painful pocket, but the present functional limitation has resolved. Repeating it solely because the image is larger adds a procedure without the former indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Aspiration helped the earlier painful pocket, but the present functional limitation has resolved. Repeating it solely because the image is larger adds a procedure without the former indication.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real option for selected difficult recurrent collections, but one recurrence with recovered function is not evidence that a drain is now needed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a real option for selected difficult recurrent collections, but one recurrence with recovered function is not evidence that a drain is now needed.

questions.explanation: Interpret recurrence and current effect separately. The earlier aspiration addressed pain and restricted use; those effects are no longer present despite a persistent image. Observation with reassessment fits this current uncomplicated pocket. Repeat aspiration and catheter drainage remain real interventions for different clinical burdens, not automatic responses to persistence.

questions.stem: Which agent-specific hypersensitivity entry is supported by {patientName}’s original records?

answerChoices.label: Gadobutrol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction
answerChoices.rationale: The administration record links the generalized wheal-type event to gadobutrol. The iohexol event has an isolated warmth phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Iohexol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction
answerChoices.rationale: This preserves the referral’s agent attribution even though the original iohexol event describes warmth without the generalized skin findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This preserves the referral’s agent attribution even though the original iohexol event describes warmth without the generalized skin findings.

answerChoices.label: Hypersensitivity-type reactions to both named agents
answerChoices.rationale: This merges a physiologic warmth event with a separate generalized skin event and loses the distinction needed for future planning.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This merges a physiologic warmth event with a separate generalized skin event and loses the distinction needed for future planning.

questions.explanation: Interpret the event phenotype, then check which agent was actually administered for that event. The generalized wheal-type event follows gadobutrol, while the iohexol visit records isolated transient warmth. Document the actual agent and symptoms. This does not prove an IgE mechanism, permit every other agent or select a premedication protocol.

questions.stem: Which next action best fits {patientName} at that earlier CT decision point?

answerChoices.label: Obtain urgent hand-surgical assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive tense swelling, sensory change and marked pain after extravasation require urgent severity-based surgical assessment.

answerChoices.label: Continue elevation with serial injection-site assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.

answerChoices.label: Treat the episode with systemic antihistamine therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.

questions.explanation: Interpret the worsening local course after initial care, then escalate for threatened tissue assessment. Keep the prior hives event separately documented; this item prescribes no pressure cutoff, contrast-volume trigger or operation.

questions.stem: Which allergy-evaluation plan fits {patientName}'s retrieved reaction history?

answerChoices.label: Retain the reaction record and refer to a drug-allergy specialist
answerChoices.rationale: Blistering, mucosal injury and organ involvement are severe delayed-reaction features outside routine skin-test or direct-challenge pathways.

answerChoices.label: Perform penicillin skin testing followed by an oral challenge
answerChoices.rationale: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.

answerChoices.label: Perform a supervised direct oral amoxicillin challenge
answerChoices.rationale: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.

questions.explanation: Interpret the retrieved phenotype rather than the short allergy header. Severe delayed features change testing eligibility. Retain the history and obtain specialist assessment; no challenge protocol or perioperative antibiotic is chosen here.

questions.stem: Which preoperative cardiac-evaluation strategy best fits {patientName}'s planned procedure?

answerChoices.label: Clinical assessment without additional ischemia testing
answerChoices.rationale: Unknown walking capacity does not establish a stress-testing indication before this low-risk procedure without symptoms.

answerChoices.label: Pharmacologic stress echocardiography before the procedure
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.

answerChoices.label: Coronary CT angiography before the procedure
answerChoices.rationale: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.

questions.explanation: Decide whether testing is indicated before choosing how to test. An orthopedic limitation and a low-risk local procedure do not create an independent ischemia-testing indication.

questions.stem: Which preparation plan best fits {patientName} before the abdominal operation?

answerChoices.label: Defer the elective operation for valve-team assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Severe valve measurements plus exertional presyncope warrant evaluation for valve intervention before nonurgent surgery.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with the operation and perioperative surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.

answerChoices.label: Defer the operation for dobutamine stress testing
answerChoices.rationale: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.

questions.explanation: The measurements and exertional presyncope support a symptomatic severe aortic stenosis concern despite preserved systolic function. Arrange valve-team assessment before the nonurgent major operation rather than treat surveillance as a substitute.

questions.stem: Which scheduling target best fits {patientName}’s elective repair, using the original PCI indication?

answerChoices.label: Aim for at least twelve months after PCI
answerChoices.rationale: The original ischemic presentation and dynamic injury with a culprit coronary lesion establish an ACS-related PCI context rather than a chronic-coronary-disease elective PCI. The represented elective interruption pathway ideally waits at least twelve months.

answerChoices.label: Aim for at least six months after PCI
answerChoices.rationale: This uses the chronic-coronary-disease DES pathway instead of the original acute presentation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses the chronic-coronary-disease DES pathway instead of the original acute presentation.

answerChoices.label: Use the current four-month interval
answerChoices.rationale: A shorter interval can be considered for selected time-sensitive surgery, but the represented repair is elective and its indication does not erase the ACS-related pathway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A shorter interval can be considered for selected time-sensitive surgery, but the represented repair is elective and its indication does not erase the ACS-related pathway.

questions.explanation: First reconstruct why the stent was placed from the original admission rather than the broad header. Then apply the elective operation’s need for antiplatelet interruption to that ACS-related DES pathway. The guideline ideally delays this elective interruption to at least twelve months; the six-month chronic-disease pathway and selected time-sensitive exception address different circumstances.

questions.stem: Which referral should be added to {patientName}’s routine surgical follow-up for the recorded troponin course?

answerChoices.label: Outpatient cardiology review
answerChoices.rationale: The postoperative dynamic rise is distinct from his stable preoperative elevation and unchanged renal function. The ischemic supply-demand context warrants cardiovascular follow-up; current recovery supports an outpatient phase.

answerChoices.label: An earlier routine nephrology review
answerChoices.rationale: CKD is relevant to the background troponin elevation, but stable renal function does not account for the new postoperative trajectory or replace cardiovascular assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CKD is relevant to the background troponin elevation, but stable renal function does not account for the new postoperative trajectory or replace cardiovascular assessment.

answerChoices.label: Urgent hospital cardiac reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Urgent reassessment would be appropriate for current acute ischemic findings, but the represented record is a resolved event and he has returned to usual activity without new symptoms or ECG change.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Urgent reassessment would be appropriate for current acute ischemic findings, but the represented record is a resolved event and he has returned to usual activity without new symptoms or ECG change.

questions.explanation: First compare the postoperative rise/fall with the stable preoperative values and renal course: CKD does not make this new trajectory merely the old background result. Then use the current clinical phase. A resolved perioperative injury in the represented supply-demand context merits cardiovascular review; it neither establishes plaque rupture nor requires emergency transfer from an otherwise stable follow-up visit.

authorChecks.decidingObservation: The dispensed supply is untouched and Marcus describes setting it aside; normal treated blood pressure does not establish a new beta-blocker requirement.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the dispensing and administration record instead showed uninterrupted daily metoprolol use with current tolerance, give the listed dose tomorrow becomes the appropriate continuation plan.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Without actual administration evidence, the imported list cannot distinguish continuation from initiation. The established indication and tomorrow timing resolve whether earlier reassessment or operative-day action is being asked. No dose or titration interval is invented.

authorChecks.stageAudit: One instruction for the immediately upcoming operative day; all options address metoprolol administration/preparation.

optionAudit.correctUnder: Recurrent meaningful pain, restricted movement or wound tension from a demonstrated collection could support aspiration.

optionAudit.temptation: Escalate after any recurrence rather than assess the current clinical burden and course.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This is a real option for selected difficult recurrent collections, but one recurrence with recovered function is not evidence that a drain is now needed.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A persistently symptomatic collection requiring repeated drainage could prompt specialist procedural planning; no universal catheter threshold is claimed.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Distinguish a generalized wheal-type event from isolated warmth using distribution and observed skin findings.
authorChecks.apply: Use the administration provenance to correct the named-agent record instead of carrying forward an iodinated-contrast label or merging both events.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: The generalized raised skin findings follow the MRI administration record for gadobutrol; iohexol belongs to the separate warmth event.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the original administration names were exchanged while the symptom records remained in their respective visits, the supported hypersensitivity entry would switch to iohexol.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Deleting administration provenance leaves the clinical phenotype recognizable but cannot identify the correct agent. Deleting symptoms leaves agent names without a supported reaction classification. Neither record alone answers the complete documentation decision.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Removed the explained local leakage event and the simple “which symptom is allergic” task. All choices are agent-specific record entries with parallel scope; the copied header is a credible conflict rather than the only place a diagnosis appears.
authorChecks.stageAudit: One documentation correction that affects the next imaging referral, not premedication, agent substitution or proof of mechanism.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: A familiar allergic phenotype must be reconciled with the actual contrast class and administration record; accepting the header yields a credible wrong agent.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone and independent of the frozen extravasation case.
authorChecks.limitation: ESUR supports agent-specific documentation. The current exercise records a hypersensitivity-type pattern only; it does not establish immunologic mechanism or prescribe a future imaging protocol.

optionAudit.temptation: Separate the actual administered agent from the copied contrast-family label.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The administration record links the generalized wheal-type event to gadobutrol. The iohexol event has an isolated warmth phenotype.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The represented agent/event pairing applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Trust the copied iodinated-contrast label over the medication administration record.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This preserves the referral’s agent attribution even though the original iohexol event describes warmth without the generalized skin findings.
optionAudit.correctUnder: If the generalized wheal event had followed iohexol administration rather than gadobutrol, this entry would be supported.

optionAudit.temptation: Apply one contrast-reaction label to every temporally associated sensation across agents.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This merges a physiologic warmth event with a separate generalized skin event and loses the distinction needed for future planning.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Separate original records of generalized hypersensitivity-type findings after each agent would support two distinct agent-specific entries.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Worsening local pain/sensation after actual initial measures is a different problem from prior generalized hives.
authorChecks.apply: Escalate local injury assessment rather than repeat an inadequate earlier plan or treat a copied mechanism.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Progression despite elevation with sensory loss and pain on passive extension.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If pain and swelling were improving and sensation remained normal, continued monitored local care would become reasonable.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The worsening trajectory is indispensable; without it conservative care remains reasonable. The older hives record is a purposeful competing attribution.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Three specific actions. No named missing consultation or transfer-availability permission. The question asks action, not a compartment label matched by one option.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Immediate next management action at the recorded scan, with initial injection stop already completed.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: A pre-existing allergy label and the expectation of benign resolution can misdirect urgency and mechanism.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; historical N2 v3 assessment-ranking version remains source-held and unchanged.
authorChecks.limitation: One direct guideline; new evidence supports this different severity-based escalation task, not automatic unpark/approval of the frozen N2 v3 assessment comparison.

optionAudit.temptation: Use trajectory and local injury rather than a copied historical mechanism.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Progressive tense swelling, sensory change and marked pain after extravasation require urgent severity-based surgical assessment.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The worsening local course applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Underweight the changing tissue/sensory findings after initial care.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Improving pain/swelling without sensory or skin change could support ongoing monitored conservative care.

optionAudit.temptation: Use the prior allergy entry as the current mechanism.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A current generalized urticarial episode would need an appropriate reaction-treatment assessment.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Delayed blistering with mucosal and organ injury is materially different from an isolated benign childhood rash.
authorChecks.apply: Avoid routine immediate-allergy testing or direct challenge and preserve specialist review.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Severe delayed mucosal/organ involvement in the actual retrieved record.
authorChecks.counterfactual: A verified immediate-type reaction without severe delayed features would change the evaluation to a specialist-selected immediate-allergy testing pathway.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The old vague label cannot determine the pathway; the retrieved timing/severity observations change it. No demographic probability or exact reaction interval invented.
authorChecks.cueAttack: No named severe-reaction diagnosis in the stem. All options specify evaluation plans; the key is shorter than the two testing competitors. Both testing choices have previews.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Select evaluation pathway, not choose prophylactic antibiotics or conduct a challenge now.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The plausible error is using a familiar penicillin skin-test sequence for a severe delayed phenotype.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Prior history-first feedback is not treated as permission for a protocol.
authorChecks.limitation: The inherited allergy-protocol teaching hold remains. This is a sourced exclusion boundary, not approval of a challenge, delabeling or prophylactic antibiotic.

optionAudit.temptation: Let actual severity change the pathway despite an old vague header.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Blistering, mucosal injury and organ involvement are severe delayed-reaction features outside routine skin-test or direct-challenge pathways.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The retrieved severe delayed features apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Use an immediate-allergy testing pathway for a different mechanism.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A compatible immediate-type history without severe delayed features could justify a specialist-selected skin-test/challenge pathway.

optionAudit.temptation: Use time since the event as the only risk classifier.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A validated low-risk history without severe delayed features could support an appropriate supervised protocol.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: The walking limit is orthopedic and the procedure has little physiologic burden.
authorChecks.apply: Avoid automatic stress or coronary-anatomic testing just because exercise capacity is uncertain.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: A superficial local procedure with no independent cardiac symptoms.
authorChecks.counterfactual: With an elevated-risk operation, elevated validated risk, poor capacity and a result that would change care, selective pharmacologic stress testing could become appropriate.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Procedure type changes the testing decision. The knee explanation prevents inability to exercise from being silently treated as cardiac symptoms.
authorChecks.cueAttack: No task term such as low-risk or unnecessary matches the key. All labels describe an evaluation strategy; both testing paths receive previews.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Whether and how to perform preoperative ischemia evaluation.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The credible error picks a pharmacologic modality before establishing indication.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no earlier risk-category teaching.
authorChecks.limitation: No numerical risk score or exam-weight assertion. One primary guideline; selective testing is conditional, not automatic.

optionAudit.temptation: Interpret why activity is limited and what operation is planned.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Unknown walking capacity does not establish a stress-testing indication before this low-risk procedure without symptoms.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The low-risk procedure and absent independent cardiac indication apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Select a nonexercise modality before deciding whether testing is indicated.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An elevated-risk operation with elevated predicted risk and poor capacity, where testing would change management, could justify selective stress testing.

optionAudit.temptation: Escalate modality to compensate for unavailable exercise data.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Selected elevated-risk cases with a management-changing high-risk coronary-anatomy question need a separate assessment.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Use the actual area/gradient/velocity pattern and exertional symptom, rather than a supplied severe-AS label.
authorChecks.apply: Change preparation to valve evaluation before a nonurgent major operation.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Exertional presyncope accompanies severe high-gradient measurements.
authorChecks.counterfactual: With no symptoms, preserved function and a low-risk planned procedure, proceeding with an appropriate perioperative plan could become reasonable.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Preserved EF sustains the competing reassurance error; urgency determines whether deferral is feasible. Every echo value is concordant, not an extra unrelated workup.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Three actual preparation plans. The task does not announce a safety hazard. Numeric findings are constructed patient values interpreted using directly sourced thresholds.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Preoperative preparation, not valve procedure selection.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: Preserved EF can be mistaken for absence of perioperative valve risk.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no preceding valve interpretation supplies the diagnosis.
authorChecks.limitation: One current primary guideline; no TAVR-versus-SAVR rank, exact delay or invented valve cutoff. The stress-test counterfactual remains specialist scope.

optionAudit.temptation: Integrate symptoms and valve physiology rather than rely on preserved EF.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Severe valve measurements plus exertional presyncope warrant evaluation for valve intervention before nonurgent surgery.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The severe symptomatic findings apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Generalize an asymptomatic low-risk-surgery pathway.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An asymptomatic patient with preserved function undergoing a low-risk procedure can represent a different supported pathway.

optionAudit.temptation: Use another test instead of acting on adequate measured valve evidence.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Discordant low-flow/low-gradient findings may create a separate specialist diagnostic question; no stress protocol is prescribed here.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Integrate new rest symptoms, dynamic troponin/ECG findings and the culprit thrombus record to identify an acute-coronary presentation rather than merely “a stent.”
authorChecks.apply: Choose the ACS-related elective antiplatelet-interruption timeline rather than the chronic-disease or time-sensitive pathway.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: The original PCI followed an acute ischemic presentation with a thrombus-containing culprit lesion, not a stable elective coronary-disease procedure.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the original PCI were instead elective treatment for chronic coronary disease, with no acute ischemic presentation, the offered six-month target would be the guideline-supported elective interruption pathway.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Removing the original indication leaves insufficient information to distinguish six from twelve months. The four-month current interval avoids an extremely early stent case in which nearly every pathway leads to the same obvious delay. Elective status and required clopidogrel interruption are necessary eligibility facts.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Removed redundant scheduling-permission language and therapeutic-heparin substitution. All choices are actual scheduling targets. No ACS diagnosis label or recommendation interval appears in the presentation.
authorChecks.stageAudit: One elective scheduling target under a represented antiplatelet-interruption requirement; all options share multidisciplinary antiplatelet planning after the scheduling decision.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The six-month alternative is a credible competing guideline pathway unless the resident reconstructs the actual PCI indication. The shorter current interval reflects a real exception with different urgency criteria.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone with no preceding PCI-interval teaching.
authorChecks.limitation: AHA-hosted 2024 guidance directly supports each timeline. Twelve months is an ideal elective pathway, not a universal prohibition under urgent or time-sensitive circumstances. No MI numeric-subtype teaching is introduced.

optionAudit.temptation: Recover the actual PCI indication before applying a generic post-stent calendar.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The original ischemic presentation and dynamic injury with a culprit coronary lesion establish an ACS-related PCI context rather than a chronic-coronary-disease elective PCI. The represented elective interruption pathway ideally waits at least twelve months.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The represented ACS-related DES and elective antiplatelet interruption apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Apply a familiar six-month DES interval without checking why PCI occurred.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This uses the chronic-coronary-disease DES pathway instead of the original acute presentation.
optionAudit.correctUnder: If the original procedure were elective PCI for chronic coronary disease rather than ACS, the six-month elective interruption target would fit the cited guideline.

optionAudit.temptation: Transfer a time-sensitive-surgery exception to this elective scheduling question.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A shorter interval can be considered for selected time-sensitive surgery, but the represented repair is elective and its indication does not erase the ACS-related pathway.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A time-sensitive condition whose harm from delay outweighed cardiovascular risk could lead the multidisciplinary team to consider surgery after three months; that is not automatic permission.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Distinguish an acute postoperative biomarker change from stable chronic elevation by using both the preoperative values and unchanged renal course, while considering the blood-loss/hypotension setting and recorded alternatives.
authorChecks.apply: Select outpatient cardiovascular review appropriate to a resolved event instead of diverting it to renal follow-up or treating it as a current acute presentation.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Troponin rises far above the stable preoperative pattern and then falls while renal function remains in its prior range; current function and ECG are unchanged.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If new rest chest pressure or a new ischemic ECG change appeared at today’s clinic visit, urgent hospital cardiac reassessment would become the appropriate offered referral.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Without baseline/serial biomarkers and renal course, chronic versus acute contribution cannot be separated. Without current recovery findings, outpatient versus urgent assessment cannot be fairly ranked. The record supplies observations for relevant alternative causes rather than an attributed diagnosis.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Removed the supplied ischemic-injury attribution, dismissive copied summary and immediate angiography foil. Three short parallel referral destinations avoid a uniquely comprehensive “review and optimize” key. Clinical interpretation is still required; no medication regimen is promised.
authorChecks.stageAudit: One referral/triage decision at current postoperative follow-up, based on a historical event and present status.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: Stable CKD makes the background elevation a credible alternative explanation, while the serial change and current phase must each alter the referral choice. This is a fair moderate ceiling rather than an unverified difficult-MI diagnosis task.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no preceding interpretation or future angiographic result supplies the answer.
authorChecks.limitation: The 2024 AHA perioperative guidance supports acute rise/fall evaluation and MINS follow-up. No specific MI subtype, assay-independent delta threshold, routine invasive test or antithrombotic regimen is asserted. The 2026 definition update is recorded as a current nomenclature boundary for clinician review.

optionAudit.temptation: Use baseline and serial data to distinguish a new perioperative event from the chronic background elevation.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The postoperative dynamic rise is distinct from his stable preoperative elevation and unchanged renal function. The ischemic supply-demand context warrants cardiovascular follow-up; current recovery supports an outpatient phase.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The represented resolved perioperative injury pattern and present stable phase apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Attribute the entire biomarker record to the known chronic condition.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: CKD is relevant to the background troponin elevation, but stable renal function does not account for the new postoperative trajectory or replace cardiovascular assessment.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A different record dominated by worsening kidney disease without a superimposed dynamic cardiac-injury pattern would shift the referral question toward renal review.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat any historical troponin event as proof of a current emergency.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Urgent reassessment would be appropriate for current acute ischemic findings, but the represented record is a resolved event and he has returned to usual activity without new symptoms or ECG change.
optionAudit.correctUnder: New rest chest pain, acute breathlessness or new ischemic ECG findings at today’s visit would change the phase to urgent hospital reassessment.

parkedAttempts.name: Elena Foster
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after colorectal cancer surgery. The founder reviews the outside hospital prevention decision after reoperation for bleeding. She had a previous postoperative DVT and still needed two people to help her from bed to chair. At this later decision, hemoglobin was 9.4, 9.5 and 9.4 g/dL on successive checks, the drain contained a small amount of straw-colored fluid, and no transfusion had been required since reoperation. Creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL (laboratory interval 0.6–1.1), platelets were 224 × 10^9/L (150–400), and the record contained no heparin-associated thrombocytopenia or drug allergy. Pneumatic compression remained ordered.

nodes.objective: Reassess a temporary pharmacologic-prophylaxis contraindication using the actual hemostatic course.
nodes.task: Which inpatient VTE-prevention plan best fits Elena at this later decision?

choices.label: Use prophylactic LMWH with pneumatic compression
choices.rationale: The observations support reconsidering the initial bleeding restriction. Prior DVT, major cancer surgery and marked mobility limitation favor combined prevention among these options.
choices.temptation: Reassess both current bleeding observations and unusually strong continuing VTE risk.
choices.correctUnder: The represented stable recovery and multiple VTE factors apply.

choices.label: Use pneumatic compression without prophylactic LMWH
choices.rationale: This carries the earlier restriction forward despite the later observations and leaves the strong current VTE indication incompletely addressed.
choices.temptation: Treat a previous bleeding episode as an unchanged contraindication.
choices.correctUnder: New bloody drainage, falling hemoglobin or another current pharmacologic contraindication could favor mechanical prevention.

choices.label: Use prophylactic LMWH without pneumatic compression
choices.rationale: Pharmacologic prevention is appropriate to reconsider, but the prior DVT and severe mobility limitation favor adding the mechanical method rather than withdrawing it.
choices.temptation: Resume the medicine but treat it as replacing the existing mechanical measure.
choices.correctUnder: A different, lower VTE-risk context or a mechanical-method contraindication could support pharmacologic prevention without compression.

nodes.explanation: Infer the current bleeding balance from the serial course rather than an eligibility label. Then account for the prior DVT and continuing functional limitation after a major cancer operation. ASH particularly favors combined prophylaxis in patients at high VTE risk when bleeding risk permits; it does not mandate the same combination for every surgical patient.

gate.interpret: Serial blood counts, drainage and transfusion course differ from the earlier blood-loss phase; the prior restriction needs reassessment.
gate.apply: Use the continuing prior-DVT/cancer/mobility risk to choose combined prevention rather than either preserve the hold or replace the mechanical method.
gate.decidingObservation: A previous DVT and persisting two-person transfer requirement remain despite the later stable blood-loss observations.
gate.counterfactual: If fresh bloody drainage and a new falling hemoglobin series returned, pneumatic compression without prophylactic LMWH would become the best offered interim plan.
gate.deletionTest: Without the recovery observations the previous bleeding restriction cannot be reassessed. Without the high-VTE-risk history, the evidence would not as strongly favor combination over LMWH by itself. Normal renal/platelet observations close the named medication eligibility gaps without proposing dose cutoffs.
gate.cueAttack: Removed “satisfactory hemostasis,” vague “prevention change,” baseline-only renal wording and therapeutic-heparin foil. All three options are complete same-stage modality combinations; the combination key is justified by the risk history, not a uniquely cautious phrase. The component-majority pattern does not assemble the key: the two LMWH rows and two compression rows would otherwise converge, so clinical interpretation remains necessary and this is a residual reviewer concern explicitly acknowledged.
gate.stageAudit: One inpatient prophylaxis plan, comparing modality combinations at identical prophylactic intensity.
gate.difficultyReason: A prior bleeding hold and the temptation to replace rather than combine modalities compete with the later recovery and VTE-risk profile. The ASH conditional preference limits claims of exclusivity.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone chart review; no prior mechanical-prevention explanation supplies a resumption rule.
gate.limitation: Conditional ASH preference, not proof that a noncombined plan is invariably wrong. If independent review finds combination versus pharmacologic-only insufficiently exclusive, park rather than force this key.

nodes.parkingReason: The one repair resolves clarity and medication-eligibility gaps, but the conditional combination preference does not make LMWH without compression unequivocally wrong. The three-row component matrix also converges on the combination key. Park rather than force a difficult exclusive ranking.
nodes.authorDisposition: The one repair resolves clarity and medication-eligibility gaps, but the conditional combination preference does not make LMWH without compression unequivocally wrong. The three-row component matrix also converges on the combination key. Park rather than force a difficult exclusive ranking.

parkedAttempts.name: Priya Shah
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside postoperative diabetes-medication decision after ketone-associated acidosis had resolved. At the decision time she was alert, blood pressure and renal function had returned to baseline, and she retained water. Both breakfast and lunch were vomited. The record was being reviewed before today’s empagliflozin administration.

nodes.objective: Use actual recovery of intake and clinical state rather than glucose or elapsed time to reassess resumption.
nodes.task: Which empagliflozin order should Priya’s hospital team enter at that current review?

choices.label: Keep empagliflozin withheld at this review
choices.rationale: Current repeated meal intolerance does not meet the labeled stability/intake prerequisites. This does not decide eventual re-exposure after the ketoacidosis episode.
choices.temptation: Separate the present administration decision from future restart eligibility.
choices.correctUnder: The represented current meal intolerance applies.

choices.label: Resume empagliflozin at this review
choices.rationale: This addresses the current decision but does not satisfy the represented intake boundary.
choices.temptation: Treat resolved laboratory abnormalities as complete recovery.
choices.correctUnder: A later sustained recovery plus completed reassessment of the episode and contributors would be prerequisites for an individualized future decision, not automatic restart.

choices.label: Permanently discontinue empagliflozin at this review
choices.rationale: The exact record does not establish a universally correct future re-exposure decision.
choices.temptation: Convert a present withholding decision into an unqualified permanent drug rule.
choices.correctUnder: A clinician may select permanent cessation after evaluating the episode, contributors, indications and alternatives.

nodes.explanation: Current meal intolerance supports withholding today. The choice does not determine whether empagliflozin should ever be restarted after this episode.

gate.interpret: Distinguish biochemical resolution from actual tolerance of intake.
gate.apply: Address administration now without teaching an automatic future restart rule.
gate.decidingObservation: Two attempted meals were vomited despite retained water.
gate.counterfactual: A later sustained intake recovery would require a separate reassessment of post-ketoacidosis re-exposure rather than automatically change this draft’s key.
gate.deletionTest: The meal record is decisive but leaves a focused safety recognition task, not an additional difficult inference.
gate.cueAttack: Repaired all labels to the same current decision and removed meal-intolerance rationale from the key label. The permanent-cessation alternative remains a discretionary clinical question rather than a clean wrong answer.
gate.stageAudit: Present administration is now separated from future re-exposure.
gate.difficultyReason: Attempt did not substantiate moderate difficulty; it remains easy current-withholding recognition and the future decision cannot fairly supply a third alternative.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair, excluded from scored exports.
gate.limitation: PARK: present hold is clear, but a fair harder three-option comparison and unique post-DKA re-exposure ranking were not established.

nodes.parkingReason: Present withholding is supported but remains easy. Permanent cessation versus eventual re-exposure after ketoacidosis needs an individualized clinical decision; no fair, independent moderate/hard comparison was established.
nodes.authorDisposition: Present withholding is supported but remains easy. Permanent cessation versus eventual re-exposure after ketoacidosis needs an individualized clinical decision; no fair, independent moderate/hard comparison was established.

parkedAttempts.name: Lena Morris
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic before elective hernia repair at a referring hospital. Her partner reports loud snoring and nocturnal breathing pauses. The outside screening report names STOP-Bang and records 6 of 8; it does not claim a diagnostic sleep-study result. Her daytime sleepiness questionnaire is within its reference interval. Awake oxygenation and chemistry are in range. Diagnostic sleep testing is booked.

nodes.conceptVersionReason: Changes risk-screen selection into perioperative planning while diagnostic confirmation is pending.
nodes.objective: Apply a discordant sleepiness/risk report to the operative planning phase without treating it as a diagnosis or automatic cancellation.
nodes.task: Which anesthesia and recovery plan should Lena’s referral request for the planned repair?

choices.label: Proceed with an OSA-conscious anesthetic and monitored recovery plan
choices.rationale: The screen and history merit planning, but the exact anesthetic, observation level and facility suitability require procedure- and setting-specific assessment.
choices.temptation: Use a risk screen for planning without calling it a diagnosis.
choices.correctUnder: A team-agreed procedure and observation plan could support proceeding.

choices.label: Postpone repair for diagnostic sleep testing and a revised plan
choices.rationale: This can be defensible when the needed perioperative plan or resources have not been established; the draft does not provide an exclusive boundary against it.
choices.temptation: Require diagnostic confirmation before acting on suspected risk.
choices.correctUnder: Unresolved comorbidity, postoperative observation or facility-suitability concerns could make postponement appropriate.

choices.label: Proceed with the hospital’s routine anesthetic and recovery plan
choices.rationale: A routine pathway might itself incorporate appropriate risk management, so its label cannot establish a different or inadequate plan.
choices.temptation: Treat a normal sleepiness questionnaire as negating the other observations.
choices.correctUnder: A routine pathway explicitly shown to meet the patient’s risk needs could be appropriate.

nodes.explanation: The report is a risk screen, not a diagnosis. The actual anesthesia, opioid and observation plan would need to be specified before these preparation choices can be exclusively ranked.

gate.interpret: Read the named risk instrument and corroborating history separately from diagnostic confirmation and daytime sleepiness.
gate.apply: Use suspected risk in a procedure- and resource-specific plan.
gate.decidingObservation: The draft still does not define an exclusive procedure/observation boundary between proceeding with a suitable plan and delaying to complete one.
gate.counterfactual: If major unresolved comorbidity or an unmet monitoring requirement were present, postponement could become the appropriate offered plan.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the screening result leaves the witnessed breathing history; the exact decision still depends on an unprovided concrete pathway rather than a second inference.
gate.cueAttack: Named STOP-Bang/result, removed “all” and made the preparation plans comparable. “Routine” could nevertheless conceal an adequate plan, creating overlap.
gate.stageAudit: All options now address a complete anesthesia/recovery preparation plan.
gate.difficultyReason: Attempt failed the unique-key gate; the plan labels cannot establish fair moderate difficulty.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair, excluded from scored supply.
gate.limitation: PARK: no local procedure/monitoring protocol is invented to force one key. The constructed screening result is not a teaching cutoff or reproduced instrument.

nodes.parkingReason: A named screen and balanced labels do not establish a unique anesthesia/recovery plan. Proceeding and postponement depend on procedure, monitoring and facility details not supplied by the permitted evidence; ordinary planning remains held for a concrete pathway.
nodes.authorDisposition: A named screen and balanced labels do not establish a unique anesthesia/recovery plan. Proceeding and postponement depend on procedure, monitoring and facility details not supplied by the permitted evidence; ordinary planning remains held for a concrete pathway.

parkedAttempts.name: Thomas Wells
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old man with treated OSA, attends clinic to review an outside ambulatory recovery record. After surgery he spoke comfortably when engaged. During repeated unstimulated checks he stopped breathing, oxygen readings fell and staff woke him. His usual PAP device was available. The founder reviews the disposition selected while these events continued.

nodes.objective: Distinguish stimulated wakeful recovery from continuing unstimulated respiratory risk before an unmonitored discharge.
nodes.task: Which disposition should Thomas’s team select at that recovery decision?

choices.label: Continue monitored recovery at the current hospital unit
choices.rationale: Persistent events preclude an unmonitored destination, but adequacy of the unit and escalation resources must still be assessed.
choices.temptation: Do not substitute the stimulated appearance for actual unstimulated recovery.
choices.correctUnder: An adequately resourced current unit may continue monitoring.

choices.label: Discharge home with his usual PAP plan
choices.rationale: The represented rescue requirements have not resolved.
choices.temptation: Treat possession of the home device as proof of readiness.
choices.correctUnder: Satisfactory unstimulated recovery with resolved risk could support the home plan.

choices.label: Transfer to a higher-acuity monitored hospital unit
choices.rationale: This may also be reasonable depending on support requirements and the current unit’s capabilities, which are not defined.
choices.temptation: Escalate the monitoring level rather than simply extend observation.
choices.correctUnder: Ongoing events exceeding current-unit resources would support transfer.

nodes.explanation: The warning signs must remain visible. They support continued monitored care, but the exact current-unit-versus-transfer decision needs a defined support and resource boundary.

gate.interpret: Recognize the unstimulated respiratory course despite a reassuring stimulated appearance.
gate.apply: Choose a monitored care setting, then assess whether the current unit can meet the actual needs.
gate.decidingObservation: The draft supplies continuing rescue needs but does not supply the capabilities that would distinguish the two monitored destinations.
gate.counterfactual: If the events exceeded documented current-unit resources, transfer would become the appropriate offered disposition.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the warning signs would create unsafe artificial ambiguity. Retaining them makes home discharge plainly premature; resource details are needed for a harder remaining decision.
gate.cueAttack: Removed the explicit PAP-failure clause and replaced oxygen-only home management with a real monitored-transfer alternative. That repair exposes overlap between the monitored plans.
gate.stageAudit: All options are actual dispositions at the same historical recovery decision.
gate.difficultyReason: Attempt failed unique-key and resident-difficulty gates: the supported safety lesson is easy, while the two monitored plans require additional clinical context.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair; no new ICU or ED setting is requested.
gate.limitation: PARK: no permission to hide apnea/rescue findings or invent a monitored-unit protocol. A basic-safety role would need explicit manager/independent acceptance.

nodes.parkingReason: Do not hide ongoing apnea/rescue needs. The supported no-unmonitored-discharge lesson remains easy; current monitored unit versus transfer cannot be uniquely ranked without real capability/support criteria.
nodes.authorDisposition: Do not hide ongoing apnea/rescue needs. The supported no-unmonitored-discharge lesson remains easy; current monitored unit versus transfer cannot be uniquely ranked without real capability/support criteria.

parkedAttempts.name: Maria Collins
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old woman, attends clinic before nonurgent abdominal surgery. During the last month she has reduced her usual walking because of breathlessness and developed ankle swelling. Examination finds basal crackles. She has no rest chest pain. The preoperative team is choosing the next cardiac investigation.

nodes.objective: Distinguish current signs of possible ventricular dysfunction from an unchanged stable patient with an old normal test.
nodes.task: Which cardiac investigation should Maria’s team prioritize for the new findings?

choices.label: Transthoracic echocardiography
choices.rationale: New dyspnea and congestion findings support assessment of ventricular function.
choices.temptation: Use changed symptoms to investigate structure and function.
choices.correctUnder: The represented new findings apply.

choices.label: Pharmacologic stress imaging
choices.rationale: An ischemia investigation can become relevant, but the draft does not establish a genuinely competing priority that makes this a difficult separate inference.
choices.temptation: Treat dyspnea as an ischemic equivalent before clarifying ventricular function.
choices.correctUnder: A different resolved structural assessment with a remaining ischemia question could support stress testing.

choices.label: Ambulatory ECG monitoring
choices.rationale: No sufficiently specific rhythm observations have been supplied to make this a strong alternative.
choices.temptation: Investigate intermittent rhythm disturbance as an explanation for limited activity.
choices.correctUnder: Documented intermittent palpitations or unexplained episodic syncope could support rhythm evaluation.

nodes.explanation: The new findings justify ventricular-function assessment. This repaired wording remains a straightforward syndrome-to-test task rather than a supported difficult diagnostic-priority comparison.

gate.interpret: Read the new breathlessness and congestion findings rather than a named old study.
gate.apply: Select ventricular assessment for a new preoperative change.
gate.decidingObservation: The represented new findings support ventricular assessment, but there is no credible competing acquired result or pathway boundary.
gate.counterfactual: If ventricular assessment had already resolved the structural question and an independently indicated ischemia question remained, stress imaging could be appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: Removed the named prior echo and redundant textbook congestion cluster. The remaining task still largely associates a syndrome with its familiar test.
gate.cueAttack: Old-test priming is removed and labels are specific; the rhythm foil remains weak. Adding unrelated warning signs just to strengthen it would manufacture ambiguity.
gate.stageAudit: Three cardiac investigations at the same evaluation stage.
gate.difficultyReason: Attempt did not establish a fair moderate/hard competing-priority decision; the supported task remains easy recognition.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair. The RAAS companion is separately parked; no mixed case remains.
gate.limitation: PARK: retain the valid guideline fact in the ledger, but do not present author labels as an independently accepted basic exception.

nodes.parkingReason: The fair supported rule remains straightforward ventricular-assessment recognition. The one repair did not produce credible independent diagnostic-priority reasoning; no accepted basic role exists.
nodes.authorDisposition: The fair supported rule remains straightforward ventricular-assessment recognition. The one repair did not produce credible independent diagnostic-priority reasoning; no accepted basic role exists.

parkedAttempts.name: Maria Collins
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old woman, attends clinic before rescheduled elective abdominal surgery after treatment for systolic heart failure. She now lies flat, walks her usual route and has no edema or crackles. Blood pressure, renal function and potassium are stable on lisinopril. The team is comparing the following precise perioperative instructions.

nodes.objective: Apply current compensated HFrEF and the treatment indication to perioperative RAAS reconciliation.
nodes.task: Which lisinopril instruction should Maria’s team select for the perioperative interval?

choices.label: Continue the established lisinopril schedule
choices.rationale: Continuation is reasonable for compensated HFrEF, but that permissive recommendation does not itself exclude a brief omission under a suitable anesthetic plan.
choices.temptation: Distinguish HFrEF therapy from hypertension-only instructions.
choices.correctUnder: A coordinated continuation plan can be appropriate in this represented clinical state.

choices.label: Omit lisinopril for the 24 hours before surgery
choices.rationale: A short omission is different from prolonged withdrawal. The evidence and provided record do not make it unequivocally inferior in every stable HFrEF patient.
choices.temptation: Apply an omission policy based on perioperative blood-pressure concerns.
choices.correctUnder: A selected controlled-hypertension/elevated-risk-surgery context supports this guideline option; HFrEF timing still requires clinical adjudication.

choices.label: Omit the operative-morning lisinopril dose
choices.rationale: This is another short omission plan whose ranking depends on dose timing, hemodynamic history and the actual anesthetic plan.
choices.temptation: Use a familiar morning-medication instruction without reconciling indication and hemodynamic context.
choices.correctUnder: An exact individualized perioperative plan could select a morning omission; the current sources do not uniquely rank it here.

nodes.explanation: The guideline permits continuation for stable HFrEF. It does not support turning that permissive option into an exclusive requirement over every short omission plan in this vignette.

gate.interpret: Recognize compensation and the HFrEF indication from the recovery record.
gate.apply: Compare explicitly timed administration plans without importing a hypertension-only instruction as a universal rule.
gate.decidingObservation: The exact interval is now specified, but the source still does not uniquely rank continuation against brief omission in this represented HFrEF context.
gate.counterfactual: An explicit current hypotension-related contraindication could change the plan toward omission, but an exact reviewed context and administration interval would be required.
gate.deletionTest: Removed “generic” and made team coordination shared. Defining the interval reveals rather than solves the clinical permissiveness boundary.
gate.cueAttack: Removed key-only coordination and unjustified dose escalation. Three real medication schedules remain potentially overlapping acceptable approaches.
gate.stageAudit: One precisely timed medication administration plan around surgery.
gate.difficultyReason: No fair unique key exists from the supplied permissive recommendation, regardless of a difficulty label.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair, excluded from scored exports.
gate.limitation: PARK: Melissa must adjudicate an exact clinical context if this exclusive ranking is to be taught. No automatic HFrEF continuation or mandatory omission rule is authored.

nodes.parkingReason: Continuation and short omission can remain acceptable depending on the precise hemodynamic/anesthetic context. A permissive HFrEF recommendation cannot support the exclusive key; Melissa must adjudicate a new exact case.
nodes.authorDisposition: Continuation and short omission can remain acceptable depending on the precise hemodynamic/anesthetic context. A permissive HFrEF recommendation cannot support the exclusive key; Melissa must adjudicate a new exact case.

parkedAttempts.name: Isabel Moore
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic before elective surgery under general anesthesia. Semaglutide was recently increased. She vomited her last two meals. Her preparation sheet specifies a medication hold, which she has completed. The anesthesia team is reviewing preparation before proceeding.

nodes.objective: Apply actual severe GI symptoms during GLP-1 escalation rather than infer readiness from a fixed interruption calendar.
nodes.task: Which preparation plan should Isabel’s team select for this elective procedure?

choices.label: Postpone for prescriber and anesthesia reassessment
choices.rationale: Persistent significant symptoms support reassessment rather than treating a completed calendar as readiness.
choices.temptation: Use current clinical response rather than the calendar in isolation.
choices.correctUnder: The represented significant symptoms apply.

choices.label: Proceed with rapid-sequence induction and tracheal intubation
choices.rationale: This is a real aspiration-risk mitigation strategy, but the exact indication, risk discussion and local pathway needed to rank it against postponement are not provided.
choices.temptation: Treat an airway technique as a complete solution to an unresolved preparation question.
choices.correctUnder: A team-reviewed situation requiring proceeding despite elevated aspiration risk could support a modified airway plan.

choices.label: Proceed after a revised liquid-diet preparation plan
choices.rationale: Diet modifications appear in guidance for selected patients, but ongoing significant symptoms and differing policies prevent this draft from asserting that a diet change establishes readiness.
choices.temptation: Apply a selected mitigation plan as a universal substitute for clinical reassessment.
choices.correctUnder: A different asymptomatic or appropriately reassessed context under a current team-approved policy could support a diet modification.

nodes.explanation: The severe-symptom boundary merits reassessment. A harder comparison between postponement, airway mitigation and diet modification requires exact clinical goals, urgency and an approved local pathway, rather than an invented universal GLP-1 rule.

gate.interpret: Recognize continuing significant intake symptoms after medication escalation despite completion of a calendar hold.
gate.apply: Use current symptoms and an actual preparation pathway rather than elapsed time alone.
gate.decidingObservation: The current symptoms are necessary safety data, but the draft lacks a supported exclusive boundary among real mitigation plans.
gate.counterfactual: A time-sensitive operation with a completed multidisciplinary risk discussion could support proceeding with an aspiration-risk airway plan; the exact indication must be separately authored and reviewed.
gate.deletionTest: Removed duplicate nonurgency and the editorial “old” label. Removing vomiting would enter disputed asymptomatic policies rather than make the current item difficult.
gate.cueAttack: Replaced antiemetic-only management with real airway and diet strategies. Their actual appropriateness cannot be established by short labels, so the comparison remains unfit for a forced key.
gate.stageAudit: All options address elective anesthesia preparation, with no invented exact hold or fasting duration.
gate.difficultyReason: The supported symptom-recognition lesson is easy; the attempted harder comparison exposes policy/context uncertainty rather than fair difficulty.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone attempted repair, excluded from scored supply.
gate.limitation: PARK: preserve differing GLP-1 policy boundaries. No universal washout, fasting rule, gastric threshold or mandatory airway technique is asserted.

nodes.parkingReason: Significant symptoms must remain visible. The supported lesson stays foundational, while real airway/diet alternatives require exact policy and clinical context. Do not force an exclusive preparation rule across differing guidance.
nodes.authorDisposition: Significant symptoms must remain visible. The supported lesson stays foundational, while real airway/diet alternatives require exact policy and clinical context. Do not force an exclusive preparation rule across differing guidance.

parkedAttempts.name: Daniel Price
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after recovery from an outside hospital operation. The founder reviews an episode of fluctuating inattention and visual misperceptions with repeated attempts to climb over bed rails and remove a fresh drain. Reorientation, family presence and de-escalation had failed. Pain, oxygenation, glucose and bladder distension had been addressed. He had no regular alcohol or benzodiazepine exposure, Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia or recorded QT prolongation.

nodes.objective: Distinguish dangerous nonwithdrawal agitation after nonpharmacologic measures from routine delirium or withdrawal treatment.
nodes.task: Which symptom-directed medicine best fits Daniel at that recorded decision point?

choices.label: Cautiously titrated haloperidol
choices.rationale: A short symptom-directed antipsychotic can be considered for dangerous agitation after nonpharmacologic measures fail, with contraindications assessed.
choices.temptation: Use the severe-symptom boundary without calling the drug a delirium cure.
choices.correctUnder: The current danger and prior measures apply.

choices.label: Cautiously titrated lorazepam
choices.rationale: No withdrawal indication is represented; benzodiazepines are not the routine first-line response to this delirium pattern.
choices.temptation: Generalize the withdrawal exception to all postoperative agitation.
choices.correctUnder: A documented benzodiazepine or alcohol interruption with a compatible withdrawal course would change the indication.

choices.label: Cautiously titrated diphenhydramine
choices.rationale: An anticholinergic sedating drug can worsen cognitive risk and does not address this delirium indication.
choices.temptation: Substitute a familiar sleep/sedation medicine for a symptom-specific plan.
choices.correctUnder: A separate histamine-mediated allergic indication would be a different therapeutic task, not treatment of delirium.

nodes.explanation: First distinguish immediate danger after failed de-escalation from routine quiet delirium, then check the withdrawal history and contraindications. Antipsychotic use here is short and symptom-directed, with low-certainty evidence; cause-directed care continues.

gate.interpret: Danger persists despite actual nonpharmacologic and cause-directed measures; no withdrawal exposure is present.
gate.apply: Consider a cautious short antipsychotic strategy rather than a withdrawal drug or anticholinergic sedative.
gate.decidingObservation: Absent regular alcohol/benzodiazepine exposure distinguishes the withdrawal exception.
gate.counterfactual: A verified abrupt interruption of chronic benzodiazepine use with compatible withdrawal findings would favor benzodiazepine treatment of that driver.
gate.deletionTest: Danger and failed measures establish the medication stage; exposure history separates lorazepam. Contraindication negatives are necessary, not decorative exclusions.
gate.cueAttack: All labels use the same cautious-titration grammar. No generic safe-plan option. No new dose or observation period.
gate.stageAudit: One symptom-directed medicine at the same recorded stage.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error extends a real withdrawal exception to a nonwithdrawal episode.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Does not modify or append to the frozen B2B21 withdrawal version.
gate.limitation: Diphenhydramine is a weaker competitor; three choices retained without padding. Evidence low; exact rank needs clinician/independent review.

parkedAttempts.name: Peter Hayes
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic before an outside MRI. His device card describes an MR Conditional generator. Since his prior uneventful scan, a lead revision left an additional implanted lead. The current referral contains the generator card and old MRI clearance; it does not identify conditions for the entire current implanted system.

nodes.objective: Recognize that a changed implanted system invalidates using generator-only or prior-scan clearance as the current system assessment.
nodes.task: Which device record should Peter's MRI team verify for the proposed examination?

choices.label: The complete current implanted system and current scan conditions
choices.rationale: The generator card does not describe the additional lead; assessment must use the actual present devices and proposed examination.
choices.temptation: Match identity and conditions to the same current system.
choices.correctUnder: The post-scan system change applies.

choices.label: The current generator model and current scan conditions
choices.rationale: This verifies the right generator but leaves another implanted component outside the safety assessment.
choices.temptation: Treat the conditional generator label as a whole-system label.
choices.correctUnder: A verified single-device system without additional components would be a different identity problem.

choices.label: The prior implanted system and prior scan conditions
choices.rationale: That record belongs to an earlier system and examination; past tolerance does not establish current conditions.
choices.temptation: Let a successful prior scan serve as reusable clearance.
choices.correctUnder: An unchanged fully identified system under the same verified conditions could make that record useful to the current team, with current confirmation.

nodes.explanation: First reconcile what is implanted now, then match the current system to the proposed examination. This does not declare the added lead safe or unsafe for all MRI; qualified MR/device review determines an appropriate pathway.

gate.interpret: An intervening lead revision changes the identity covered by the old clearance.
gate.apply: Request current whole-system verification rather than extrapolate from one component or past tolerance.
gate.decidingObservation: An additional lead remains after the prior scan.
gate.counterfactual: If records established that the generator was the only implanted device, generator-specific current-condition verification would cover the relevant system.
gate.deletionTest: The intervening component change is the consequential observation; deleting it reduces the case to generic repeat clearance.
gate.cueAttack: Balanced record-comparison options; the key is not a generic cautious plan. No invented MR field-strength or device protocol.
gate.stageAudit: Which identification/conditions record to verify, not choosing an MRI protocol or treatment.
gate.difficultyReason: A valid-looking MR Conditional generator card is a credible partial-evidence trap.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no prior MRI physics task reveals the safety answer.
gate.limitation: No device/lead-specific permission or prohibition, no claim that the clinic can clear scanning.

nodes.authorDisposition: UNKEYED: failed deletion and counterfactual gates

reviewDispositions.response: Removed the initiation label; specified tomorrow’s decision, original hypertension indication and neutral dispensing/administration evidence. Re-solved against both literal continuation and unnecessary delay.
reviewDispositions.remainingLimitation: One current guideline supports the medication rule. Fictional tablet counts and vital signs are observations, not evidence-derived treatment cutoffs.

reviewDispositions.response: Preserved the exact reviewed question, options, explanation, evidence claims, patient header and finite profile. PASS suggestions are not authorization to edit this exact version.
reviewDispositions.remainingLimitation: No high-risk bridging exception is keyed or resolved; CHEST and AHA scope differences are preserved. No exact interruption timing.

reviewDispositions.response: Removed supplied bleeding interpretation and the filter foil; made the competing thrombosis history explicit and compared actual prophylactic modalities. Standalone context prevents feedback scaffolding.
reviewDispositions.remainingLimitation: ASH recommendations are conditional and evidence certainty is low/very low. This is the best offered immediate modality, not a quantitative bleeding threshold or universal timing rule.
reviewDispositions.composition: Revised attempt isolated from all prior and future scored companions pending independent re-review.

reviewDispositions.response: Removed the hemostasis conclusion; supplied current renal/platelet eligibility, named VTE prevention and replaced therapeutic dosing with same-stage modality plans. Rechecked the conditional combination preference and recorded its exclusivity limit.
reviewDispositions.remainingLimitation: The one repair resolves clarity and medication-eligibility gaps, but the conditional combination preference does not make LMWH without compression unequivocally wrong. reviewItems.title: Actual beta-blocker exposure before surgery
clarityIssues: The visit-to-operation interval is unstated; the task could mean an immediate operative-day instruction or a longer preparation plan.

cues.phrase: first replacement dose for cardiac risk reduction
cues.why: The presentation classifies the order as new initiation and supplies its purpose, doing the decisive reconciliation inference.

fairness: Omitting new operative-day beta blockade is the best offered plan. No confident clinical error identified in that narrow rule. Absence of current symptoms does not establish absence of a chronic cardiac indication, so the rationale for not reassessing earlier needs clearer indication history.
Standalone. As written, explicit cessation months ago followed by a familiar initiation rule is easy rather than two consequential inferences.
suggestions: Specify the decision time and relevant established indication history. Show neutral administration/dispensing observations rather than calling the order a first replacement dose.
Compare credible plans requiring actual exposure and indication to be interpreted; do not invent a dose or titration interval.

reviewItems.title: Warfarin interruption for colectomy
fairness: Temporary interruption without routine therapeutic bridging is the best offered plan for the represented AF history and major bowel resection. The operation and anticoagulant indication both matter.
The bridge is a credible perioperative error; continuing therapeutic warfarin misapplies a minor-procedure strategy. No competing best answer identified in this scope.
Standalone. The explanation appropriately separates therapeutic bridging from surgical VTE prophylaxis. Exact timing and high-risk exceptions are not tested.
suggestions: Retain the indication, relevant embolic history and procedure. Delete the sentence merely announcing that the surgeon is comparing instructions.

reviewItems.title: VTE prevention during postoperative bleeding

cues.phrase: during active bleeding assessment
cues.why: The presentation interprets the raw blood-loss findings.

cues.phrase: during the active bleeding assessment
cues.why: The task repeats the interpretation that determines the answer.

cues.phrase: No VTE had been diagnosed.
