gate.interpret: Differentiate acute fluctuating attention from baseline memory impairment and small voids from proof of bladder emptying.
gate.apply: Select a targeted residual-volume assessment for a reversible cause.
gate.decidingObservation: Tender postvoid lower-abdominal fullness with repeated small voids and no focal deficit.
gate.counterfactual: A new focal neurologic deficit with an unremarkable bladder examination would prioritize head imaging.
gate.deletionTest: The new examination changes the investigation. Necessary glucose/oxygen/focal checks preserve fairness; no unused laboratory panel or exact urine-time trigger.
gate.cueAttack: No bladder-scan omission is named. All three choices are investigations with equivalent metadata treatment; the previous task did not teach retention.
gate.stageAudit: Current cause investigation rather than sedation or definitive treatment.
gate.difficultyReason: Two reassuring shortcuts compete: quiet behavior and apparent continued urination.
gate.sequenceAudit: The new postoperative examination earns the later node; the earlier medication answer cannot determine the current investigation.
gate.limitation: NIDDK supports residual assessment, delirium guidelines support cause evaluation; the clinical ranking is bounded synthesis requiring review. No CT/EEG protocol taught.

definitions.name: Maya Lewis
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 47-year-old woman, attends clinic after recovery from an outside abdominal operation. The founder reviews a period of bowel dysfunction. Nasogastric suction continued; each clamping attempt caused vomiting, and administered oral tablets returned in the drainage. Her ART was prescribed as a complete oral regimen. A completed pharmacist/HIV-clinician review documented no complete non-enteral substitute in the hospital formulary.

nodes.objective: Apply the unavoidable complete-regimen interruption boundary after actual route/formulation review.
nodes.task: Which ART plan should Maya's team have used during that documented interval?

choices.label: Coordinate temporary interruption of the complete oral regimen
choices.rationale: When the complete regimen cannot be delivered despite route review, expert-coordinated interruption avoids unplanned partial treatment.
choices.temptation: Recognize that continuity efforts have reached an actual route boundary.
choices.correctUnder: The verified unavoidable interval applies.

choices.label: Continue the regimen components that can be obtained separately
choices.rationale: Availability of individual agents does not establish an effective complete regimen.
choices.temptation: Equate partial administration with preserved ART continuity.
choices.correctUnder: A complete alternative regimen explicitly designed by the HIV clinician would be a different plan.

choices.label: Continue the complete regimen with repeated tube dosing
choices.rationale: The actual repeated vomiting and return of administered tablets show that repeated dosing is not reliable delivery of the regimen.
choices.temptation: Apply a continuation rule without checking the actual route review.
choices.correctUnder: A functioning enteral route with verified compatible formulations would support continuation.

nodes.explanation: Avoid routine interruption when ART can be delivered. Here actual route and formulation review establishes an unavoidable interval, so coordinate the complete-regimen plan with the HIV clinician rather than improvise partial treatment.

gate.interpret: Interpret failed clamping attempts and returned tablets as ineffective enteral delivery, rather than a generic fasting prohibition.
gate.apply: Use an expert-coordinated complete-regimen interruption rather than partial substitution.
gate.decidingObservation: Repeated clamping/dosing attempts failed, with tablets returned in drainage and no complete non-enteral substitute after expert review.
gate.counterfactual: If functioning enteral access and verified compatible full-regimen formulations were available, continue the complete regimen through that route.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the actual route review makes the key premature. The named roles establish that the prior review occurred, not that a convenient resource can be summoned to reveal the key.
gate.cueAttack: The task does not announce interruption is unavoidable. Every option is a complete ART instruction of comparable scope; no booster-only cue or midazolam comparison.
gate.stageAudit: Regimen administration during one defined historical interval.
gate.difficultyReason: The resident must reconcile the valid continuity rule with a documented route failure.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. The exact passed ART/midazolam case and its anesthesia companion are preserved.
gate.limitation: One accessible primary guideline; no drug-specific conversion, washout, component restart or dose taught.

definitions.name: Grace Turner
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 53-year-old woman, attends clinic after excision of a benign breast lesion. A new superficial fullness lies under the healed incision. Palpation cannot distinguish fluid from soft tissue. Her preoperative mammogram showed the original lesion, but was obtained before the excision. The incision is intact; she has no fever or redness and no breast implant.

nodes.objective: Match imaging to the current superficial postoperative target rather than reuse a preoperative study or escalate modality.
nodes.task: Which investigation should Grace undergo next for the new incision-site fullness?

choices.label: Targeted ultrasound at the incision site
choices.rationale: The current focused question is fluid versus soft tissue at a new superficial postoperative target.
choices.temptation: Match the acquisition to the actual new target.
choices.correctUnder: The palpable postoperative target applies.

choices.label: Diagnostic mammography of the affected breast
choices.rationale: The uncertain superficial postoperative collection is better characterized initially by targeted ultrasound; prior mammography predates it.
choices.temptation: Use the familiar breast modality without matching the question.
choices.correctUnder: A new mammographic calcification or architectural-distortion question would require a different imaging pathway.

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the affected breast
choices.rationale: The focused superficial question has not exhausted targeted ultrasound; advanced imaging is not selected by postoperative status itself.
choices.temptation: Treat a new postoperative finding as requiring the most extensive modality.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent unresolved findings after appropriate first evaluation could justify a different specialist imaging plan.

nodes.explanation: The target is new and postoperative, so the old acquisition cannot characterize it. Targeted ultrasound addresses the fluid-versus-soft-tissue question before a more extensive imaging pathway.

gate.interpret: Separate a preoperative study of the original lesion from the new postoperative palpable target.
gate.apply: Select target-matched ultrasound rather than assume prior imaging answers the current question.
gate.decidingObservation: The finding is a new superficial post-excision fullness, not a calcification target.
gate.counterfactual: If the new target were suspicious mammographic calcifications rather than superficial fullness, diagnostic mammography would become the relevant offered investigation.
gate.deletionTest: Chronology prevents false reassurance from prior imaging. Palpation uncertainty makes testing useful; no report declares a seroma before the choice.
gate.cueAttack: Three breast imaging modalities, with all wait profiles present. Removed chest-CT and pathology-review category foils.
gate.stageAudit: Initial imaging of the new target.
gate.difficultyReason: Target and acquisition chronology create the error beyond simply recognizing ultrasound.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node; no future fluid result appears in presentation or explanation.
gate.limitation: Narrow inherited institutional atom; no new mammographic criteria or escalation algorithm asserted. Independent difficulty review may judge this lower moderate.

nodes.objective: Use current symptoms and wound effect, rather than persistence of fluid alone, to rank intervention versus observation.
nodes.task: Which management plan best fits Grace after the later review?
nodes.update: Ultrasound showed a small smooth-walled fluid pocket with no solid component or internal vascularity. On later review the pocket was still palpable, but incisional discomfort had resolved, shoulder movement was unrestricted and the overlying wound was not stretched. There was still no erythema or systemic illness.

choices.label: Clinical observation with reassessment for new symptoms
choices.rationale: The current collection is simple and causes no meaningful symptom, wound effect or functional limitation.
choices.temptation: Use the response trajectory rather than persistence alone.
choices.correctUnder: The present uncomplicated asymptomatic state applies.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with clinical reassessment
choices.rationale: Persistent palpability alone does not establish benefit from aspiration when symptoms and wound effects have resolved.
choices.temptation: Treat any persistent postoperative fluid as requiring drainage.
choices.correctUnder: Meaningful pain, functional limitation or wound tension attributable to the collection could justify intervention.

choices.label: Antibiotic treatment with clinical reassessment
choices.rationale: No clinical infection signal is represented; antibiotics do not remove a simple uninfected fluid pocket.
choices.temptation: Treat a postoperative collection as infected by default.
choices.correctUnder: New erythema, warmth, systemic illness or other infection evidence would require reassessment for an infection-directed plan.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the current clinical effect of the collection. Persistence does not equal an intervention indication when discomfort and limitation resolve and the wound remains uncompromised. A new symptom, wound change or infection concern warrants reassessment.

gate.interpret: The image remains a small fluid pocket while the meaningful clinical effects have resolved.
gate.apply: Rank observation above routine aspiration or infection treatment.
gate.decidingObservation: Resolved pain, unrestricted movement and no wound tension despite persistent palpability.
gate.counterfactual: New meaningful pain or wound tension from the same collection would make aspiration a reasonable offered intervention.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the update removes both characterization and current response. The first node only chose imaging and did not rehearse observation.
gate.cueAttack: The task omits “small uncomplicated collection.” All labels are follow-up plans with similar grammar; aspiration gets its own preview.
gate.stageAudit: Current management after characterization and actual symptom reassessment.
gate.difficultyReason: Persistence creates a credible aspiration temptation despite clinical improvement.
gate.sequenceAudit: Earlier feedback does not teach the management rule; later actual symptom course earns this node.
gate.limitation: Inherited single-institution management detail with general NCI cross-check. No aspiration-volume cutoff or antibiotic regimen.

definitions.name: Laura Kim
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, brings three outside imaging-event notes to clinic before another imaging discussion. The referral header groups all three under one allergy entry. The founder reviews the original time-stamped symptoms rather than the copied header.

nodes.objective: Separate event-specific distribution and timing before deciding which event supports an allergic-like history.
nodes.task: Which of Laura's recorded events supports an allergic-like contrast-reaction entry?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Examination A
items.value: Brief generalized warmth during injection; no skin eruption; resolved fully

items.label: Examination B
items.value: Itchy raised wheals across chest and arms during injection; resolved under radiology care

items.label: Examination C
items.value: Pain and swelling confined to the IV site as contrast leaked locally; no generalized skin or breathing symptoms

choices.label: The generalized wheal event at examination B
choices.rationale: The actual distribution and morphology support an allergic-like pattern; a later local event does not erase it.
choices.temptation: Use the original symptoms rather than the grouped header.
choices.correctUnder: The time-stamped wheals apply.

choices.label: The transient warmth event at examination A
choices.rationale: Isolated resolved warmth can be physiologic/chemotoxic and does not establish the allergic-like pattern described in B.
choices.temptation: Treat any sensation after contrast as the same reaction class.
choices.correctUnder: If A instead documented immediate hives or another supported hypersensitivity pattern, its classification would change.

choices.label: The focal injection-site event at examination C
choices.rationale: Local leakage and swelling describe extravasation; this does not replace the separate generalized wheal history.
choices.temptation: Copy a prior allergy label onto a differently distributed event.
choices.correctUnder: If C also documented a distinct generalized urticarial event, that separate reaction would need its own record.

nodes.explanation: Reconstruct each exposure separately. The generalized wheals support an allergic-like history, while isolated warmth and focal leakage describe different events. This classification does not prove IgE causation or select a premedication regimen.

gate.interpret: The copied header combines three different distributions and timepoints.
gate.apply: Preserve the actual hypersensitivity-pattern event without extending it to every exposure.
gate.decidingObservation: Generalized wheals at B versus strictly local leakage at C.
gate.counterfactual: If generalized wheals were documented at C and B instead contained only a localized leakage event, C would be the correct event.
gate.deletionTest: The event exhibit is essential; neither a generic allergy header nor another event can answer the provenance question.
gate.cueAttack: Every option names one event and its finding; no key-only diagnosis in a complaint. Equivalent letters/chronology labels prevent word-matching a task phrase to the key.
gate.stageAudit: Which documented event supports the same history category.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error is conflating a prior allergic event with a subsequent injection injury.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. No earlier physiology explanation labels the exhibit rows.
gate.limitation: Classification/documentation only. No future contrast agent, skin test or prophylactic drug selected.

definitions.name: Amelia Stone
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside CT-related hand injury. The founder reviews the earlier management decision. Injection stopped when contrast leaked around a dorsal-hand catheter. Despite elevation, swelling became tense, finger sensation decreased and passive finger extension caused marked pain. Breathing and blood pressure were unchanged. A different prior scan had caused generalized hives.

nodes.objective: Use progressive local injury after initial care to select urgent surgical escalation without relabeling it as a prior systemic reaction.
nodes.task: Which next action best fits Amelia at that earlier CT decision point?

choices.label: Obtain urgent hand-surgical assessment
choices.rationale: Progressive tense swelling, sensory change and marked pain after extravasation require urgent severity-based surgical assessment.
choices.temptation: Use trajectory and local injury rather than a copied historical mechanism.
choices.correctUnder: The worsening local course applies.

choices.label: Continue elevation with serial injection-site assessment
choices.rationale: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.
choices.temptation: Underweight the changing tissue/sensory findings after initial care.
choices.correctUnder: Improving pain/swelling without sensory or skin change could support ongoing monitored conservative care.

choices.label: Treat the episode with systemic antihistamine therapy
choices.rationale: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.
choices.temptation: Use the prior allergy entry as the current mechanism.
choices.correctUnder: A current generalized urticarial episode would need an appropriate reaction-treatment assessment.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the worsening local course after initial care, then escalate for threatened tissue assessment. Keep the prior hives event separately documented; this item prescribes no pressure cutoff, contrast-volume trigger or operation.

gate.interpret: Worsening local pain/sensation after actual initial measures is a different problem from prior generalized hives.
gate.apply: Escalate local injury assessment rather than repeat an inadequate earlier plan or treat a copied mechanism.
gate.decidingObservation: Progression despite elevation with sensory loss and pain on passive extension.
gate.counterfactual: If pain and swelling were improving and sensation remained normal, continued monitored local care would become reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: The worsening trajectory is indispensable; without it conservative care remains reasonable. The older hives record is a purposeful competing attribution.
gate.cueAttack: Three specific actions. No named missing consultation or transfer-availability permission. The question asks action, not a compartment label matched by one option.
gate.stageAudit: Immediate next management action at the recorded scan, with initial injection stop already completed.
gate.difficultyReason: A pre-existing allergy label and the expectation of benign resolution can misdirect urgency and mechanism.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; historical N2 v3 assessment-ranking version remains source-held and unchanged.
gate.limitation: One direct guideline; new evidence supports this different severity-based escalation task, not automatic unpark/approval of the frozen N2 v3 assessment comparison.

definitions.name: Evelyn Scott
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends clinic before ambulatory surgery. The penicillin-allergy entry says “rash years ago.” Retrieved hospital records instead describe widespread blistering, painful oral erosions and liver injury developing after several days of amoxicillin, with hospital treatment. She has not taken a penicillin since.

nodes.conceptVersionReason: Changes initial history gathering into the severe-delayed-reaction exclusion from routine skin-test/direct-challenge pathways after actual records are obtained.
nodes.objective: Use severe delayed reaction findings to avoid an inappropriate routine allergy-testing pathway.
nodes.task: Which allergy-evaluation plan fits Evelyn's retrieved reaction history?

choices.label: Retain the reaction record and refer to a drug-allergy specialist
choices.rationale: Blistering, mucosal injury and organ involvement are severe delayed-reaction features outside routine skin-test or direct-challenge pathways.
choices.temptation: Let actual severity change the pathway despite an old vague header.
choices.correctUnder: The retrieved severe delayed features apply.

choices.label: Perform penicillin skin testing followed by an oral challenge
choices.rationale: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.
choices.temptation: Use an immediate-allergy testing pathway for a different mechanism.
choices.correctUnder: A compatible immediate-type history without severe delayed features could justify a specialist-selected skin-test/challenge pathway.

choices.label: Perform a supervised direct oral amoxicillin challenge
choices.rationale: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.
choices.temptation: Use time since the event as the only risk classifier.
choices.correctUnder: A validated low-risk history without severe delayed features could support an appropriate supervised protocol.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the retrieved phenotype rather than the short allergy header. Severe delayed features change testing eligibility. Retain the history and obtain specialist assessment; no challenge protocol or perioperative antibiotic is chosen here.

gate.interpret: Delayed blistering with mucosal and organ injury is materially different from an isolated benign childhood rash.
gate.apply: Avoid routine immediate-allergy testing or direct challenge and preserve specialist review.
gate.decidingObservation: Severe delayed mucosal/organ involvement in the actual retrieved record.
gate.counterfactual: A verified immediate-type reaction without severe delayed features would change the evaluation to a specialist-selected immediate-allergy testing pathway.
gate.deletionTest: The old vague label cannot determine the pathway; the retrieved timing/severity observations change it. No demographic probability or exact reaction interval invented.
gate.cueAttack: No named severe-reaction diagnosis in the stem. All options specify evaluation plans; the key is shorter than the two testing competitors. Both testing choices have previews.
gate.stageAudit: Select evaluation pathway, not choose prophylactic antibiotics or conduct a challenge now.
gate.difficultyReason: The plausible error is using a familiar penicillin skin-test sequence for a severe delayed phenotype.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Prior history-first feedback is not treated as permission for a protocol.
gate.limitation: The inherited allergy-protocol teaching hold remains. This is a sourced exclusion boundary, not approval of a challenge, delabeling or prophylactic antibiotic.

definitions.name: Samuel Ortiz
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic before removal of a superficial forearm lipoma under local anaesthesia. Knee arthritis limits walking, so the intake form cannot estimate exercise capacity from stairs. He has no exertional chest pressure, new dyspnea or known cardiovascular disease. The referral requests cardiac testing because of the walking limitation.

nodes.objective: Apply procedure risk before turning a noncardiac exercise limitation into routine ischemia testing.
nodes.task: Which preoperative cardiac-evaluation strategy best fits Samuel's planned procedure?

choices.label: Clinical assessment without additional ischemia testing
choices.rationale: Unknown walking capacity does not establish a stress-testing indication before this low-risk procedure without symptoms.
choices.temptation: Interpret why activity is limited and what operation is planned.
choices.correctUnder: The low-risk procedure and absent independent cardiac indication apply.

choices.label: Pharmacologic stress echocardiography before the procedure
choices.rationale: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.
choices.temptation: Select a nonexercise modality before deciding whether testing is indicated.
choices.correctUnder: An elevated-risk operation with elevated predicted risk and poor capacity, where testing would change management, could justify selective stress testing.

choices.label: Coronary CT angiography before the procedure
choices.rationale: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.
choices.temptation: Escalate modality to compensate for unavailable exercise data.
choices.correctUnder: Selected elevated-risk cases with a management-changing high-risk coronary-anatomy question need a separate assessment.

nodes.explanation: Decide whether testing is indicated before choosing how to test. An orthopedic limitation and a low-risk local procedure do not create an independent ischemia-testing indication.

gate.interpret: The walking limit is orthopedic and the procedure has little physiologic burden.
gate.apply: Avoid automatic stress or coronary-anatomic testing just because exercise capacity is uncertain.
gate.decidingObservation: A superficial local procedure with no independent cardiac symptoms.
gate.counterfactual: With an elevated-risk operation, elevated validated risk, poor capacity and a result that would change care, selective pharmacologic stress testing could become appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: Procedure type changes the testing decision. The knee explanation prevents inability to exercise from being silently treated as cardiac symptoms.
gate.cueAttack: No task term such as low-risk or unnecessary matches the key. All labels describe an evaluation strategy; both testing paths receive previews.
gate.stageAudit: Whether and how to perform preoperative ischemia evaluation.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error picks a pharmacologic modality before establishing indication.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no earlier risk-category teaching.
gate.limitation: No numerical risk score or exam-weight assertion. One primary guideline; selective testing is conditional, not automatic.

definitions.name: Maria Collins
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old woman, attends clinic before nonurgent abdominal surgery. An echocardiogram obtained last year was normal. She now sleeps propped on several pillows, stops while walking across her room and has new ankle swelling. Examination shows raised jugular venous pressure and basal crackles. She has no chest pressure.

nodes.objective: Distinguish current signs of possible ventricular dysfunction from an unchanged stable patient with an old normal test.
nodes.task: Which cardiac investigation should be prioritized for Maria's changed preoperative status?

choices.label: Transthoracic echocardiography
choices.rationale: New dyspnea and congestion findings warrant reassessment of ventricular function despite the old normal study.
choices.temptation: Use the actual interval change rather than the age of the prior report alone.
choices.correctUnder: The new congestion pattern applies.

choices.label: Pharmacologic myocardial perfusion imaging
choices.rationale: The immediate question is new ventricular dysfunction/congestion; stress testing is not the first substitute for resolving that state.
choices.temptation: Treat all preoperative cardiac concerns as ischemia screening.
choices.correctUnder: A stable elevated-risk patient with a remaining management-changing ischemia question could need selective stress assessment.

choices.label: Ambulatory ECG rhythm monitoring
choices.rationale: There is no rhythm-symptom pattern supplied to make a prolonged rhythm study the prioritized assessment of these new findings.
choices.temptation: Choose a cardiac test without matching it to the clinical question.
choices.correctUnder: Intermittent palpitations or unexplained episodic syncope with an unresolved rhythm concern would be a different targeted question.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the changed symptoms and examination, then choose a study of ventricular function. A prior normal result is not current evidence when the clinical state has changed. This is evaluation of a possible active cardiac problem, not routine screening.

gate.interpret: Orthopnea-pattern symptoms, venous pressure and crackles suggest a current congestion/function problem.
gate.apply: Reassess ventricular function rather than rely on last year or begin stress screening.
gate.decidingObservation: New congestion at the current review.
gate.counterfactual: After congestion resolved, a persistent management-changing ischemia question in an elevated-risk patient could make stress imaging the relevant next cardiac test.
gate.deletionTest: The old normal study makes interval change meaningful. Each current finding supports the syndrome, rather than being a checklist excluding all competitors.
gate.cueAttack: No diagnosis or named missing echo appears before the choices. Three named tests, all with wait profiles. No clinic treatment of acute failure is implied.
gate.stageAudit: Prioritized cardiac investigation before final elective planning.
gate.difficultyReason: A recent normal report and absent chest pressure can falsely redirect toward clearance or ischemia testing.
gate.sequenceAudit: First node; later function findings and treatment response are hidden.
gate.limitation: No emergent stabilization regimen or guarantee that testing can wait; actual clinical urgency remains the treating team's responsibility.

nodes.objective: Apply current compensated HFrEF and the treatment indication to perioperative RAAS reconciliation.
nodes.task: Which lisinopril plan best fits Maria before the rescheduled operation?
nodes.update: Hospital evaluation showed a reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction. After treatment she again lay flat, walked her usual route and had no edema or crackles. Blood pressure, potassium and renal function were stable on lisinopril, now prescribed for systolic heart failure. A generic hypertension instruction sheet proposed omitting it before the rescheduled operation.

choices.label: Continue the tolerated lisinopril with the perioperative team
choices.rationale: Continuation is reasonable for compensated HFrEF with stable tolerance; the hypertension-only omission rule is not universal across indications.
choices.temptation: Reconcile indication and response, not just drug class.
choices.correctUnder: Current compensated HFrEF and stable monitoring apply.

choices.label: Omit lisinopril for the preoperative interval
choices.rationale: Temporary omission can be reasonable in selected controlled-hypertension patients, but this record establishes a different indication and stable tolerance.
choices.temptation: Apply an indication-specific hypotension-reduction policy to every RAAS prescription.
choices.correctUnder: Controlled hypertension without HFrEF before an elevated-risk operation could support the selected omission plan.

choices.label: Increase lisinopril for the preoperative interval
choices.rationale: Neither the operation nor unchanged reduced systolic function establishes a need for immediate dose escalation after a stable response.
choices.temptation: Treat a persistently abnormal EF as proof the current perioperative dose is inadequate.
choices.correctUnder: An outpatient heart-failure titration decision with a documented remaining indication and monitoring would be a separate stage.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the response as compensated clinical status, then use why the medicine is prescribed. Continuing tolerated chronic RAAS therapy is reasonable in HFrEF; a selected hypertension omission policy is not a blanket drug-class instruction.

gate.interpret: Actual symptom, examination and laboratory response establishes current compensation and tolerance despite reduced systolic function.
gate.apply: Use the heart-failure indication rather than the generic hypertension sheet.
gate.decidingObservation: Stable tolerated therapy for HFrEF rather than controlled hypertension alone.
gate.counterfactual: If lisinopril were used for controlled hypertension without HFrEF before an elevated-risk operation, temporary omission could become reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the later response leaves active symptoms and unknown renal/hemodynamic tolerance, so the continuation decision is not earned.
gate.cueAttack: Three named dose instructions. No exact BP threshold or “all medicines available” permission. The question does not say the sheet is wrong.
gate.stageAudit: Chronic medicine continuation/temporary adjustment, not acute heart-failure treatment.
gate.difficultyReason: A familiar anesthesia instruction competes with an indication-specific exception and actual treatment response.
gate.sequenceAudit: First feedback asks for evaluation only. The new EF, actual response and medicine indication are needed for this separate decision.
gate.limitation: One guideline with conditional advice; no universal policy or exact dose. The treating team can change the plan for new instability.

definitions.name: Walter Evans
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 73-year-old man, attends clinic before nonurgent major abdominal surgery. He recently nearly fainted while climbing stairs. Echocardiography shows an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg and peak velocity 4.3 m/s, with preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction. The abdominal condition has no current obstruction, infection or bleeding.

nodes.objective: Interpret severe aortic valve measurements with exertional symptoms before accepting a nonurgent major-surgery plan.
nodes.task: Which preparation plan best fits Walter before the abdominal operation?

choices.label: Defer the elective operation for valve-team assessment
choices.rationale: Severe valve measurements plus exertional presyncope warrant evaluation for valve intervention before nonurgent surgery.
choices.temptation: Integrate symptoms and valve physiology rather than rely on preserved EF.
choices.correctUnder: The severe symptomatic findings apply.

choices.label: Proceed with the operation and perioperative surveillance
choices.rationale: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.
choices.temptation: Generalize an asymptomatic low-risk-surgery pathway.
choices.correctUnder: An asymptomatic patient with preserved function undergoing a low-risk procedure can represent a different supported pathway.

choices.label: Defer the operation for dobutamine stress testing
choices.rationale: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.
choices.temptation: Use another test instead of acting on adequate measured valve evidence.
choices.correctUnder: Discordant low-flow/low-gradient findings may create a separate specialist diagnostic question; no stress protocol is prescribed here.

nodes.explanation: The measurements and exertional presyncope support a symptomatic severe aortic stenosis concern despite preserved systolic function. Arrange valve-team assessment before the nonurgent major operation rather than treat surveillance as a substitute.

gate.interpret: Use the actual area/gradient/velocity pattern and exertional symptom, rather than a supplied severe-AS label.
gate.apply: Change preparation to valve evaluation before a nonurgent major operation.
gate.decidingObservation: Exertional presyncope accompanies severe high-gradient measurements.
gate.counterfactual: With no symptoms, preserved function and a low-risk planned procedure, proceeding with an appropriate perioperative plan could become reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Preserved EF sustains the competing reassurance error; urgency determines whether deferral is feasible. Every echo value is concordant, not an extra unrelated workup.
gate.cueAttack: Three actual preparation plans. The task does not announce a safety hazard. Numeric findings are constructed patient values interpreted using directly sourced thresholds.
gate.stageAudit: Preoperative preparation, not valve procedure selection.
gate.difficultyReason: Preserved EF can be mistaken for absence of perioperative valve risk.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no preceding valve interpretation supplies the diagnosis.
gate.limitation: One current primary guideline; no TAVR-versus-SAVR rank, exact delay or invented valve cutoff. The stress-test counterfactual remains specialist scope.

definitions.name: Olivia James
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic for a reducible incisional hernia that is not obstructed. Six weeks earlier she had a myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting coronary stent. She takes aspirin and clopidogrel. The proposed elective abdominal repair would require interrupting clopidogrel, and the current hernia symptoms can be managed while scheduling is reviewed.

nodes.objective: Integrate ACS stent indication, early interval and operation urgency before accepting antiplatelet interruption.
nodes.task: Which scheduling and antiplatelet plan best fits Olivia now?

choices.label: Defer elective repair and retain the cardiology antiplatelet plan
choices.rationale: This nonurgent repair would interrupt antiplatelet treatment early after DES PCI for ACS; defer and coordinate timing rather than create an avoidable early interruption.
choices.temptation: Use the stent indication and surgical urgency together.
choices.correctUnder: The recent ACS stent and nonurgent operation apply.

choices.label: Proceed with elective repair after interrupting clopidogrel
choices.rationale: A short surgical hold does not resolve the early post-ACS stent-risk problem.
choices.temptation: Treat interruption duration as the only timing question.
choices.correctUnder: A later appropriately reviewed interval after DES PCI with a supported interruption plan could allow surgery.

choices.label: Proceed with elective repair after substituting therapeutic heparin
choices.rationale: Therapeutic heparin is not a substitute for the coronary-stent antiplatelet strategy.
choices.temptation: Apply anticoagulant bridging logic to platelet-dependent stent protection.
choices.correctUnder: A separate anticoagulant indication can require its own plan; it would not replace this antiplatelet decision.

nodes.explanation: The clinical question is whether to create an elective antiplatelet interruption now. After DES PCI for ACS, the guideline ideally defers elective surgery requiring interruption for at least twelve months; urgent or time-sensitive surgery requires a separate team assessment.

gate.interpret: The stent treated ACS and the current hernia has no urgent complication.
gate.apply: Defer elective interruption rather than choose a hold schedule or heparin substitute.
gate.decidingObservation: Only six weeks have elapsed after DES PCI for an infarction, while the repair is nonurgent.
gate.counterfactual: After an appropriately reviewed later interval meeting the guideline timing and with a cardiology-supported interruption plan, the proceed-after-interruption option could become reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: The PCI indication and timing distinguish the decision; the hernia urgency is necessary to support deferral, not a convenience permission.
gate.cueAttack: All choices pair timing and medication strategy; the key is no more comprehensive. No twelve-month answer is disclosed in the task.
gate.stageAudit: Elective scheduling and antiplatelet plan at one timepoint.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error focuses on how to hold clopidogrel before deciding whether elective interruption should occur.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no anticoagulant-bridge companion repeats the answer.
gate.limitation: One guideline; no actual hold duration, antiplatelet dose or bridging protocol authored.

definitions.name: George Miller
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside colectomy. His hospital record shows troponin rose above the assay upper reference limit during postoperative hypotension and then fell. The hospital assessment attributed the episode to ischemic myocardial injury after evaluating alternative causes. He recalls no chest pain and is now asymptomatic. A copied discharge summary calls the troponin change “expected after surgery.”

nodes.objective: Apply a documented ischemic perioperative injury to follow-up without mistaking absent pain for no consequence or inferring plaque rupture.
nodes.task: Which follow-up request best fits George's recorded cardiac event?

choices.label: Arrange cardiovascular review and risk-factor optimization
choices.rationale: A documented ischemic injury can merit follow-up even without reported chest pain.
choices.temptation: Use the event assessment rather than the copied reassuring label.
choices.correctUnder: The hospital-attributed ischemic injury applies.

choices.label: Retain routine surgical follow-up with no cardiac review
choices.rationale: Absence of pain does not erase a documented ischemic postoperative troponin event.
choices.temptation: Treat a silent event as clinically irrelevant.
choices.correctUnder: An adequately evaluated nonischemic or artifactual result without another cardiac indication would require a different follow-up decision.

choices.label: Arrange immediate invasive coronary angiography from clinic
choices.rationale: The resolved event and current asymptomatic state do not independently establish an acute invasive indication or plaque rupture.
choices.temptation: Equate any troponin rise with a current type-1 infarction pathway.
choices.correctUnder: New acute ischemic symptoms or another acute coronary indication would require urgent reassessment in the appropriate setting.

nodes.explanation: Use the hospital's completed attribution and current clinical phase. A silent ischemic postoperative injury can justify cardiovascular follow-up; it does not by itself prove plaque rupture or select immediate angiography or an antithrombotic regimen.

gate.interpret: Distinguish a documented rise/fall attributed to ischemic injury from an expected harmless postoperative label.
gate.apply: Select follow-up appropriate to a resolved event rather than dismiss it or treat it as a current acute coronary presentation.
gate.decidingObservation: Completed hospital assessment attributes the dynamic biomarker event to ischemic injury.
gate.counterfactual: If the completed assessment instead established an analytical artifact with no cardiac disease indication, routine surgical follow-up could suffice.
gate.deletionTest: Attribution is needed to avoid calling every troponin rise MINS; the current symptom-free phase separates follow-up from acute invasive evaluation.
gate.cueAttack: The diagnosis is supplied only because follow-up is the objective. Three concrete referral strategies; no vague individualized-plan key.
gate.stageAudit: Follow-up referral intensity after a resolved event.
gate.difficultyReason: The resident must avoid both silent-event dismissal and reflex acute angiography.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Does not ask the same event's diagnosis after supplying its interpretation.
gate.limitation: One guideline; hospital attribution is a constructed prerequisite, not independent proof. No routine drug regimen or surveillance schedule.

definitions.name: Isabel Moore
definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic before nonurgent elective surgery under general anaesthesia. Semaglutide was recently increased. She has repeated vomiting and cannot retain her usual meals. An old instruction sheet says the procedure can proceed once a calendar-based medication hold is completed. Her surgical condition has no current urgent complication.

nodes.objective: Apply actual severe GI symptoms during GLP-1 escalation rather than infer readiness from a fixed interruption calendar.
nodes.task: Which preparation plan best fits Isabel before this elective procedure?

choices.label: Defer the procedure for prescriber and anaesthesia reassessment
choices.rationale: Significant symptoms and poor intake require reassessment before a nonurgent procedure; a completed hold clock does not establish readiness.
choices.temptation: Use actual response and urgency rather than an old universal schedule.
choices.correctUnder: Current repeated vomiting during escalation applies.

choices.label: Proceed once the calendar-based medication hold is complete
choices.rationale: Elapsed time does not establish symptom resolution or gastric-emptying readiness in this symptomatic patient.
choices.temptation: Treat one historical holding rule as a complete risk assessment.
choices.correctUnder: A clinically stable asymptomatic patient with a current team-approved plan would support proceeding on that agreed schedule.

choices.label: Proceed after premedication with ondansetron
choices.rationale: Reducing nausea does not establish that the unresolved intake/emptying concern has resolved.
choices.temptation: Substitute symptom suppression for assessment of the actual perioperative concern.
choices.correctUnder: An independently assessed transient nausea indication could merit an antiemetic without being a surgery-readiness test.

nodes.explanation: Recognize the significant current symptoms, then apply the nonurgent setting. Reassess with the prescribing and anaesthesia teams before proceeding. This tests a shared severe-symptom boundary, not a universal GLP-1 hold or fasting duration.

gate.interpret: Repeated vomiting and inability to retain meals during dose escalation are more than mild fullness.
gate.apply: Defer nonurgent preparation for reassessment rather than use a clock or symptom-suppression shortcut.
gate.decidingObservation: Significant symptoms persist, and the operation is nonurgent.
gate.counterfactual: With sustained usual intake, no significant symptoms and a current agreed preparation plan, proceeding on the agreed schedule could become reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Without actual symptoms the old schedule question enters disputed asymptomatic policies. Urgency is essential to support deferral.
gate.cueAttack: No quoted safety rule, exact hold interval or named missing test. Three preparation plans with similar scope; none depends on a newly available device.
gate.stageAudit: Readiness/preparation before one elective procedure.
gate.difficultyReason: An old holding rule and an antiemetic can each seem to solve a different problem than actual readiness.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no future gastric ultrasound result or postoperative recovery is exposed.
gate.limitation: Fasting/hold policies disagree across sources and remain withheld; no medication washout, fasting interval or exact gastric threshold.

decisionNodes.stem: Which metoprolol instruction should {patientName} receive for the planned operation?

answerChoices.label: Omit the operative-day start and reassess the indication
answerChoices.rationale: The record shows new exposure rather than continuation. With no immediate indication, surgery-day initiation for risk reduction is inappropriate.

answerChoices.label: Give the listed dose on the morning of surgery
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a historical prescription as evidence of current tolerance.

answerChoices.label: Delay surgery to restart and assess metoprolol
answerChoices.rationale: A stale prescription without a current treatment indication does not require delaying an otherwise planned operation to create new beta-blocker exposure.

decisionNodes.explanation: First establish actual exposure. A drug still listed in the chart is not necessarily chronic treatment. The continuation recommendation does not justify initiating beta blockade on the operative day for risk reduction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which anticoagulation plan fits {patientName} before the colectomy?

answerChoices.label: Interrupt warfarin with no therapeutic heparin bridge
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary interruption for major surgery does not create a routine therapeutic-bridging indication for this AF history.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt warfarin and use a therapeutic heparin bridge
answerChoices.rationale: This adds treatment-level anticoagulation despite the represented AF indication, increasing bleeding exposure without the routine benefit assumed.

answerChoices.label: Continue therapeutic warfarin at the usual dose

decisionNodes.stem: Which VTE-prevention plan best fits {patientName} during the active bleeding assessment?

answerChoices.label: Intermittent pneumatic compression with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Current bleeding can outweigh the immediate pharmacologic-prevention benefit; mechanical prevention is retained while that balance changes.

answerChoices.label: Prophylactic LMWH with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The cancer operation and immobility support prevention, but active blood loss changes the immediate balance.

answerChoices.label: Prophylactic IVC filter placement with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: An inability to give prophylactic anticoagulation does not itself establish an IVC-filter indication without VTE.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the current blood-loss trajectory before applying a prevention plan. Mechanical prevention can be used while active bleeding is assessed; the cancer operation still matters when the balance is reassessed.
sourceLabels: ASH surgical VTE prevention guideline

decisionNodes.stem: Which prevention change fits {patientName} at this later hospital review?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At a later review the bleeding source had been controlled. Serial hemoglobin measurements were unchanged, the wound and drain showed no further bleeding, and the treating team recorded satisfactory hemostasis. She still needed help walking from the bed to a chair; renal function was unchanged from baseline. Pneumatic compression continued.

answerChoices.label: Add prophylactic LMWH to pneumatic compression
answerChoices.rationale: The temporary bleeding constraint has changed while the major cancer operation and restricted mobility remain.

answerChoices.label: Continue pneumatic compression without pharmacologic prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: This carries the earlier active-bleeding decision forward despite its documented resolution.

answerChoices.label: Replace pneumatic compression with therapeutic heparin
answerChoices.rationale: Ongoing prevention risk does not establish a treatment-dose indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: The previous decision was conditional on active bleeding. Reassess it after actual hemostatic recovery rather than preserve the hold by habit. Prevention intensity remains different from treatment intensity.
sourceLabels: ASH surgical VTE prevention guideline

decisionNodes.stem: Which total postoperative LMWH course best fits {patientName} at discharge?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: By discharge {patientName} was retaining meals and the bleeding had not recurred. LMWH prophylaxis was tolerated. She could walk short distances with assistance but had not resumed her usual mobility. The discharge date fell well before four weeks after the operation. There was no diagnosed VTE.

answerChoices.label: Complete about four weeks from the operation
answerChoices.rationale: Selected high-risk abdominopelvic cancer-surgery patients can receive an extended total postoperative course when bleeding risk is acceptable.

answerChoices.label: Complete the course on the day of discharge
answerChoices.rationale: Leaving the hospital does not mean the operation-related VTE risk and mobility impairment have ended.

answerChoices.label: Complete three months from the operation
answerChoices.rationale: A treatment-length course does not follow from a prophylaxis indication without diagnosed VTE.

decisionNodes.explanation: The total course is counted from the operation, with the treating team accounting for any interruption. Discharge and partial walking recovery do not automatically end a selected extended-prophylaxis indication. This is prevention, not treatment of a diagnosed clot.

decisionNodes.stem: Which medication-associated complication best fits {patientName} at the earlier admission?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Glucose
items.value: 168 mg/dL

items.label: Serum bicarbonate
items.value: 12 mmol/L

items.label: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate
items.value: Markedly above the laboratory reference interval

items.label: Lactate
items.value: Within the laboratory reference interval

answerChoices.label: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis
answerChoices.rationale: Acidemia, low bicarbonate and marked ketone elevation form the pattern despite modest glucose; fasting and SGLT2 exposure fit the association.

answerChoices.label: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis
answerChoices.rationale: The lactate does not account for the supplied acid-base abnormality and ketone excess.

answerChoices.label: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
answerChoices.rationale: The glucose and marked ketone-associated acidemia do not fit a predominantly hyperosmolar hyperglycemic presentation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the pH, bicarbonate and ketones together. A modest glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis during SGLT2 exposure. This association warrants urgent hospital evaluation of the episode and other contributors; it does not prove a unique cause.

decisionNodes.stem: Which empagliflozin instruction fits {patientName} at the later recovery review?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Later records show that the acidosis and ketone elevation resolved. Blood pressure and renal function returned to her baseline. She could retain water, but each meal still led to vomiting. Her fasting glucose was 176 mg/dL. The discharge template scheduled her usual diabetes medicines to restart.

answerChoices.label: Continue withholding empagliflozin during meal intolerance
answerChoices.rationale: Resolution of acidosis does not establish resumed oral intake when meals still cause vomiting.

answerChoices.label: Resume empagliflozin with the next retained meal
answerChoices.rationale: A planned or single retained meal does not establish recovery when the current record shows repeated meal intolerance.

answerChoices.label: Resume empagliflozin after the next fasting glucose check
answerChoices.rationale: Glucose does not measure recovery of oral intake or resolve the current fasting risk.

decisionNodes.explanation: Recheck present clinical stability and oral intake after the acute episode. Resolved acidosis and a glucose rise do not override continuing meal intolerance. The eventual restart remains a treating-team decision.

answerChoices.rationale: The risk report and breathing history remain relevant despite limited daytime sleepiness; confirmation is a different question.

decisionNodes.stem: Which of {patientName}'s recorded events supports an allergic-like contrast-reaction entry?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Examination A
items.value: Brief generalized warmth during injection; no skin eruption; resolved fully

items.label: Examination B
items.value: Itchy raised wheals across chest and arms during injection; resolved under radiology care

items.label: Examination C
items.value: Pain and swelling confined to the IV site as contrast leaked locally; no generalized skin or breathing symptoms

answerChoices.label: The generalized wheal event at examination B
answerChoices.rationale: The actual distribution and morphology support an allergic-like pattern; a later local event does not erase it.

answerChoices.label: The transient warmth event at examination A
answerChoices.rationale: Isolated resolved warmth can be physiologic/chemotoxic and does not establish the allergic-like pattern described in B.

answerChoices.label: The focal injection-site event at examination C
answerChoices.rationale: Local leakage and swelling describe extravasation; this does not replace the separate generalized wheal history.

decisionNodes.explanation: Reconstruct each exposure separately. The generalized wheals support an allergic-like history, while isolated warmth and focal leakage describe different events. This classification does not prove IgE causation or select a premedication regimen.

decisionNodes.stem: Which cardiac investigation should be prioritized for {patientName}'s changed preoperative status?

answerChoices.label: Transthoracic echocardiography
answerChoices.rationale: New dyspnea and congestion findings warrant reassessment of ventricular function despite the old normal study.

answerChoices.label: Pharmacologic myocardial perfusion imaging
answerChoices.rationale: The immediate question is new ventricular dysfunction/congestion; stress testing is not the first substitute for resolving that state.

answerChoices.rationale: There is no rhythm-symptom pattern supplied to make a prolonged rhythm study the prioritized assessment of these new findings.

decisionNodes.stem: Which lisinopril plan best fits {patientName} before the rescheduled operation?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Hospital evaluation showed a reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction. After treatment she again lay flat, walked her usual route and had no edema or crackles. Blood pressure, potassium and renal function were stable on lisinopril, now prescribed for systolic heart failure. A generic hypertension instruction sheet proposed omitting it before the rescheduled operation.

answerChoices.label: Continue the tolerated lisinopril with the perioperative team
answerChoices.rationale: Continuation is reasonable for compensated HFrEF with stable tolerance; the hypertension-only omission rule is not universal across indications.

answerChoices.label: Omit lisinopril for the preoperative interval
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary omission can be reasonable in selected controlled-hypertension patients, but this record establishes a different indication and stable tolerance.

answerChoices.label: Increase lisinopril for the preoperative interval
answerChoices.rationale: Neither the operation nor unchanged reduced systolic function establishes a need for immediate dose escalation after a stable response.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the response as compensated clinical status, then use why the medicine is prescribed. Continuing tolerated chronic RAAS therapy is reasonable in HFrEF; a selected hypertension omission policy is not a blanket drug-class instruction.

answerChoices.label: Arrange immediate invasive coronary angiography from clinic

questions.stem: Which metoprolol instruction should {patientName} receive for the planned operation?

answerChoices.label: Omit the operative-day start and reassess the indication
answerChoices.rationale: The record shows new exposure rather than continuation. With no immediate indication, surgery-day initiation for risk reduction is inappropriate.

answerChoices.label: Give the listed dose on the morning of surgery
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a historical prescription as evidence of current tolerance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This treats a historical prescription as evidence of current tolerance.

answerChoices.label: Delay surgery to restart and assess metoprolol
answerChoices.rationale: A stale prescription without a current treatment indication does not require delaying an otherwise planned operation to create new beta-blocker exposure.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A stale prescription without a current treatment indication does not require delaying an otherwise planned operation to create new beta-blocker exposure.

questions.explanation: First establish actual exposure. A drug still listed in the chart is not necessarily chronic treatment. The continuation recommendation does not justify initiating beta blockade on the operative day for risk reduction.

questions.stem: Which anticoagulation plan fits {patientName} before the colectomy?

answerChoices.label: Interrupt warfarin with no therapeutic heparin bridge
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary interruption for major surgery does not create a routine therapeutic-bridging indication for this AF history.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt warfarin and use a therapeutic heparin bridge
answerChoices.rationale: This adds treatment-level anticoagulation despite the represented AF indication, increasing bleeding exposure without the routine benefit assumed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This adds treatment-level anticoagulation despite the represented AF indication, increasing bleeding exposure without the routine benefit assumed.

answerChoices.label: Continue therapeutic warfarin at the usual dose
answerChoices.rationale: The bleeding implications of major resection differ from a minor low-bleeding-risk procedure.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The bleeding implications of major resection differ from a minor low-bleeding-risk procedure.

questions.explanation: Interpret both the planned resection and why warfarin is prescribed. Avoid routine therapeutic bridging for this AF interruption. Postoperative surgical VTE prevention has its own indication and must be planned separately.

questions.stem: Which VTE-prevention plan best fits {patientName} during the active bleeding assessment?

answerChoices.label: Intermittent pneumatic compression with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Current bleeding can outweigh the immediate pharmacologic-prevention benefit; mechanical prevention is retained while that balance changes.

answerChoices.label: Prophylactic LMWH with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The cancer operation and immobility support prevention, but active blood loss changes the immediate balance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The cancer operation and immobility support prevention, but active blood loss changes the immediate balance.

answerChoices.label: Prophylactic IVC filter placement with bleeding reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: An inability to give prophylactic anticoagulation does not itself establish an IVC-filter indication without VTE.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An inability to give prophylactic anticoagulation does not itself establish an IVC-filter indication without VTE.

questions.explanation: Interpret the current blood-loss trajectory before applying a prevention plan. Mechanical prevention can be used while active bleeding is assessed; the cancer operation still matters when the balance is reassessed.

questions.stem: Which prevention change fits {patientName} at this later hospital review?

answerChoices.label: Add prophylactic LMWH to pneumatic compression
answerChoices.rationale: The temporary bleeding constraint has changed while the major cancer operation and restricted mobility remain.

answerChoices.label: Continue pneumatic compression without pharmacologic prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: This carries the earlier active-bleeding decision forward despite its documented resolution.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This carries the earlier active-bleeding decision forward despite its documented resolution.

answerChoices.label: Replace pneumatic compression with therapeutic heparin
answerChoices.rationale: Ongoing prevention risk does not establish a treatment-dose indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ongoing prevention risk does not establish a treatment-dose indication.

questions.explanation: The previous decision was conditional on active bleeding. Reassess it after actual hemostatic recovery rather than preserve the hold by habit. Prevention intensity remains different from treatment intensity.

questions.stem: Which total postoperative LMWH course best fits {patientName} at discharge?

answerChoices.label: Complete about four weeks from the operation
answerChoices.rationale: Selected high-risk abdominopelvic cancer-surgery patients can receive an extended total postoperative course when bleeding risk is acceptable.

answerChoices.label: Complete the course on the day of discharge
answerChoices.rationale: Leaving the hospital does not mean the operation-related VTE risk and mobility impairment have ended.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Leaving the hospital does not mean the operation-related VTE risk and mobility impairment have ended.

answerChoices.label: Complete three months from the operation
answerChoices.rationale: A treatment-length course does not follow from a prophylaxis indication without diagnosed VTE.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A treatment-length course does not follow from a prophylaxis indication without diagnosed VTE.

questions.explanation: The total course is counted from the operation, with the treating team accounting for any interruption. Discharge and partial walking recovery do not automatically end a selected extended-prophylaxis indication. This is prevention, not treatment of a diagnosed clot.

questions.stem: Which minimum preoperative interruption should {patientName} record for his current medicine?

answerChoices.label: Withhold the current medicine at least four days beforehand
answerChoices.rationale: The actual current drug has a four-day label minimum when possible.

answerChoices.label: Withhold the current medicine at least three days beforehand
answerChoices.rationale: This carries empagliflozin instructions forward after the actual drug changed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This carries empagliflozin instructions forward after the actual drug changed.

answerChoices.label: Withhold the current medicine from the operative morning
answerChoices.rationale: A morning-only omission does not address this drug-specific fasting risk plan.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A morning-only omission does not address this drug-specific fasting risk plan.

questions.explanation: Reconcile the current bottle, not just the old calendar. U.S. labels distinguish empagliflozin (at least three days) and ertugliflozin (at least four days), when possible, before surgery or prolonged fasting.

questions.stem: Which medication-associated complication best fits {patientName} at the earlier admission?

answerChoices.label: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis
answerChoices.rationale: Acidemia, low bicarbonate and marked ketone elevation form the pattern despite modest glucose; fasting and SGLT2 exposure fit the association.

answerChoices.label: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis
answerChoices.rationale: The lactate does not account for the supplied acid-base abnormality and ketone excess.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The lactate does not account for the supplied acid-base abnormality and ketone excess.

answerChoices.label: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
answerChoices.rationale: The glucose and marked ketone-associated acidemia do not fit a predominantly hyperosmolar hyperglycemic presentation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The glucose and marked ketone-associated acidemia do not fit a predominantly hyperosmolar hyperglycemic presentation.

questions.explanation: Interpret the pH, bicarbonate and ketones together. A modest glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis during SGLT2 exposure. This association warrants urgent hospital evaluation of the episode and other contributors; it does not prove a unique cause.

questions.stem: Which empagliflozin instruction fits {patientName} at the later recovery review?

answerChoices.label: Continue withholding empagliflozin during meal intolerance
answerChoices.rationale: Resolution of acidosis does not establish resumed oral intake when meals still cause vomiting.

answerChoices.label: Resume empagliflozin with the next retained meal
answerChoices.rationale: A planned or single retained meal does not establish recovery when the current record shows repeated meal intolerance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A planned or single retained meal does not establish recovery when the current record shows repeated meal intolerance.

answerChoices.label: Resume empagliflozin after the next fasting glucose check
answerChoices.rationale: Glucose does not measure recovery of oral intake or resolve the current fasting risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Glucose does not measure recovery of oral intake or resolve the current fasting risk.

questions.explanation: Recheck present clinical stability and oral intake after the acute episode. Resolved acidosis and a glucose rise do not override continuing meal intolerance. The eventual restart remains a treating-team decision.

questions.stem: Which investigation should {patientName} undergo next to clarify these preoperative findings?

answerChoices.label: Arterial blood-gas analysis
answerChoices.rationale: The combined obesity, breathing history and persistent bicarbonate/oxygenation observations raise an awake ventilation question that requires PaCO2 assessment.

answerChoices.label: Attended overnight polysomnography
answerChoices.rationale: A sleep study addresses nocturnal disease but does not replace assessing the current awake ventilation concern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A sleep study addresses nocturnal disease but does not replace assessing the current awake ventilation concern.

answerChoices.label: Overnight pulse-oximetry recording
answerChoices.rationale: An oxygen trace does not measure awake arterial carbon dioxide.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An oxygen trace does not measure awake arterial carbon dioxide.

questions.explanation: The clinical combination raises suspicion for awake hypoventilation. Measure arterial carbon dioxide rather than diagnose it from bicarbonate or dismiss it because daytime dozing is limited. Sleep-disordered breathing still needs its own assessment.

questions.stem: Which request should {patientName} send with the hospital preoperative referral?

answerChoices.label: Plan anaesthesia and postoperative observation using suspected OSA risk
answerChoices.rationale: The risk report and breathing history remain relevant despite limited daytime sleepiness; confirmation is a different question.

answerChoices.label: Defer all perioperative planning until diagnostic polysomnography
answerChoices.rationale: This makes diagnostic confirmation a prerequisite for planning on current risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This makes diagnostic confirmation a prerequisite for planning on current risk.

answerChoices.label: Use the usual pathway based on the sleepiness report
answerChoices.rationale: A sleepiness report does not cancel witnessed breathing pauses or the separate apnoea-risk assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A sleepiness report does not cancel witnessed breathing pauses or the separate apnoea-risk assessment.

questions.explanation: Sleepiness and apnoea probability measure different things. Communicate suspected risk now so the actual hospital team can plan anaesthesia and recovery; neither a screen nor this question grants a confirmed diagnosis or unrestricted clearance.

questions.stem: Which disposition best fits {patientName} while these recovery episodes continue?

answerChoices.label: Continue recovery in a hospital setting with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated events during unstimulated observation represent continuing risk despite a reassuring conversation.

answerChoices.label: Discharge home using his usual positive-airway-pressure treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Usual treatment has not controlled the currently observed postoperative events.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Usual treatment has not controlled the currently observed postoperative events.

answerChoices.label: Discharge home with supplemental oxygen during sleep
answerChoices.rationale: An oxygen prescription does not establish resolution of recurrent obstruction or remove the need for an appropriate monitored assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An oxygen prescription does not establish resolution of recurrent obstruction or remove the need for an appropriate monitored assessment.

questions.explanation: Assess the unstimulated course, not just the response to conversation. Continuing postoperative respiratory events can make an unmonitored discharge inappropriate even when usual home PAP is available.

questions.stem: Which assessment should be added to {patientName}'s preoperative evaluation?

answerChoices.label: Validated frailty assessment across function and other domains
answerChoices.rationale: The observed changes extend beyond knee pain and diagnosis count. A validated multidomain assessment characterizes reserve for planning.

answerChoices.label: Orthopedic assessment focused on knee-related mobility
answerChoices.rationale: The knee deserves care, but an isolated mobility assessment does not account for medication support and decline on comfortable days.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The knee deserves care, but an isolated mobility assessment does not account for medication support and decline on comfortable days.

answerChoices.label: Cardiac assessment focused on exercise-induced ischemia
answerChoices.rationale: Limited walking does not by itself establish ischemic symptoms or replace assessment of the broader decline.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Limited walking does not by itself establish ischemic symptoms or replace assessment of the broader decline.

questions.explanation: A short diagnosis list does not exclude loss of reserve. Interpret the actual trajectory across domains, then characterize it with a validated assessment rather than assign frailty from age or a knee complaint.

questions.stem: Which discharge-support request best fits {patientName}'s later hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Arrange supervised rehabilitation and reassess home transfers and steps
answerChoices.rationale: A level walk with a therapist does not establish the tasks needed to manage at home without daytime assistance.

answerChoices.label: Arrange home discharge with the daughter's evening assistance
answerChoices.rationale: Evening help does not cover the represented daytime transfer and entrance needs.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Evening help does not cover the represented daytime transfer and entrance needs.

answerChoices.label: Arrange home discharge with intermittent therapy visits
answerChoices.rationale: Intermittent visits do not cover the documented person-assisted transfers needed between visits.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Intermittent visits do not cover the documented person-assisted transfers needed between visits.

questions.explanation: Read function against what was actually attempted. Supported corridor walking does not establish independent transfers or entrance steps. Ask for a support plan that covers current needs and reassesses recovery rather than assuming a periodic visit supplies continuous assistance.

questions.stem: Which scheduled medicine should {patientName}'s team remove from this prevention plan?

answerChoices.label: Remove the bedtime diphenhydramine
answerChoices.rationale: Its anticholinergic exposure adds a preventable cognitive risk in this older vulnerable patient; no separate allergy indication is supplied.

answerChoices.label: Remove the scheduled acetaminophen
answerChoices.rationale: Undertreated pain can contribute to delirium; this plan has a current analgesic purpose.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Undertreated pain can contribute to delirium; this plan has a current analgesic purpose.

answerChoices.label: Remove the opioid-associated senna
answerChoices.rationale: Bowel care has a stated role during opioid exposure; it is not the anticholinergic sleep order.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bowel care has a stated role during opioid exposure; it is not the anticholinergic sleep order.

questions.explanation: A prevention bundle can still contain a conflicting medication order. Review the actual indication and anticholinergic exposure while retaining appropriate pain and bowel care.
