questions.stem: Which investigation should {patientName}'s hospital team prioritize for this new episode?

answerChoices.label: Bedside postvoid bladder ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: Acute fluctuating inattention warrants cause assessment; small voids do not exclude retention when postvoid lower-abdominal fullness persists.

answerChoices.label: Noncontrast head CT
answerChoices.rationale: The local urinary observations identify a current targeted question; no focal finding or head-injury history is supplied to prioritize CT.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The local urinary observations identify a current targeted question; no focal finding or head-injury history is supplied to prioritize CT.

answerChoices.label: Electroencephalography
answerChoices.rationale: The voiding/examination observations warrant assessment before choosing a seizure investigation for this course.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The voiding/examination observations warrant assessment before choosing a seizure investigation for this course.

questions.explanation: Quiet behavior can still be an acute delirium pattern. Interpret the postvoid fullness and small-volume voids, then assess residual bladder volume. This does not establish urinary retention as the only contributor.

questions.stem: Which ART plan should {patientName}'s team have used during that documented interval?

answerChoices.label: Coordinate temporary interruption of the complete oral regimen
answerChoices.rationale: When the complete regimen cannot be delivered despite route review, expert-coordinated interruption avoids unplanned partial treatment.

answerChoices.label: Continue the regimen components that can be obtained separately
answerChoices.rationale: Availability of individual agents does not establish an effective complete regimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Availability of individual agents does not establish an effective complete regimen.

answerChoices.label: Continue the complete regimen with repeated tube dosing
answerChoices.rationale: The actual repeated vomiting and return of administered tablets show that repeated dosing is not reliable delivery of the regimen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The actual repeated vomiting and return of administered tablets show that repeated dosing is not reliable delivery of the regimen.

questions.explanation: Avoid routine interruption when ART can be delivered. Here actual route and formulation review establishes an unavoidable interval, so coordinate the complete-regimen plan with the HIV clinician rather than improvise partial treatment.

questions.stem: Which investigation should {patientName} undergo next for the new incision-site fullness?

answerChoices.label: Targeted ultrasound at the incision site
answerChoices.rationale: The current focused question is fluid versus soft tissue at a new superficial postoperative target.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic mammography of the affected breast
answerChoices.rationale: The uncertain superficial postoperative collection is better characterized initially by targeted ultrasound; prior mammography predates it.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The uncertain superficial postoperative collection is better characterized initially by targeted ultrasound; prior mammography predates it.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the affected breast
answerChoices.rationale: The focused superficial question has not exhausted targeted ultrasound; advanced imaging is not selected by postoperative status itself.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The focused superficial question has not exhausted targeted ultrasound; advanced imaging is not selected by postoperative status itself.

questions.explanation: The target is new and postoperative, so the old acquisition cannot characterize it. Targeted ultrasound addresses the fluid-versus-soft-tissue question before a more extensive imaging pathway.

questions.stem: Which management plan best fits {patientName} after the later review?

answerChoices.label: Clinical observation with reassessment for new symptoms
answerChoices.rationale: The current collection is simple and causes no meaningful symptom, wound effect or functional limitation.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with clinical reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent palpability alone does not establish benefit from aspiration when symptoms and wound effects have resolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Persistent palpability alone does not establish benefit from aspiration when symptoms and wound effects have resolved.

answerChoices.label: Antibiotic treatment with clinical reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: No clinical infection signal is represented; antibiotics do not remove a simple uninfected fluid pocket.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No clinical infection signal is represented; antibiotics do not remove a simple uninfected fluid pocket.

questions.explanation: Interpret the current clinical effect of the collection. Persistence does not equal an intervention indication when discomfort and limitation resolve and the wound remains uncompromised. A new symptom, wound change or infection concern warrants reassessment.

questions.stem: Which of {patientName}'s recorded events supports an allergic-like contrast-reaction entry?

answerChoices.label: The generalized wheal event at examination B
answerChoices.rationale: The actual distribution and morphology support an allergic-like pattern; a later local event does not erase it.

answerChoices.label: The transient warmth event at examination A
answerChoices.rationale: Isolated resolved warmth can be physiologic/chemotoxic and does not establish the allergic-like pattern described in B.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Isolated resolved warmth can be physiologic/chemotoxic and does not establish the allergic-like pattern described in B.

answerChoices.label: The focal injection-site event at examination C
answerChoices.rationale: Local leakage and swelling describe extravasation; this does not replace the separate generalized wheal history.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local leakage and swelling describe extravasation; this does not replace the separate generalized wheal history.

questions.explanation: Reconstruct each exposure separately. The generalized wheals support an allergic-like history, while isolated warmth and focal leakage describe different events. This classification does not prove IgE causation or select a premedication regimen.

questions.stem: Which next action best fits {patientName} at that earlier CT decision point?

answerChoices.label: Obtain urgent hand-surgical assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive tense swelling, sensory change and marked pain after extravasation require urgent severity-based surgical assessment.

answerChoices.label: Continue elevation with serial injection-site assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Conservative care fits mild stable injuries, but the actual course has progressed despite that initial care.

answerChoices.label: Treat the episode with systemic antihistamine therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The current episode is a progressive local leakage injury; a separate prior hives event does not establish that this is a systemic reaction.

questions.explanation: Interpret the worsening local course after initial care, then escalate for threatened tissue assessment. Keep the prior hives event separately documented; this item prescribes no pressure cutoff, contrast-volume trigger or operation.

questions.stem: Which allergy-evaluation plan fits {patientName}'s retrieved reaction history?

answerChoices.label: Retain the reaction record and refer to a drug-allergy specialist
answerChoices.rationale: Blistering, mucosal injury and organ involvement are severe delayed-reaction features outside routine skin-test or direct-challenge pathways.

answerChoices.label: Perform penicillin skin testing followed by an oral challenge
answerChoices.rationale: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is not the routine evaluation route for the represented severe delayed reaction.

answerChoices.label: Perform a supervised direct oral amoxicillin challenge
answerChoices.rationale: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A remote date does not make severe delayed mucosal/organ injury a low-risk history.

questions.explanation: Interpret the retrieved phenotype rather than the short allergy header. Severe delayed features change testing eligibility. Retain the history and obtain specialist assessment; no challenge protocol or perioperative antibiotic is chosen here.

questions.stem: Which preoperative cardiac-evaluation strategy best fits {patientName}'s planned procedure?

answerChoices.label: Clinical assessment without additional ischemia testing
answerChoices.rationale: Unknown walking capacity does not establish a stress-testing indication before this low-risk procedure without symptoms.

answerChoices.label: Pharmacologic stress echocardiography before the procedure
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Avoiding exercise does not make stress imaging useful when the procedure and current clinical assessment do not justify it.

answerChoices.label: Coronary CT angiography before the procedure
answerChoices.rationale: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An anatomic coronary study does not solve the lack of a testing indication in this low-risk setting.

questions.explanation: Decide whether testing is indicated before choosing how to test. An orthopedic limitation and a low-risk local procedure do not create an independent ischemia-testing indication.

questions.stem: Which cardiac investigation should be prioritized for {patientName}'s changed preoperative status?

answerChoices.label: Transthoracic echocardiography
answerChoices.rationale: New dyspnea and congestion findings warrant reassessment of ventricular function despite the old normal study.

answerChoices.label: Pharmacologic myocardial perfusion imaging
answerChoices.rationale: The immediate question is new ventricular dysfunction/congestion; stress testing is not the first substitute for resolving that state.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The immediate question is new ventricular dysfunction/congestion; stress testing is not the first substitute for resolving that state.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory ECG rhythm monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: There is no rhythm-symptom pattern supplied to make a prolonged rhythm study the prioritized assessment of these new findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: There is no rhythm-symptom pattern supplied to make a prolonged rhythm study the prioritized assessment of these new findings.

questions.explanation: Interpret the changed symptoms and examination, then choose a study of ventricular function. A prior normal result is not current evidence when the clinical state has changed. This is evaluation of a possible active cardiac problem, not routine screening.

questions.stem: Which lisinopril plan best fits {patientName} before the rescheduled operation?

answerChoices.label: Continue the tolerated lisinopril with the perioperative team
answerChoices.rationale: Continuation is reasonable for compensated HFrEF with stable tolerance; the hypertension-only omission rule is not universal across indications.

answerChoices.label: Omit lisinopril for the preoperative interval
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary omission can be reasonable in selected controlled-hypertension patients, but this record establishes a different indication and stable tolerance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Temporary omission can be reasonable in selected controlled-hypertension patients, but this record establishes a different indication and stable tolerance.

answerChoices.label: Increase lisinopril for the preoperative interval
answerChoices.rationale: Neither the operation nor unchanged reduced systolic function establishes a need for immediate dose escalation after a stable response.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neither the operation nor unchanged reduced systolic function establishes a need for immediate dose escalation after a stable response.

questions.explanation: Interpret the response as compensated clinical status, then use why the medicine is prescribed. Continuing tolerated chronic RAAS therapy is reasonable in HFrEF; a selected hypertension omission policy is not a blanket drug-class instruction.

questions.stem: Which preparation plan best fits {patientName} before the abdominal operation?

answerChoices.label: Defer the elective operation for valve-team assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Severe valve measurements plus exertional presyncope warrant evaluation for valve intervention before nonurgent surgery.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with the operation and perioperative surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.

answerChoices.label: Defer the operation for dobutamine stress testing
answerChoices.rationale: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.

questions.explanation: The measurements and exertional presyncope support a symptomatic severe aortic stenosis concern despite preserved systolic function. Arrange valve-team assessment before the nonurgent major operation rather than treat surveillance as a substitute.

questions.stem: Which scheduling and antiplatelet plan best fits {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Defer elective repair and retain the cardiology antiplatelet plan
answerChoices.rationale: This nonurgent repair would interrupt antiplatelet treatment early after DES PCI for ACS; defer and coordinate timing rather than create an avoidable early interruption.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with elective repair after interrupting clopidogrel
answerChoices.rationale: A short surgical hold does not resolve the early post-ACS stent-risk problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A short surgical hold does not resolve the early post-ACS stent-risk problem.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with elective repair after substituting therapeutic heparin
answerChoices.rationale: Therapeutic heparin is not a substitute for the coronary-stent antiplatelet strategy.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Therapeutic heparin is not a substitute for the coronary-stent antiplatelet strategy.

questions.explanation: The clinical question is whether to create an elective antiplatelet interruption now. After DES PCI for ACS, the guideline ideally defers elective surgery requiring interruption for at least twelve months; urgent or time-sensitive surgery requires a separate team assessment.

questions.stem: Which follow-up request best fits {patientName}'s recorded cardiac event?

answerChoices.label: Arrange cardiovascular review and risk-factor optimization
answerChoices.rationale: A documented ischemic injury can merit follow-up even without reported chest pain.

answerChoices.label: Retain routine surgical follow-up with no cardiac review
answerChoices.rationale: Absence of pain does not erase a documented ischemic postoperative troponin event.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Absence of pain does not erase a documented ischemic postoperative troponin event.

answerChoices.label: Arrange immediate invasive coronary angiography from clinic
answerChoices.rationale: The resolved event and current asymptomatic state do not independently establish an acute invasive indication or plaque rupture.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The resolved event and current asymptomatic state do not independently establish an acute invasive indication or plaque rupture.

questions.explanation: Use the hospital's completed attribution and current clinical phase. A silent ischemic postoperative injury can justify cardiovascular follow-up; it does not by itself prove plaque rupture or select immediate angiography or an antithrombotic regimen.

questions.stem: Which preparation plan best fits {patientName} before this elective procedure?

answerChoices.label: Defer the procedure for prescriber and anaesthesia reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Significant symptoms and poor intake require reassessment before a nonurgent procedure; a completed hold clock does not establish readiness.

answerChoices.label: Proceed once the calendar-based medication hold is complete
answerChoices.rationale: Elapsed time does not establish symptom resolution or gastric-emptying readiness in this symptomatic patient.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Elapsed time does not establish symptom resolution or gastric-emptying readiness in this symptomatic patient.

answerChoices.label: Proceed after premedication with ondansetron
answerChoices.rationale: Reducing nausea does not establish that the unresolved intake/emptying concern has resolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reducing nausea does not establish that the unresolved intake/emptying concern has resolved.

questions.explanation: Recognize the significant current symptoms, then apply the nonurgent setting. Reassess with the prescribing and anaesthesia teams before proceeding. This tests a shared severe-symptom boundary, not a universal GLP-1 hold or fasting duration.

authorChecks.apply: Use the new-exposure boundary rather than the continuation recommendation.

authorChecks.counterfactual: If dispensing and administration instead confirmed stable tolerated daily use, giving the usual dose would become appropriate.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The exposure discrepancy changes the answer. The current symptom/indication statement prevents an acute indication from overriding the elective rule; no arbitrary pulse cutoff is used.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Removed the legacy stable/well-tolerated conclusion and dose-doubling foil. All choices are specific instructions; the key is not longer than both competitors. No future case feedback is visible.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Three operative-day medication instructions.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: A familiar continuation rule competes with the less obvious need to establish actual exposure.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no earlier continuation explanation rehearses the answer.
authorChecks.limitation: One guideline; no exact starting dose or titration schedule. New construct gets a separate history.

optionAudit.temptation: Reconcile actual administration before applying a continuation rule.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The record shows new exposure rather than continuation. With no immediate indication, surgery-day initiation for risk reduction is inappropriate.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The documented absence of ongoing exposure applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Apply the chronic-continuation rule to a stale list.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This treats a historical prescription as evidence of current tolerance.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Verified ongoing stable use with current tolerance would support giving the usual dose.

optionAudit.temptation: Recognize new exposure but assume the old prescription establishes a current initiation indication.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A stale prescription without a current treatment indication does not require delaying an otherwise planned operation to create new beta-blocker exposure.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A verified new treatment indication with time for tolerability assessment could require a revised elective preparation plan.

authorChecks.interpret: A major bowel resection and AF without represented prior embolic events are distinct inputs.
authorChecks.apply: Interrupt therapeutic warfarin without automatically adding a treatment-dose bridge.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: The anticoagulant indication is AF, with the documented thromboembolic history shown.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the operation were canceled and no procedure or new bleeding problem remained, continuing the established therapeutic warfarin regimen would replace perioperative interruption.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The operation makes uninterrupted warfarin a meaningful competitor; the indication/history distinguishes interruption from bridging. The prior beta-blocker story is removed.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Deleted the legacy sentence announcing that interruption is required and the permanent-cessation caricature. Three concrete anticoagulation plans answer the same task.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Preoperative therapeutic anticoagulation, not a matrix of pre- and postoperative phases.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The credible error is unnecessary treatment-dose bridging during an anticipated low-INR interval.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; frozen N2 order reconciliation is not appended.
authorChecks.limitation: No high-risk bridging exception is keyed or resolved; CHEST and AHA scope differences are preserved. No exact interruption timing.

optionAudit.temptation: Separate procedural interruption from thromboembolic indication.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Temporary interruption for major surgery does not create a routine therapeutic-bridging indication for this AF history.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The represented AF and operation apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat any subtherapeutic interval as requiring a bridge.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This adds treatment-level anticoagulation despite the represented AF indication, increasing bleeding exposure without the routine benefit assumed.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A different very-high-risk thrombotic indication would require specialist assessment; this option is not endorsed as an automatic exception.

optionAudit.temptation: Generalize an uninterrupted plan from minor procedures.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The bleeding implications of major resection differ from a minor low-bleeding-risk procedure.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A low-bleeding-risk procedure with a supported uninterrupted-warfarin protocol would be a different decision.

authorChecks.interpret: New bloody drainage plus falling hemoglobin represents current bleeding risk, not just a drain being present.
authorChecks.apply: Choose mechanical prevention while the bleeding question is resolved.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Active blood loss at this decision point.
authorChecks.counterfactual: With controlled bleeding and a stable hemostatic review, the persistent cancer-surgery/immobility risk would favor adding pharmacologic prevention.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Removing the bleeding trajectory makes the pharmacologic option reasonable. No drain-volume cutoff or fabricated risk score.
authorChecks.cueAttack: All options include reassessment; the key is not uniquely cautious. The stem does not announce high bleeding risk or name compression.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Three prevention strategies before any established VTE.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: Cancer and immobility make LMWH tempting; the resident must update a competing risk.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: First chart timepoint; later hemostatic findings and duration are not shown.
authorChecks.limitation: Guideline recommendations conditional; this is not acute VTE treatment.

optionAudit.temptation: Account for present bleeding rather than only a static risk label.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Current bleeding can outweigh the immediate pharmacologic-prevention benefit; mechanical prevention is retained while that balance changes.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Active bleeding and no established VTE apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Use the thrombotic-risk finding without updating bleeding risk.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The cancer operation and immobility support prevention, but active blood loss changes the immediate balance.
optionAudit.correctUnder: After hemostasis and reassessment establish acceptable bleeding risk, pharmacologic prophylaxis may be appropriate.

optionAudit.temptation: Substitute an invasive preventive device for a temporarily contraindicated drug.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: An inability to give prophylactic anticoagulation does not itself establish an IVC-filter indication without VTE.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Established acute VTE with an anticoagulation contraindication is a different specialist treatment problem.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: The bleeding trajectory has changed; immobility has not.
authorChecks.apply: Restore pharmacologic prevention rather than escalate to treatment or preserve the old hold.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Completed source control with serial stability and explicit hemostatic assessment.
authorChecks.counterfactual: Renewed bloody output and falling hemoglobin would return the balance toward the mechanical plan during reassessment.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Deleting this update leaves the earlier bleeding contraindication in force. Every trend establishes whether that constraint changed.
authorChecks.cueAttack: No fixed waiting period or statement that she is eligible for LMWH. Three specific intensity/route plans; the first feedback did not state this later answer.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Prevention/intensity adjustment at the later review.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: Requires reversing an initially correct decision after actual new evidence.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Earlier feedback explains conditional bleeding balance, not the later regimen. New hemostatic observations earn the second node.
authorChecks.limitation: No exact safe-start time, dose or renal adjustment specified.

optionAudit.temptation: Reassess the original contraindication at the current phase.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The temporary bleeding constraint has changed while the major cancer operation and restricted mobility remain.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The documented hemostatic course and persisting VTE risk apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat a temporary drug hold as a continuing contraindication.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This carries the earlier active-bleeding decision forward despite its documented resolution.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Recurrent bleeding or another current anticoagulant contraindication would favor this plan.

optionAudit.temptation: Confuse high prevention risk with an established clot.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Ongoing prevention risk does not establish a treatment-dose indication.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A newly established VTE would change the decision to a treatment pathway.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Partial mobility recovery at discharge is not restored baseline mobility; no VTE has appeared.
authorChecks.apply: Choose an extended total prophylactic course rather than a discharge endpoint or treatment duration.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Major cancer resection with persistent restricted mobility and current LMWH tolerance.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If discharge followed a lower-risk operation with full mobility and no extended-course indication, stopping at discharge could be appropriate.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Current tolerance and no recurrent bleed prevent the earlier hemorrhage from remaining an unresolved contraindication. No irrelevant antibiotic/drain story remains.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Removed indefinite therapy foil and the authored high-VTE-risk conclusion. All options give total-course endpoints, with no uniquely qualified key.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Duration of an already selected agent.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The closest error mistakes discharge and walking a little for risk resolution.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Earlier nodes do not teach an exact duration. The discharge update resolves current tolerance and preserves a separate duration inference.
authorChecks.limitation: LMWH is an established option, not the only contemporary drug; no dose or universal cancer-surgery mandate.

optionAudit.temptation: Use operation type, mobility and current tolerance together.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Selected high-risk abdominopelvic cancer-surgery patients can receive an extended total postoperative course when bleeding risk is acceptable.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The current risk/bleeding context applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Use discharge as a surrogate for risk resolution.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Leaving the hospital does not mean the operation-related VTE risk and mobility impairment have ended.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A lower-risk procedure/patient without an extended-course indication would be a different plan.

optionAudit.temptation: Confuse postoperative prevention with clot treatment.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A treatment-length course does not follow from a prophylaxis indication without diagnosed VTE.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A diagnosed VTE would require a separate evidence-supported treatment-duration decision.

authorChecks.apply: Recognize the SGLT2 warning despite the modest glucose and postoperative intake restriction.

authorChecks.limitation: Counterfactual is a changed whole metabolic record, not a claim that one lactate proves drug causality.

optionAudit.temptation: Interpret the metabolic findings before using glucose as reassurance.

optionAudit.correctUnder: The supplied ketone/acidosis pattern and exposure apply.

optionAudit.correctUnder: Marked lactate elevation during metformin exposure with a compatible clinical cause would redirect the medication-associated concern.

optionAudit.correctUnder: Marked hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality with minimal ketone-associated acidosis would support that alternative.

optionAudit.correctUnder: Current meal intolerance persists.

authorChecks.cueAttack: Three named dose instructions. No exact BP threshold or “all medicines available” permission. The question does not say the sheet is wrong.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Chronic medicine continuation/temporary adjustment, not acute heart-failure treatment.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: A familiar anesthesia instruction competes with an indication-specific exception and actual treatment response.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: First feedback asks for evaluation only. The new EF, actual response and medicine indication are needed for this separate decision.
authorChecks.limitation: One guideline with conditional advice; no universal policy or exact dose. The treating team can change the plan for new instability.

optionAudit.temptation: Reconcile indication and response, not just drug class.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Continuation is reasonable for compensated HFrEF with stable tolerance; the hypertension-only omission rule is not universal across indications.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Current compensated HFrEF and stable monitoring apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Apply an indication-specific hypotension-reduction policy to every RAAS prescription.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Temporary omission can be reasonable in selected controlled-hypertension patients, but this record establishes a different indication and stable tolerance.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Controlled hypertension without HFrEF before an elevated-risk operation could support the selected omission plan.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat a persistently abnormal EF as proof the current perioperative dose is inadequate.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Neither the operation nor unchanged reduced systolic function establishes a need for immediate dose escalation after a stable response.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An outpatient heart-failure titration decision with a documented remaining indication and monitoring would be a separate stage.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Use the actual area/gradient/velocity pattern and exertional symptom, rather than a supplied severe-AS label.
authorChecks.apply: Change preparation to valve evaluation before a nonurgent major operation.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Exertional presyncope accompanies severe high-gradient measurements.
authorChecks.counterfactual: With no symptoms, preserved function and a low-risk planned procedure, proceeding with an appropriate perioperative plan could become reasonable.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Preserved EF sustains the competing reassurance error; urgency determines whether deferral is feasible. Every echo value is concordant, not an extra unrelated workup.
authorChecks.cueAttack: Three actual preparation plans. The task does not announce a safety hazard. Numeric findings are constructed patient values interpreted using directly sourced thresholds.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Preoperative preparation, not valve procedure selection.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: Preserved EF can be mistaken for absence of perioperative valve risk.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no preceding valve interpretation supplies the diagnosis.
authorChecks.limitation: One current primary guideline; no TAVR-versus-SAVR rank, exact delay or invented valve cutoff. The stress-test counterfactual remains specialist scope.

optionAudit.temptation: Integrate symptoms and valve physiology rather than rely on preserved EF.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Severe valve measurements plus exertional presyncope warrant evaluation for valve intervention before nonurgent surgery.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The severe symptomatic findings apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Generalize an asymptomatic low-risk-surgery pathway.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Preserved EF does not cancel the severe symptomatic valve problem before a nonurgent major operation.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An asymptomatic patient with preserved function undergoing a low-risk procedure can represent a different supported pathway.

optionAudit.temptation: Use another test instead of acting on adequate measured valve evidence.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This clear high-gradient symptomatic pattern does not require a stress study to establish the represented severe valve problem.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Discordant low-flow/low-gradient findings may create a separate specialist diagnostic question; no stress protocol is prescribed here.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: The stent treated ACS and the current hernia has no urgent complication.
authorChecks.apply: Defer elective interruption rather than choose a hold schedule or heparin substitute.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Only six weeks have elapsed after DES PCI for an infarction, while the repair is nonurgent.
authorChecks.counterfactual: After an appropriately reviewed later interval meeting the guideline timing and with a cardiology-supported interruption plan, the proceed-after-interruption option could become reasonable.
authorChecks.deletionTest: The PCI indication and timing distinguish the decision; the hernia urgency is necessary to support deferral, not a convenience permission.
authorChecks.cueAttack: All choices pair timing and medication strategy; the key is no more comprehensive. No twelve-month answer is disclosed in the task.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Elective scheduling and antiplatelet plan at one timepoint.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The credible error focuses on how to hold clopidogrel before deciding whether elective interruption should occur.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no anticoagulant-bridge companion repeats the answer.
authorChecks.limitation: One guideline; no actual hold duration, antiplatelet dose or bridging protocol authored.

optionAudit.temptation: Use the stent indication and surgical urgency together.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: This nonurgent repair would interrupt antiplatelet treatment early after DES PCI for ACS; defer and coordinate timing rather than create an avoidable early interruption.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The recent ACS stent and nonurgent operation apply.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat interruption duration as the only timing question.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A short surgical hold does not resolve the early post-ACS stent-risk problem.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A later appropriately reviewed interval after DES PCI with a supported interruption plan could allow surgery.

optionAudit.temptation: Apply anticoagulant bridging logic to platelet-dependent stent protection.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Therapeutic heparin is not a substitute for the coronary-stent antiplatelet strategy.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A separate anticoagulant indication can require its own plan; it would not replace this antiplatelet decision.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Distinguish a documented rise/fall attributed to ischemic injury from an expected harmless postoperative label.
authorChecks.apply: Select follow-up appropriate to a resolved event rather than dismiss it or treat it as a current acute coronary presentation.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Completed hospital assessment attributes the dynamic biomarker event to ischemic injury.
authorChecks.counterfactual: If the completed assessment instead established an analytical artifact with no cardiac disease indication, routine surgical follow-up could suffice.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Attribution is needed to avoid calling every troponin rise MINS; the current symptom-free phase separates follow-up from acute invasive evaluation.
authorChecks.cueAttack: The diagnosis is supplied only because follow-up is the objective. Three concrete referral strategies; no vague individualized-plan key.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Follow-up referral intensity after a resolved event.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: The resident must avoid both silent-event dismissal and reflex acute angiography.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Does not ask the same event's diagnosis after supplying its interpretation.
authorChecks.limitation: One guideline; hospital attribution is a constructed prerequisite, not independent proof. No routine drug regimen or surveillance schedule.

optionAudit.temptation: Use the event assessment rather than the copied reassuring label.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: A documented ischemic injury can merit follow-up even without reported chest pain.
optionAudit.correctUnder: The hospital-attributed ischemic injury applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat a silent event as clinically irrelevant.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Absence of pain does not erase a documented ischemic postoperative troponin event.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An adequately evaluated nonischemic or artifactual result without another cardiac indication would require a different follow-up decision.

optionAudit.temptation: Equate any troponin rise with a current type-1 infarction pathway.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: The resolved event and current asymptomatic state do not independently establish an acute invasive indication or plaque rupture.
optionAudit.correctUnder: New acute ischemic symptoms or another acute coronary indication would require urgent reassessment in the appropriate setting.

authorChecks.authorDisposition: Ready for independent scrutiny; author checks confer no PASS
authorChecks.interpret: Repeated vomiting and inability to retain meals during dose escalation are more than mild fullness.
authorChecks.apply: Defer nonurgent preparation for reassessment rather than use a clock or symptom-suppression shortcut.
authorChecks.decidingObservation: Significant symptoms persist, and the operation is nonurgent.
authorChecks.counterfactual: With sustained usual intake, no significant symptoms and a current agreed preparation plan, proceeding on the agreed schedule could become reasonable.
authorChecks.deletionTest: Without actual symptoms the old schedule question enters disputed asymptomatic policies. Urgency is essential to support deferral.
authorChecks.cueAttack: No quoted safety rule, exact hold interval or named missing test. Three preparation plans with similar scope; none depends on a newly available device.
authorChecks.stageAudit: Readiness/preparation before one elective procedure.
authorChecks.difficultyReason: An old holding rule and an antiemetic can each seem to solve a different problem than actual readiness.
authorChecks.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no future gastric ultrasound result or postoperative recovery is exposed.
authorChecks.limitation: Fasting/hold policies disagree across sources and remain withheld; no medication washout, fasting interval or exact gastric threshold.

optionAudit.temptation: Use actual response and urgency rather than an old universal schedule.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Significant symptoms and poor intake require reassessment before a nonurgent procedure; a completed hold clock does not establish readiness.
optionAudit.correctUnder: Current repeated vomiting during escalation applies.

optionAudit.temptation: Treat one historical holding rule as a complete risk assessment.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Elapsed time does not establish symptom resolution or gastric-emptying readiness in this symptomatic patient.
optionAudit.correctUnder: A clinically stable asymptomatic patient with a current team-approved plan would support proceeding on that agreed schedule.

optionAudit.temptation: Substitute symptom suppression for assessment of the actual perioperative concern.
optionAudit.whyRankedHere: Reducing nausea does not establish that the unresolved intake/emptying concern has resolved.
optionAudit.correctUnder: An independently assessed transient nausea indication could merit an antiemetic without being a surgery-readiness test.

parkedAttempts.name: Daniel Price
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after recovery from an outside hospital operation. The founder reviews an episode of fluctuating inattention and visual misperceptions with repeated attempts to climb over bed rails and remove a fresh drain. Reorientation, family presence and de-escalation had failed. Pain, oxygenation, glucose and bladder distension had been addressed. He had no regular alcohol or benzodiazepine exposure, Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia or recorded QT prolongation.

nodes.objective: Distinguish dangerous nonwithdrawal agitation after nonpharmacologic measures from routine delirium or withdrawal treatment.
nodes.task: Which symptom-directed medicine best fits Daniel at that recorded decision point?

choices.label: Cautiously titrated haloperidol
choices.rationale: A short symptom-directed antipsychotic can be considered for dangerous agitation after nonpharmacologic measures fail, with contraindications assessed.
choices.temptation: Use the severe-symptom boundary without calling the drug a delirium cure.
choices.correctUnder: The current danger and prior measures apply.

choices.label: Cautiously titrated lorazepam
choices.rationale: No withdrawal indication is represented; benzodiazepines are not the routine first-line response to this delirium pattern.
choices.temptation: Generalize the withdrawal exception to all postoperative agitation.
choices.correctUnder: A documented benzodiazepine or alcohol interruption with a compatible withdrawal course would change the indication.

choices.label: Cautiously titrated diphenhydramine
choices.rationale: An anticholinergic sedating drug can worsen cognitive risk and does not address this delirium indication.
choices.temptation: Substitute a familiar sleep/sedation medicine for a symptom-specific plan.
choices.correctUnder: A separate histamine-mediated allergic indication would be a different therapeutic task, not treatment of delirium.

nodes.explanation: First distinguish immediate danger after failed de-escalation from routine quiet delirium, then check the withdrawal history and contraindications. Antipsychotic use here is short and symptom-directed, with low-certainty evidence; cause-directed care continues.

gate.interpret: Danger persists despite actual nonpharmacologic and cause-directed measures; no withdrawal exposure is present.
gate.apply: Consider a cautious short antipsychotic strategy rather than a withdrawal drug or anticholinergic sedative.
gate.decidingObservation: Absent regular alcohol/benzodiazepine exposure distinguishes the withdrawal exception.
gate.counterfactual: A verified abrupt interruption of chronic benzodiazepine use with compatible withdrawal findings would favor benzodiazepine treatment of that driver.
gate.deletionTest: Danger and failed measures establish the medication stage; exposure history separates lorazepam. Contraindication negatives are necessary, not decorative exclusions.
gate.cueAttack: All labels use the same cautious-titration grammar. No generic safe-plan option. No new dose or observation period.
gate.stageAudit: One symptom-directed medicine at the same recorded stage.
gate.difficultyReason: The credible error extends a real withdrawal exception to a nonwithdrawal episode.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone. Does not modify or append to the frozen B2B21 withdrawal version.
gate.limitation: Diphenhydramine is a weaker competitor; three choices retained without padding. Evidence low; exact rank needs clinician/independent review.

nodes.authorDisposition: UNKEYED: failed credible-option and comparative-evidence gate; excluded from scored exports

parkedAttempts.name: Peter Hayes
parkedAttempts.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic before an outside MRI. His device card describes an MR Conditional generator. Since his prior uneventful scan, a lead revision left an additional implanted lead. The current referral contains the generator card and old MRI clearance; it does not identify conditions for the entire current implanted system.

nodes.objective: Recognize that a changed implanted system invalidates using generator-only or prior-scan clearance as the current system assessment.
nodes.task: Which device record should Peter's MRI team verify for the proposed examination?

choices.label: The complete current implanted system and current scan conditions
choices.rationale: The generator card does not describe the additional lead; assessment must use the actual present devices and proposed examination.
choices.temptation: Match identity and conditions to the same current system.
choices.correctUnder: The post-scan system change applies.

choices.label: The current generator model and current scan conditions
choices.rationale: This verifies the right generator but leaves another implanted component outside the safety assessment.
choices.temptation: Treat the conditional generator label as a whole-system label.
choices.correctUnder: A verified single-device system without additional components would be a different identity problem.

choices.label: The prior implanted system and prior scan conditions
choices.rationale: That record belongs to an earlier system and examination; past tolerance does not establish current conditions.
choices.temptation: Let a successful prior scan serve as reusable clearance.
choices.correctUnder: An unchanged fully identified system under the same verified conditions could make that record useful to the current team, with current confirmation.

nodes.explanation: First reconcile what is implanted now, then match the current system to the proposed examination. This does not declare the added lead safe or unsafe for all MRI; qualified MR/device review determines an appropriate pathway.

gate.interpret: An intervening lead revision changes the identity covered by the old clearance.
gate.apply: Request current whole-system verification rather than extrapolate from one component or past tolerance.
gate.decidingObservation: An additional lead remains after the prior scan.
gate.counterfactual: If records established that the generator was the only implanted device, generator-specific current-condition verification would cover the relevant system.
gate.deletionTest: The intervening component change is the consequential observation; deleting it reduces the case to generic repeat clearance.
gate.cueAttack: Balanced record-comparison options; the key is not a generic cautious plan. No invented MR field-strength or device protocol.
gate.stageAudit: Which identification/conditions record to verify, not choosing an MRI protocol or treatment.
gate.difficultyReason: A valid-looking MR Conditional generator card is a credible partial-evidence trap.
gate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no prior MRI physics task reveals the safety answer.
gate.limitation: No device/lead-specific permission or prohibition, no claim that the clinic can clear scanning.

nodes.authorDisposition: UNKEYED: complete-current-system key remains preferable after deleting the update; counterfactual overlaps generator-only evidence. Requires a new actual decision, not cosmetic wording.

plan.milestone: One bounded repair per each of 20 REVISE items, exact preservation of eight PASS items, and fair/moderate ceiling or explicit parking.
plan.constraints: Five-file lane only. No agents, external messages, shared files, installs or Git writes. Source and clinical-review restrictions remain in force.
plan.composition: Split passing recovery-support and delirium-quiet-cause nodes into self-contained cases without changing reviewed clinical wording. Keep all revised nodes standalone pending independent re-review so no multipart case mixes PASS with pending or parked nodes.

Captured complete pre-repair sidecar proposals and owned-file hashes.
Completed one concrete repair attempt for every returned item; thirteen remain scored pending independent review and seven are parked for documented fairness/difficulty boundaries.
Final focused validation passed 22/22, including exact PASS question/node/header hashes and no mixed multipart case. Typecheck reports only the existing concurrent pancreas TS2322 at (997,48).
plan.nextAction: Manager reviews the five-file diff, the eight exact preserved PASS versions, thirteen revised candidates and seven parks; obtains independent re-review and named clinical decisions; handles shared integration and concurrent typecheck repair.

beforeCoverage.title: Selective cardiac evaluation
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.
beforeCoverage.decision: Decide whether a test is indicated and what current physiology needs evaluation.
beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Orthopedic walking limitation versus new congestion; prior test chronology.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Choose stress imaging before establishing indication, or trust an old normal echo.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Unnecessary testing or missed changed ventricular function.
beforeCoverage.coverage: No assigned live construct for these important preoperative decisions. New cases cover indication before modality.

beforeCoverage.title: VTE prevention across bleeding and discharge
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.
beforeCoverage.decision: Reassess mechanical versus pharmacologic prevention and select a total prevention course.
beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Active blood loss, later serial hemostatic recovery and actual mobility.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Carry an initial drug hold forward or stop an extended plan at discharge.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Avoidable bleeding or loss of indicated prevention.
beforeCoverage.coverage: Four repetitive duration items are represented; the dynamic bleeding/recovery phases are new.

beforeCoverage.title: Antithrombotic indication and intensity
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.
beforeCoverage.decision: Separate chronic AF interruption/bridging from surgical VTE prophylaxis.
beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Actual indication/history, planned operation and the purpose of two orders.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Use any low INR as a bridge trigger or cancel prophylaxis with the bridge.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Unnecessary treatment-dose exposure or omitted surgical prevention.
beforeCoverage.coverage: Keep the strong exact accepted N2 v3; rewrite one generic AF variant and propose consolidating weaker duplicates. Exceptional-risk/DOAC/neuraxial policies remain separate research gaps.

beforeCoverage.title: SGLT2 interruption, metabolic event and resumption
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.
beforeCoverage.decision: Reconcile current drug, interpret ketone/acidemia and reassess actual oral recovery.
beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Current dispensing versus old calendar; pH/bicarbonate/ketones; later meal tolerance.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Use one class-wide interval, dismiss modest-glucose illness or restart from a calendar.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Misplanned fasting exposure or missed/recurrent metabolic complication.
beforeCoverage.coverage: Preserve frozen N2 v2 repeat-procedure schedule. Add a new variant reusing the parked restart identity; distinct case phases earn their inferences.

beforeCoverage.title: OSA risk versus awake ventilation
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.
beforeCoverage.decision: Separate screen probability, diagnosis, awake PaCO2 assessment and operative planning.
beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Discordant sleepiness/apnoea reports; obesity and repeated awake observations.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Use little sleepiness as reassurance or substitute a sleep study for awake physiology.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Missed ventilation concern or inappropriate planning delay.
beforeCoverage.coverage: F13 exact source-held PASS and live v4 fallback preserved. New constrained ATS-supported version requires fresh independent/clinical review.

beforeCoverage.title: Frailty and actual recovery function
beforeCoverage.testingRelevance: Qualitative general-surgery residency importance and consequential-error estimate; no recalled questions, exam-frequency data or official blueprint percentage.

beforeCoverage.rawEvidence: Comfortable-knee-day function, medication assistance, observed transfers/steps and caregiver coverage.
beforeCoverage.closestError: Infer frailty from age or infer independence from one supported corridor walk.
beforeCoverage.consequence: Uncharacterized vulnerability or an unsupported discharge plan.
beforeCoverage.coverage: Four proxy-label questions become one stronger assessment draft plus a genuinely later support decision. No placement rule or instrument copied.

beforeCoverage.title: Delirium: preventable exposure, quiet change and withdrawal exception
